Evidence is mixed. One short trial suggested calcitonin can meaningfully reduce metastatic bone pain for some patients [1]. A larger, longer trial showed it performed no better than placebo on pain or function—essentially ineffective at the group level [2]. So overall, calcitonin’s benefit is uncertain and likely modest, but it is not shown to be dangerous in these studies [1][2].

- **Rationale**: Two good-quality studies looked at calcitonin for bone pain from breast cancer spread to bone. One found meaningful pain relief vs placebo; the other found no benefit. Neither reported serious safety problems. So the main issue is uncertain benefit, not proven harm. Decisions should be individualized with your cancer doctor.

- **Full Answer**: Evidence on calcitonin for metastatic bone pain is mixed, not uniformly negative.

In one 40‑patient trial, women receiving daily salmon calcitonin for 4 weeks used fewer pain pills, had shorter and less intense pain, and were rated “extremely” or “moderately” helped more often than those on placebo [1].  

In another 49‑patient trial using a similar dose for at least 3 months, calcitonin did not improve pain, pain‑medicine use, or overall functioning compared with placebo [2].

Neither study showed serious toxicity; lab changes were modest [1][2].

ReviewTitle: Light‐emitting diode phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in neonates

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Phototherapy is the mainstay of treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. The commonly used light sources for providing phototherapy are special blue fluorescent tubes, compact fluorescent tubes and halogen spotlights. However, light emitting diodes (LEDs) as light sources with high luminous intensity, narrow wavelength band and higher delivered irradiance could make phototherapy more efficacious than the conventional phototherapy units.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To evaluate the effect of LED phototherapy as compared to conventional phototherapy in decreasing serum total bilirubin levels and duration of treatment in neonates with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library 2010, Issue 1), MEDLINE (1966 to April 30, 2010) and EMBASE (1988 to July 8, 2009). Handsearches of the proceedings of annual meetings of The European Society for Paediatric Research and The Society for Pediatric Research were conducted through 2010.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trials were eligible for inclusion if they enrolled neonates (term and preterm) with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and compared LED phototherapy with other light sources (fluorescent  tubes, compact fluorescent tubes, halogen spotlight; method of administration: conventional or fibreoptic).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: We used the standard methods of The Cochrane Collaboration and its Neonatal Review Group for data collection and analysis.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Six randomised controlled trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. Four studies compared LED and halogen light sources. Two studies compared LED and compact fluorescent light sources. The duration of phototherapy (six studies, 630 neonates) was comparable in LED and non-LED phototherapy groups (mean difference (hours) -0.43, 95% CI -1.91 to 1.05). The rate of decline of serum total bilirubin (STB) (four studies, 511 neonates) was also similar in the two groups (mean difference (mg/dL/hour) 0.01, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.04). Treatment failure, defined as the need of additional phototherapy or exchange blood transfusion (1 study, 272 neonates), was comparable (RR 1.83, 95% CI 0.47 to 7.17). Side effects of phototherapy such as hypothermia (RR 6.41, 95% CI 0.33 to 122.97), hyperthermia (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.18 to 2.11) and skin rash (RR 1.83, 95% CI 0.17 to 19.96) were rare and occurred with similar frequency in the two groups.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: LED light source phototherapy is efficacious in bringing down levels of serum total bilirubin at rates that are similar to phototherapy with conventional (compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) or halogen) light sources. Further studies are warranted for evaluating efficacy of LED phototherapy in neonates with haemolytic jaundice or in the presence of severe hyperbilirubinaemia (STB ≥ 20 mg/dL).

Inputs.Title: Transepidermal water loss and cerebral hemodynamics in preterm infants: conventional versus LED phototherapy.
Inputs.Abstract: The aim of our study was to evaluate whether high-intensity gallium nitride light-emitting diode (LED) phototherapy (LPT) influences transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and cerebral hemodynamics in preterm neonates in comparison with conventional phototherapy (CPT). Thirty-one preterm infants were randomized for conventional (n = 14) and for LED (n = 17) phototherapy. All infants were studied using a Tewameter TM 210 and cerebral Doppler ultrasound immediately before phototherapy (time 0), 30 min (time 1), 1-6 h (time 2), and 12-24 h (time 3) after the start of phototherapy, and 6-12 h after discontinuing phototherapy (time 4). The study shows that LPT does not induce significant changes in TEWL (time 0: 2.75 +/- 4.71 ml/m(2)/h; time 3: 14.45 +/- 3.68 ml/m(2)/h), in peak systolic, end diastolic and mean cerebral blood flow velocity (CBFV), and in the resistence index (RI). On the contrary, CPT is associated with a significant increase of TEWL (time 0: 13.22 +/- 5.61 ml/m(2)/h; time 3: 20.94 +/- 3.21 ml/m(2)/h), which disappeared at time 4, when phototherapy had stopped. The peak systolic and mean CBFV increased, respectively, from 0.11 +/- 0.03 m/s at time 0 to 0.16 +/- 0.07 m/s at time 3. We conclude that LPT, emitting light within the 450-470-nm spectrum for optimal bilirubin degradation, can be preferable to CPT for the therapy of hyperbilirubinemia in preterm infants.

Inputs.Title: A new blue light-emitting phototherapy device: a prospective randomized controlled study.
Inputs.Abstract:
To evaluate the efficacy of a new phototherapy light source with a narrow luminous blue spectrum. The device, made with high-intensity gallium nitride light-emitting diodes (LEDs), was compared with conventional phototherapy at similar light intensities.
                Two university-affiliated community hospitals in Jerusalem.
                Prospective open randomized study.
                Sixty-nine jaundiced, but otherwise healthy, term infants who met the entry criteria for phototherapy set by the American Academy of Pediatrics' Practice Parameter.
                The duration of phototherapy and the rate of decrease in total serum bilirubin (TSB) concentration.
                The mean TSB concentrations at initiation and termination of treatment did not differ between newborns receiving LED and those receiving conventional phototherapy. The duration of phototherapy and the rate of decrease in TSB concentration were not statistically different in the 2 groups. The average rate of decrease in TSB after adjustment by a linear regression analysis for confounding factors was -3.16 micromol/L/h (95% confidence limits -4.81, -1.51) in newborns receiving LED phototherapy compared with -2.19 micromol/L/h (-3.99, -0.40) in those treated with conventional phototherapy (P <.14). No side effects were noted in any of the newborns.
                The blue gallium nitride LED device is as effective as conventional phototherapy and is readily accepted by nursing staff. Future LED phototherapy devices can provide much higher irradiance, and thus greater efficacy, and offer a new highly versatile approach to the treatment of jaundice.

Inputs.Title: Light emitting diodes versus compact fluorescent tubes for phototherapy in neonatal jaundice: a multi center randomized controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract:
To evaluate whether light-emitting diode (LED) phototherapy is as efficacious as compact fluorescent tube (CFT) phototherapy for the treatment of non-hemolytic jaundice in healthy term and late preterm neonates.
                Multi centre open label randomized controlled trial.
                Four tertiary care neonatal units.
                Healthy term and late preterm neonates with non-hemolytic jaundice.
                Single-surface LED or CFT phototherapy. PRIMARY OUTCOME VARIABLE: Duration of phototherapy.
                A total of 272 neonates were randomized to receive LED (n=142) or CFT (n=130) phototherapy. The baseline demographic and biochemical variables were similar in the two groups. The median duration of phototherapy (IQR) in the two groups was comparable (26 (22-36) h vs. 25(22-36) h; P=0.44). At any time point, a similar proportion of neonates were under phototherapy in the two groups (log-rank test, P=0.38). The rate of fall of serum total bilirubin (STB) during phototherapy and the incidence of failure of phototherapy were also not different. An equal proportion of neonates had a rebound increase in STB needing restarting of phototherapy. Side effects were rare, comparable in the two groups and included hypothermia, hyperthermia, rash, skin darkening and dehydration.
                LED and CFT phototherapy units were equally efficacious in the management of non-hemolytic hyperbilirubinemia in healthy term and late preterm neonates.

Inputs.Title: Efficacy of new microprocessed phototherapy system with five high intensity light emitting diodes (Super LED).
Inputs.Abstract:
To evaluate the efficacy of a microprocessed phototherapy (PT) system with five high intensity light emitting diodes (Super LED) for the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia of premature infants.
                Randomized clinical trial using Super LED phototherapy in the study group and twin halogen spotlight phototherapy in the control group. A stratified blocked randomization, based on birth weight, was performed. The duration of phototherapy and the rate of decrease of total serum bilirubin (TSB) concentration in the first 24 hours of treatment were the main outcome measures.
                We studied 88 infants, 44 in the Super LED group and 44 in the halogen spotlight PT group. The demographic characteristics of the patients in both groups were similar. Infants in the Super LED group had a similar mean initial serum bilirubin level (10.1+/-2.4 mg%) to those receiving halogen spotlight treatment (10.9+/-2.0 mg%). After 24 hours of treatment, the decrease in total serum bilirubin levels was significantly greater in the Super LED group (27.9 vs. 10.7%, p<0.01) and duration of phototherapy was significantly shorter in this group (36.8 h vs. 63.8 h, p<0.01). After 24 hours of treatment, a significantly greater number of patients receiving Super LED phototherapy had reached serum bilirubin concentrations low enough to allow withdrawal of treatment (23 vs. 10, p<0.01).
                Our results demonstrate that the efficacy of Super LED phototherapy for treating hyperbilirubinemia in premature infants was significantly better than halogen phototherapy.

Inputs.Title: A prospective randomized controlled study of phototherapy using blue and blue-green light-emitting devices, and conventional halogen-quartz phototherapy.
Inputs.Abstract:
To determine the efficacy of blue versus blue-green phototherapy using new light sources with narrow luminous spectra. The devices made of high-intensity gallium nitride light-emitting diodes (LEDs) were also compared to conventional halogen-quartz bulbs phototherapy.
                Prospective open randomized study.
                A total of 114 jaundiced, but otherwise healthy term infants who met the entry criteria for phototherapy set by the American Academy of Pediatrics' Practice Parameter.
                The duration of phototherapy and the rate of decrease in total serum bilirubin (TSB).
                The mean TSB concentrations at initiation and termination of treatment, as well as the duration of phototherapy and the rate of decrease in TSB, were not statistically different in newborns receiving blue LED, blue-green LED or conventional phototherapy. The average rate of decrease in TSB (slope), after adjustment by a linear regression analysis for confounding factors, was -3.61 micromol/hour (95% confidence limits -5.47, -1.75) in the 25 newborns receiving blue LED phototherapy compared with -2.57 micromol/hour (-4.32, -0.82) in the 22 newborns treated with blue-green LED phototherapy and -3.42 micromol/hour (-5.02, -1.81) in the 57 newborns who received conventional phototherapy.
                When using low light irradiance, there was no statistically significant difference in the effectiveness of phototherapy using blue-green LEDs, blue LEDs or conventional halogen-quartz bulbs.

Inputs.Title: Randomized controlled trial of light-emitting diode phototherapy.
Inputs.Abstract:
We wished to compare the efficacy of light-emitting diode (LED) phototherapy with special blue fluorescent (BB) tube phototherapy in the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
                We randomly assigned 66 infants >or=35 weeks of gestation to receive phototherapy using an LED device or BB. In addition to phototherapy from above, all infants also received phototherapy from below using four BB tubes or a fiberoptic pad.
                After 15+/-5 h of phototherapy, the rate of decline in the total serum bilirubin (TSB) was 0.35+/-0.25 mg/dl/h in the LED group vs 0.27+/-0.25 mg/dl/h in the BB group (P=0.20).
                LED phototherapy is as effective as BB phototherapy in lowering serum bilirubin levels in term and near-term newborns.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is LED phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is LED phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Evidence from multiple randomized trials in jaundiced newborns (a condition dominated by unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia) compares LED phototherapy to conventional fluorescent and halogen systems. Most studies show equal effectiveness at similar light intensity, with one high‑intensity “Super LED” system performing better than halogen. Safety profiles are similar or better with LED.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across several randomized trials in jaundiced newborns, LED phototherapy lowers unconjugated bilirubin just as well as fluorescent or halogen units when light intensity is similar. Term and late‑preterm infants treated with LED had the same bilirubin fall rate, treatment duration, need to restart therapy, and side‑effect rates as those treated with conventional compact fluorescent, halogen, or special blue fluorescent lamps [2][3][5][6]. In one trial using a “Super LED” system, premature infants cleared bilirubin faster and needed fewer hours of treatment than with twin halogen spotlights [4]. Another study in preterm infants found LED light in the optimal 450–470 nm range did not disturb skin water loss or brain blood flow, whereas conventional phototherapy increased skin water loss and altered cerebral blood flow [1]. Overall, LED phototherapy is at least as effective as conventional phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and high‑intensity LED systems may be more effective with fewer side effects [1][2][3][4][5][6].

- **Full Answer**:  
Across several randomized trials in newborns with unconjugated jaundice, LED phototherapy is not less effective than traditional lamps and is sometimes more effective.  

In term infants, blue LED units lowered bilirubin at essentially the same speed and required similar treatment time as conventional fluorescent or halogen-quartz lights [2][3][5][6]. In premature infants, a higher‑intensity “Super LED” system actually removed bilirubin faster (about 28% drop in 24 hours versus 11%) and shortened treatment by roughly one day compared with halogen spotlights [4].  

Overall, available evidence shows LED phototherapy is an effective treatment for unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, at least matching, and sometimes exceeding, older light sources [2][3][4][5][6]. Thus, it should not be considered clinically ineffective.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: The common cold is one of the most common illnesses in humans and constitutes an economic burden both in terms of productivity and expenditure for treatment. There is no proven cure for the common cold and symptomatic relief is the mainstay of treatment. The use of intranasal ipratropium bromide (IB) has been addressed in several studies and might prove an effective treatment for the common cold.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To determine the effect of IB versus placebo or no treatment on severity of rhinorrhoea and nasal congestion in children and adults with the common cold. Subjective overall improvement was another primary outcome and side effects (for example, dry mucous membranes, epistaxis and systemic anticholinergic effects) were reported as a secondary outcome.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: In this updated review we searched CENTRAL 2013, Issue 3, MEDLINE (1950 to March week 4, 2013), MEDLINE in-process and other non-indexed citations (8 April 2013), EMBASE (1974 to April 2013), AMED (1985 to April 2013), Biosis (1974 to February 2011) and LILACS (1985 to April 2013).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing IB to placebo or no treatment in children and adults with the common cold.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two review authors independently extracted data and assessed trial quality. We used a standardised form to extract relevant data and we contacted trial authors for additional information.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Seven trials with a total of 2144 participants were included. Four studies (1959 participants) addressed subjective change in severity of rhinorrhoea. All studies were consistent in reporting statistically significant changes in favour of IB. Nasal congestion was reported in four studies and was found to have no significant change between the two groups. Two studies found a positive response in the IB group for the global assessment of overall improvement. Side effects were more frequent in the IB group, odds ratio (OR) 2.09 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.40 to 3.11). Commonly encountered side effects included nasal dryness, blood tinged mucus and epistaxis. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was moderate.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: For people with the common cold, the existing evidence, which has some limitations, suggests that IB is likely to be effective in ameliorating rhinorrhoea. IB had no effect on nasal congestion and its use was associated with more side effects compared to placebo or no treatment although these appeared to be well tolerated and self limiting. There is a need for larger, high-quality trials to determine the effectiveness of IB in relieving common cold symptoms.

Inputs.Title: Ipratropium nasal spray: a new treatment for rhinorrhea in the common cold.
Inputs.Abstract: A need is often present for symptomatic treatment of the common cold. A blocked nose can be opened by a vasoconstrictor, but no effective therapy is known today for rhinorrhea. The aim of the present trial was to study the effect of the topically active parasympatholytic, ipratropium, on rhinorrhea. In a placebo-controlled group comparative trial, 80 micrograms of ipratropium were taken as a nasal spray 4 times daily for 1 wk by 40 adults with spontaneously occurring common colds. All subjects administered an intranasal vasoconstrictor (xylomethazoline, 0.1%) 5 min before administering placebo or ipratropium. Ipratropium treatment resulted in a significant reduction in nasal discharge compared with that of placebo treatment during the whole treatment period (p less than 0.001), but the drug was especially effective the first 3 days, when the watery secretion was predominant. It was concluded that this new spray can be of value in the first days of a cold, when nasal discharge is a nuisance.

Inputs.Title: Common cold and high-dose ipratropium bromide: use of anticholinergic medication as an indicator of reflex-mediated hypersecretion.
Inputs.Abstract: It was our aim to study the role played by parasympathetic reflexes for the amount and physical characteristics of nasal discharge during a common cold, and to define the maximum anti-rhinorrhoea effect obtainable with anticholinergic medication. Fifty adults with naturally acquired colds were treated with a very high dose of the topically active cholinoceptor-antagonists ipratropium bromide in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of parallel groups. A dosage of 400 micrograms was given 4 times daily for 3 days, using a specially manufactured high-dosed pressurized aerosol. This treatment resulted in a 56% reduction in the number of nose blowings (p < 0.01) and a 58% reduction in the weight of blown secretions (p < 0.01). Assessment of the "pourability" of the nasal discharge indicated that ipratropium bromide mainly reduces the watery secretions but not the mucopurulent secretions. The high dose of ipratropium bromide caused nose- and mouth-dryness in a considerable number of the patients. In conclusion: (1) during the first days of a common cold about 60% of the nasal discharge is a reflex-mediated product from nasal glands; (2) this type of secretion is predominantly watery; and (3) ipratropium bromide can reduce watery rhinorrhoea in the common cold, but a lower dose is required in order to avoid side effects.

Inputs.Title: Ipratropium bromide treatment of experimental rhinovirus infection.
Inputs.Abstract: The importance of parasympathetic-cholinergic mechanisms in the production of common cold symptoms is not clear. The quaternary ammonium anticholinergic antagonist ipratropium bromide was intranasally administered under double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled conditions to assess its tolerance and efficacy in reducing nasal hypersecretion in adult volunteers with experimental rhinovirus colds. Ipratropium was sprayed intranasally three times daily (80 micrograms per treatment) for 5 days beginning 24 h after intranasal inoculation of rhinovirus type 39. Clinical colds occurred in 50% of 30 infected ipratropium recipients and in 76% of 33 infected placebo recipients (P = 0.04). The nasal mucus weights tended to be lower for ipratropium-treated persons (mean +/- standard deviation, 14.7 +/- 15.1 g/5 days) than for placebo-treated recipients (24.7 +/- 28.0 g/5 days; P = 0.076). Whereas total nasal symptom scores were similar between the two groups, the rhinorrhea score analyzed for each day of treatment showed nonsignificant trends favoring the ipratropium group over the last 4 days of treatment. Ipratropium was generally well tolerated. The results suggest that cholinergic mechanisms are at least partially responsible for nasal mucus production in rhinovirus colds but that the effect of anticholinergic compounds alone is insufficient to be of practical use in treatment, although they may have value as components of multi-ingredient preparations.

Inputs.Title: Effectiveness and safety of intranasal ipratropium bromide in common colds. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract:
To determine the tolerability and clinical effectiveness of intranasal ipratropium bromide for the treatment of symptoms of common colds.
                Multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial.
                3 university student health services.
                411 previously healthy persons 14 to 56 years of age who had cold symptoms that had lasted for no more than 36 hours, rhinorrhea subjectively judged to be of at least moderate severity, and documented nasal discharge of at least 1.5 g over a 1-hour observation period.
                Either 1) ipratropium bromide nasal spray 0.06% in buffered salt solution, two 42-micrograms sprays per nostril administered by metered pump spray; 2) control nasal spray, which consisted of buffered salt solution; or 3) no treatment. Treatments were self-administered three or four times daily during waking hours for 4 days. After receiving their morning dose, patients stayed at the study center for 6 hours on study day 1 and 3 hours on study day 2; symptom severity was recorded and nasal mucus discharges were collected and weighed hourly during these periods.
                Ipratropium recipients had 26% less nasal discharge than controls (P = 0.0024) and 34% less nasal discharge than untreated patients (P = 0.0001). Severity of rhinorrhea as judged subjectively was reduced in ipratropium recipients by 31% compared with controls and by 78% compared with untreated patients (P = 0.0001 for both comparisons). In addition to being associated with reductions in daily assessments of the severity of rhinorrhea (P < or = 0.003), ipratropium was associated with reduced sneezing on study days 2 (20% difference; P = 0.03) and 4 (30% difference; P = 0.02) but not with reduced nasal congestion compared with the control spray. Ipratropium was generally well tolerated but was associated with higher rates of blood-tinged mucus (16.8% in the ipratropium group compared with 3.6% in the control group; P = 0.01) and nasal dryness (11.7% in the ipratropium group compared with 3.6% in the control group; P = 0.021) than the control spray. Patient assessments of the overall effectiveness of treatment were more favorable for ipratropium than for the control spray (P < or = 0.026) or for no treatment (P < or = 0.002) on each day of inquiry (study days 1, 2, and 5).
                Intranasal ipratropium bromide provides specific relief of rhinorrhea and sneezing associated with common colds.

Inputs.Title: A double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the safety and efficacy of ipratropium bromide nasal spray versus placebo in patients with the common cold.
Inputs.Abstract: Ipratropium bromide (IB) has been found to reduce secretions in the upper respiratory tract; this is accomplished through competitive inhibition of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors that control rhinorrhea production. This study compared the safety and efficacy of IB with placebo in the symptomatic relief of rhinorrhea in patients with the common cold. Human subjects with symptoms of a common cold, primarily rhinorrhea, were enrolled and treated with either IB (84 micrograms/nostril) or placebo; each was administered as two sprays per nostril, four times a day, for 4 days. Primary efficacy analyses were in-clinic measurements of nasal discharge weights over a 3-hour period after administration on days 1 and 2 and assessment of rhinorrhea symptoms by use of a subjective patient-completed visual analog rating scale. IB significantly reduced rhinorrhea an average of 18% over placebo for days 1 and 2 (p = 0.01). Visual analog scale scores showed an average improvement in rhinorrhea of 22% over placebo (p = 0.001). When patients with relatively minor rhinorrhea (baseline weight of nasal discharge < or = 1.0 gm) were excluded, IB produced an average reduction in nasal discharge of 23% over placebo for days 1 and 2 (p = 0.003).

Inputs.Title: Efficacy and safety of topical combinations of ipratropium and xylometazoline for the treatment of symptoms of runny nose and nasal congestion associated with acute upper respiratory tract infection.
Inputs.Abstract:
Rhinorrhea and nasal congestion are simultaneous symptoms associated with the common cold. This study investigated the efficacy and safety of a combination nasal spray of ipratropium and xylometazoline for simultaneous treatment of these symptoms.
                The trial was a multicenter double-blind, parallel-group, randomized design on patients with common cold symptoms. Patients scored symptoms of runny nose and nasal congestion and recorded adverse events in a diary for up to 7 days. Patients also recorded tissue use. The five test treatments consisted of ipratropium, 0.6 mg/mL, and xylometazoline, 1.0 mg/mL; ipratropium, 0.6 mg/mL, and xylometazoline, 0.5 mg/mL; ipratropium, 0.6 mg/mL; xylometazoline, 1.0 mg/mL; and placebo solution.
                Eight hundred sixty-four patients were screened and 786 patients received treatment. One day after treatment there was a clear separation between the scores for the placebo and ipratropium treatment groups for rhinorrhea and between the placebo and xylometazoline treatment groups for congestion. Both ipratropium/xylometazoline 1.0 and ipratropium/xylometazoline 0.5 treatments were superior to xylometazoline with respect to rhinorrhea (p < 0.0001) and superior to ipratropium with respect to nasal congestion scores (p < 0.001). Both the ipratropium combination treatments had significantly lower tissue use than the xylometazoline treatment group (p < 0.0001). Adverse events were distributed equally between the treatments, except mucus tinged with blood, epistaxis, nasal passage irritation, and nasal dryness, which had a higher incidence in the three groups that received medicines containing ipratropium.
                The results indicate that a combination medicine of ipratropium and xylometazoline is safe and effective for treatment of rhinorrhea and nasal congestion associated with common cold.

Inputs.Title: A dose-response study of the efficacy and safety of ipratropium bromide nasal spray in the treatment of the common cold.
Inputs.Abstract: Rhinorrhea is an annoying symptom of the common cold for which effective therapy is not currently available. Ipratropium bromide (IB) is an anticholinergic drug that has been shown to decrease glandular secretion when applied topically to the nasal mucosa. The purpose of this study was to compare the efficacy and safety of three doses of IB nasal spray versus either vehicle or no treatment in relieving rhinorrhea in patients with naturally acquired colds. Rhinorrhea severity was measured objectively by determining nasal discharge weights and subjectively by means of visual analog scale scores. Compared with either vehicle or no treatment, IB nasal spray produced a significant decrease in the severity of rhinorrhea. A dose of 84 micrograms (two sprays of a 0.06% solution in buffered saline solution) in each nostril was more efficacious than a 42 microgram per nostril dose and only marginally less efficacious than a 168 micrograms per nostril dose. The 84 micrograms per nostril dose also was associated with fewer adverse events than was the higher dose. None of the adverse events related to intranasal IB therapy was of a serious nature. The use of IB nasal spray appears to be a rational and safe approach to relieving rhinorrhea associated with the common cold.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is intranasal ipratropium bromide for common cold?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is intranasal ipratropium bromide for common cold?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: The question asks how well intranasal ipratropium works for the common cold. The articles consistently show that it specifically reduces runny nose (watery discharge) and sneezing, with little effect on nasal blockage or on the overall course of the illness. I summarized the size of benefit and main side effects across multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials, using simple language and keeping technical wording to a minimum.

- **Full Answer**: Intranasal ipratropium bromide mainly helps the “runny” part of a cold, not the stuffy nose.

Across several randomized, placebo‑controlled trials, ipratropium sprays reduced the amount of nasal discharge by about 18%–34% compared with saline or no treatment, and by about 23%–58% in people with heavier, watery drainage [2][4][5][7]. Patients also rated their runny nose about 20%–30% better than with placebo [4][5][7]. One high‑dose study showed roughly 56% fewer nose blowings and 58% less nasal secretion, but at the cost of more dryness and mouth symptoms [2]. Ipratropium does not meaningfully relieve nasal blockage or overall cold severity and likely does not shorten the illness [3][4]. It works best in the first few days, when secretions are watery [1][2].

Side effects are usually local and mild, such as nasal dryness, irritation, and blood‑tinged mucus, which occur more often than with saline sprays but rarely require stopping the drug [2][4][6][7].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several randomized, placebo-controlled trials, intranasal ipratropium bromide consistently reduces the *runny nose* component of the common cold, especially watery discharge, but has little effect on nasal blockage or overall cold duration. Some researchers therefore judge it too limited to serve as a stand‑alone “cold cure,” even though it clearly helps with rhinorrhea. Side effects are usually mild nasal dryness or slight nosebleeds.

- **Full Answer**:  
Intranasal ipratropium bromide is **not ineffective**, but its benefit is narrowly focused. It does **not** cure the common cold or relieve nasal stuffiness, and overall symptom scores change little [3][4].  

However, for **runny nose**, it gives moderate, consistent relief:

- Reduces nasal discharge weight by about **18–34%** compared with placebo or no treatment in typical-dose trials [4][5].  
- High-dose studies show about **56–58%** fewer nose blowings and secretion weight, but with more dryness [2].  
- Especially helpful in the **first few days** of a cold when secretions are watery [1][2][7].  

Side effects include nasal dryness and occasional blood‑tinged mucus, usually mild [2][4][6][7].

efficacy.positive_question: Does intranasal ipratropium bromide work for common cold?
efficacy.negative_question: Does intranasal ipratropium bromide not work for common cold?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Multiple randomized trials show intranasal ipratropium bromide clearly reduces watery nasal discharge and patient‑rated runny nose in early common colds [1][2][4][5][7]. It does not relieve nasal blockage or shorten the illness [3][4]. Side effects (dryness, minor bleeding) are usually mild but more frequent than with placebo [2][4][6][7].

- **Full Answer**:  
Intranasal ipratropium bromide can help if your main common‑cold symptom is a very runny nose. Several randomized, placebo‑controlled studies in adults found that ipratropium nasal spray reduced the amount of nasal discharge by about 18% to 60% and clearly improved patient‑rated runny nose compared with saline spray or no treatment [1][2][4][5][7]. It mainly works on watery secretions and is most helpful in the first few days of a cold [1][2]. It also modestly reduces sneezing [4], but it does not open a blocked nose or shorten how long the cold lasts [3][4]. Common side effects are nasal dryness, irritation, and occasional blood‑stained mucus, which were usually mild but occurred more often than with placebo [2][4][6][7]. Overall, it is a reasonable short‑term option for bothersome runny nose, not a cure for the cold itself [1][2][4][7].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials show that intranasal ipratropium bromide reliably reduces *runny nose* (especially watery discharge) in people with common colds. It does *not* relieve nasal blockage and has little effect on overall cold duration or other symptoms. One experimental study concluded that anticholinergic treatment alone gives limited overall benefit, but still found trends toward less mucus, supporting its specific effect on rhinorrhea. Side effects such as nasal dryness and blood‑tinged mucus occur but are usually mild.

- **Full Answer**:  
Intranasal ipratropium bromide does work, but only for certain cold symptoms.  

Several controlled trials show it significantly reduces the amount of nasal discharge and the number of nose blowings, especially during the first days when the mucus is watery [1,2,4,5,7]. Patients also *feel* that their runny nose is less bothersome when using it [4,5,7].  

However, it does **not** improve nasal congestion (stuffiness) or shorten the cold itself [3,4]. One trial judged its overall benefit as modest if used alone, though it can help as part of combination sprays with a decongestant [3,6].  

Common side effects are nasal dryness and occasional blood‑tinged mucus [2,4,6].

safety.positive_question: Is intranasal ipratropium bromide safe for common cold?
safety.negative_question: Is intranasal ipratropium bromide dangerous for common cold?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: Several randomized trials tested intranasal ipratropium for colds, carefully tracking both symptom relief and short‑term side effects.

- **Full Answer**: Across multiple controlled studies in several hundred adults with early common colds, intranasal ipratropium bromide clearly reduced watery runny nose and sneezing but did not improve nasal blockage [1,3–7]. At commonly used doses (about 42–84 micrograms per nostril, 3–4 times daily for up to 7 days), the spray was “generally well tolerated” and no serious drug‑related events were reported [1,3,4,5,7]. The main side effects were local dryness, irritation, and blood‑tinged mucus or mild nosebleeds, which occurred more often than with saline or decongestant sprays and were dose‑related [2,4,6,7]. Mouth dryness also appeared with very high doses [2]. Overall, short‑term use of intranasal ipratropium is considered safe for otherwise healthy people who want relief from troublesome runny nose due to the common cold, but it may cause mild nose dryness or bleeding [3,4,6,7].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials of intranasal ipratropium bromide in otherwise healthy people with common colds show that the drug reduces watery nasal discharge by about 20–30% compared with placebo or no treatment [1][2][3][4][5][7]. Across these studies, ipratropium was generally well tolerated, even at relatively high doses [2][3][4][5][7]. The main side effects were local dryness of the nose and mouth, blood‑tinged mucus, occasional minor nosebleeds, and nasal irritation, all of which were more common at higher doses but were not serious [2][4][6][7]. No serious systemic complications were reported in these trials of short‑term use for colds [3][4][5][6][7]. Thus, for otherwise healthy adults and adolescents, short‑term use of intranasal ipratropium for common‑cold runny nose appears symptomatically helpful and not dangerous, though bothersome local side effects may limit comfort or continued use.

- **Full Answer**:  
Intranasal ipratropium bromide is not considered dangerous for short‑term relief of runny nose from the common cold [3][4][5][7] in healthy adults.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing intranasal ipratropium bromide is good for common cold?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing intranasal ipratropium bromide is harmful for common cold?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: The summaries describe several randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of intranasal ipratropium bromide in people with naturally acquired and experimental common colds. These studies consistently measure objective nasal discharge and patient‑reported symptoms, compare ipratropium with placebo or no treatment, and report side effects. Together they show a clear pattern: ipratropium helps runny nose (rhinorrhea) and sneezing, but not nasal blockage, and it can cause dryness and minor nosebleeds. I will synthesize these findings in plain language and give a clear, evidence‑based conclusion.

- **Full Answer**:  
Multiple well-designed scientific studies show that intranasal ipratropium bromide helps the runny nose of the common cold.  

Randomized, placebo‑controlled trials in adults with natural colds found that ipratropium nasal spray cut nasal discharge weights by about 18%–56% and clearly reduced how severe people rated their runny nose, especially in the first few days of illness [1][2][4][5][7]. A large student‑health study also showed less sneezing and better overall ratings of treatment compared with saline spray or no treatment [4]. In experimental rhinovirus infection, ipratropium slightly lowered mucus volume and the chance of developing a cold, but the overall symptom benefit was modest [3]. Combination sprays that include ipratropium plus a decongestant (xylometazoline) improve both runny nose and stuffiness [6].  

Across studies, ipratropium did not relieve nasal blockage by itself, and it caused more nasal dryness and occasional blood‑tinged mucus than placebo, but side effects were generally mild [2][4][6][7].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: The studies provided are randomized clinical trials of intranasal ipratropium for the common cold. They report symptom relief plus mainly local, dose‑related side effects (dryness, irritation, blood‑tinged mucus), and do not describe serious or permanent harm.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, intranasal ipratropium bromide is **not shown to be harmful** for treating runny nose from the common cold. Multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials in adults found that ipratropium significantly reduced nasal discharge and rhinorrhea symptoms compared with placebo or no treatment [0][1][3][4][6].  

Across studies, the spray was described as “generally well tolerated” or “safe” [2][3][6]. However, it did cause more local side effects than placebo, especially at higher doses: nasal and mouth dryness [1], nasal dryness and blood‑tinged mucus [3][5], epistaxis (nosebleeds), and nasal irritation [5][6]. These adverse effects were bothersome but not serious, and no systemic or long-term harms were reported [2][6].  

Overall, the evidence shows symptom benefit with mainly mild, reversible nasal side effects, not scientific proof of harm.

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is intranasal ipratropium bromide a good choice for common cold?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is intranasal ipratropium bromide a bad choice for common cold?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The articles consistently show that intranasal ipratropium bromide clearly reduces runny, watery nasal discharge and improves patients’ subjective feeling of “dripping” nose. It is most useful in the first few days of a cold and mainly targets watery secretions, not thick mucus or overall cold duration. It does not relieve nasal blockage, so it’s often paired with a decongestant if congestion is a big problem. Side effects are mostly local—dryness, irritation, and sometimes blood‑tinged mucus or minor nosebleeds—especially at higher doses, but are generally not serious. One smaller study suggests the effect alone may be modest, yet larger trials and dose‑response data support it as a rational, effective short‑term option for people whose main complaint is troublesome runny nose. It is not needed for mild symptoms and won’t cure the cold, just make the runny nose easier to live with.

- **Full Answer**:  
Intranasal ipratropium bromide is a reasonable choice if your main cold problem is a very runny, watery nose and frequent sneezing.

Multiple good-quality studies show that the nasal spray clearly reduces the amount of nasal discharge by about 20% to 30% compared with salt-water sprays or no treatment, and patients feel their runny nose is noticeably better [1][4][5][7]. It works best in the first few days of a cold, when the mucus is mostly watery rather than thick and colored [1][2][4]. It does not open a stuffy nose, so it’s often combined with a decongestant spray for congestion [1][4][6].

Side effects are usually mild but include nasal dryness, irritation, and sometimes blood‑tinged mucus or small nosebleeds, especially at higher doses [2][4][6][7]. It doesn’t cure the infection or shorten the cold, but just helps control runny‑nose symptoms [3][4].

Overall, it’s a good option for short‑term relief of bothersome runny nose.
timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: Intranasal ipratropium mainly blocks gland-driven watery nasal secretions. - **Full Answer**: Intranasal ipratropium is not a “bad” choice; it’s a reasonable short‑term option if your main cold symptom is bothersome runny nose, but it won’t help congestion and can cause nasal dryness or minor nosebleeds [1][2][4][5][6][7]. Consult your doctor first.

cost.positive_question: Is intranasal ipratropium bromide worth the money for common cold?
cost.negative_question: Is intranasal ipratropium bromide not worth the money for common cold?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:

Dryness, irritation, and blood‑tinged mucus are more common than with saline but usually mild [2][4][6][7]. One trial concluded its benefit was too small to be useful alone [3].

If your main problem is bothersome watery drip and cheaper options haven’t helped or aren’t suitable, paying for ipratropium can be reasonable, knowing the benefit is moderate and lasts a few days [1][2][4][5][7]. Expect possible nose dryness or blood‑tinged mucus [2][4][6]. If congestion or overall misery are your main issues, it’s probably not worth the cost unless used in a combination spray with a decongestant, which can help both symptoms [3][4][6].
cost.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Evidence shows intranasal ipratropium clearly reduces runny nose in common colds. Several placebo‑controlled trials found 18%–34% less nasal discharge and better patient‑rated relief when compared with salt‑water sprays or no treatment, especially in the first days and in people with heavier rhinorrhea [1][2][4][5][7]. Intranasal ipratropium bromide is not a cure for the common cold, but it does meaningfully reduce a runny nose for many people.

Usual doses are generally safe, though they increase nasal dryness and occasional blood‑streaked mucus compared with placebo [4][6][7].  

Ipratropium does not relieve nasal blockage or other cold symptoms, and one experimental study judged it too limited to be useful on its own, except possibly in combination products [3][4].  

So it may be “worth the money” if constant dripping is your main problem, but unnecessary for mild colds.

One experimental rhinovirus study saw only modest benefit and concluded that anticholinergics alone are not enough as a stand‑alone cold treatment, although they may help as part of a combination product [3]. Ipratropium does *not* relieve nasal congestion or shorten the cold, and it commonly causes nasal dryness and occasional blood‑tinged mucus, but serious harms were not reported in these trials [1][4][6][7].

- **Full Answer**:  
Evidence suggests intranasal ipratropium bromide is **not ineffective**, but its benefit is limited to runny nose. In large, well‑designed trials, it reduced the amount of nasal discharge by about 18–34% compared with saline sprays or no treatment, and patients rated their runny nose roughly 20–30% better [4][5][7]. High‑dose short‑term use cut nose blowing and secretion weight by about 50–60% but caused more nose and mouth dryness [2]. It does **not** reliably improve nasal congestion or other cold symptoms, nor does it shorten how long the cold lasts [3][4]. Side effects are mostly local—nasal dryness and blood‑tinged mucus were more common than with saline, but no serious complications were reported in these studies [1][4][6][7]. Overall, ipratropium nasal spray is a reasonably safe option if runny nose is your main problem, but it won’t fix the whole cold, and it’s also reasonable to skip it if the symptom isn’t very bothersome.

ReviewTitle: Amniotomy alone for induction of labour

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Amniotomy (deliberate rupture of the membranes) is a simple procedure which can be used alone for induction of labour if the membranes are accessible, thus avoiding the need for pharmacological intervention. However, the time interval from amniotomy to established labour may not be acceptable to clinicians and women, and in a number of cases labour may not ensue. This is one of a series of reviews of methods of cervical ripening and labour induction using standardised methodology.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To determine the effects of amniotomy alone for third trimester labour induction in women with a live fetus.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and bibliographies of relevant papers (January 2007). We updated this search on 23 May 2012 and added the results to the awaiting classification section of the review.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Clinical trials comparing amniotomy alone for third trimester cervical ripening or labour induction with placebo/no treatment or other methods listed above it on a predefined list of labour induction methods.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: A strategy was developed to deal with the large volume and complexity of trial data relating to labour induction. This involved a two-stage method of data extraction. We assessed trial quality and contacted study authors for additional information.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Two trials, comprising 50 and 260 women, respectively were eligible for inclusion in this review. No conclusions could be drawn from comparisons of amniotomy alone versus no intervention, and amniotomy alone versus oxytocin alone (small trial, only one pre-specified outcome reported). No trials compared amniotomy alone with intracervical prostaglandins. One trial compared amniotomy alone with a single dose of vaginal prostaglandins for women with a favourable cervix, and found a significant increase in the need for oxytocin augmentation in the amniotomy alone group (44% versus 15%; relative risk 2.85, 95% confidence interval 1.82 to 4.46). This should be viewed with caution as this was the result of a single-centre trial. Furthermore, secondary intervention occurred four hours after amniotomy, and this time interval may not have been appropriate.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text:
Data are lacking about the value of amniotomy alone for induction of labour. While there are now other modern methods available for induction of labour (pharmacological agents), there remain clinical scenarios where amniotomy alone may be desirable and appropriate, and this method is worthy of further research. This research should include evaluation of the appropriate time interval from amniotomy to secondary intervention, women and caregivers' satisfaction and economic analysis.
[Note: the two citations in the awaiting classification section of the review may alter the conclusions of the review once assessed.]

Inputs.Title: A randomized prospective trial comparing single dose prostaglandin E2 vaginal gel with forewater amniotomy for induction of labour.
Inputs.Abstract: A prospective randomized parallel-group study was carried out to compare the efficacy of a single dose vaginal prostaglandin E2 gel with forewater amniotomy for induction of labour at term in 260 parturients (110 primigravid and 150 parous women) with low risk pregnancy and favourable cervix. In the prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) managed group, the primigravidae were treated with 2 mg PGE2 gel and parous patients with 1 mg PGE2 gel. Forewater amniotomy was performed 4 h later, or sooner if women requested analgesia. In the amniotomy group, artificial forewater amniotomy was carried out and a repeat cervical assessment done 4 h later, or sooner if women requested analgesia. In both groups, intravenous oxytocin was established if there was evidence of disordered uterine activity, 6 h after the start of initial intervention. An assessment of consumers' views was carried out by using a standardized questionnaire completed 48 h after delivery. There was a significant reduction in the requirement for oxytocin augmentation in women treated with PGE2: primigravidae, odds ratio (OR), 0.27 and 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.12-0.61; multiparae, OR, 0.19 and 95% CI, 0.08-0.45. Fewer primigravidae managed with PGE2 gel required epidural analgesia (OR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.06-1.00). Fewer parous women managed with PGE2 gel required parenteral opiates (OR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.23-0.85) and more women required inhalation analgesia or no analgesia (OR, 2.22; 95% CI, 1.76-2.79). The intervention to delivery intervals were shortened in PGE2 groups independent of parity but the differences were not significant.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

Inputs.Title: Role of the cervix in the induction of labor.
Inputs.Abstract: A study on induction of labor was carried out to test the hypothesis that changing the cervix will enhance the effectiveness of induction of labor. Fifty pregnant women near term with Bishop scores of 4 or less were divided into 5 study groups, in which a 12-hour preparation phase procedure was carried out to produce cervical or myometrial changes. All women had continuous measurement of uterine activity by an extraovular catheter. The patients were divided into 1) control subjects, and into groups treated with 2) laminaria, 3) Foley catheter, 4) amniotomy, and 5) oxytocin infusion. These preparation techniques were used for 12 hours, after which rupture of membranes was carried out in all cases. Although all procedures significantly changed the cervix, none but oxytocin affected the induction-to-delivery interval. The authors concluded that when a study design rigidly controls for cervical Bishop score, timing of rupture of membranes, and oxytocin infusion rates, the cervical preparation alone will not enhance inducibility.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is amniotomy alone for induction of labour?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is amniotomy alone for induction of labour?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across studies, amniotomy (artificially breaking the waters) can start labour but often does not generate regular contractions on its own. In women at term with favourable cervixes, those induced by amniotomy needed oxytocin much more often than those given prostaglandin gel, showing amniotomy alone is a weaker stimulus for labour. In women with unripe cervixes, using amniotomy as a “preparation” step changed the cervix but did not shorten time from induction to birth, unlike oxytocin.

- **Full Answer**:  
Amniotomy alone is a weak method of inducing labour. In term pregnancies with a favourable cervix, breaking the waters without other medicines led to more women needing oxytocin to strengthen contractions compared with prostaglandin gel, indicating poorer effectiveness of amniotomy by itself [1]. In women with an unfavourable cervix, amniotomy changed the cervix but did not shorten the time from starting induction to delivery, whereas oxytocin did [2]. Overall, many women will still require oxytocin.
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks how ineffective amniotomy (artificially breaking the waters) is when used *alone* to induce labour. One study in women with an unripe cervix compared several 12‑hour “preparation” methods, including amniotomy, against no treatment and oxytocin; only oxytocin shortened the time from induction to birth, while amniotomy did not, showing little true induction effect [2]. Another trial in women with a favourable cervix showed that those induced mainly with amniotomy needed oxytocin augmentation far more often than those given prostaglandin gel, again indicating that amniotomy alone rarely generates adequate labour [1].

- **Full Answer**:  
Amniotomy (breaking the waters) by itself is a relatively weak method of inducing labour.  

In a rigorously controlled study of women near term with an unfavourable cervix, women assigned to amniotomy for 12 hours showed no reduction in the time from starting induction to birth compared with untreated controls; only those given oxytocin had faster labours [2]. This means amniotomy alone did not make labour progress any quicker, even though the cervix did soften and open somewhat [2].  

In another trial of low‑risk term pregnancies with favourable cervixes, women who had amniotomy as the main induction method were three to five times more likely to require extra oxytocin to keep labour going than women given prostaglandin gel first [1]. This heavy reliance on extra oxytocin shows that, in practice, amniotomy alone often fails to start or maintain effective labour and is usually insufficient as the sole induction method today [1,2].

efficacy.positive_question: Does amniotomy alone work for induction of labour?
efficacy.negative_question: Does amniotomy alone not work for induction of labour?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: In the first study, women with favorable cervixes were induced either with prostaglandin gel followed by amniotomy, or with amniotomy alone. Many more women in the amniotomy-only group needed extra oxytocin to keep labor going, showing that amniotomy by itself was less effective [1]. In a second study of women with an unfavorable cervix, using amniotomy as the only preparation did change the cervix but did not shorten the time from induction to birth [2].

- **Full Answer**: Amniotomy (breaking the waters) on its own can sometimes start labor, but it is not a reliable or especially effective way to induce labor. In women who already had a favorable cervix, amniotomy alone led to more need for oxytocin drips compared with prostaglandin gel, meaning it often could not maintain strong enough contractions [1]. In women with an unripe cervix, amniotomy alone did not speed birth at all [2].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Studies have tested whether breaking the waters (amniotomy) alone is enough to induce labour. In women at term with a favourable cervix, amniotomy did start labour in many cases, but significantly more of these women needed extra oxytocin than women who first had prostaglandin gel, meaning amniotomy was less effective on its own [1]. In women with an unripe cervix, amniotomy used alone did not shorten the time from induction to birth [2].

- **Full Answer**:  
Amniotomy alone can sometimes start labour, particularly if the cervix is already soft and open, but it is often not enough to complete induction. Compared with prostaglandin gel, women induced by amniotomy needed oxytocin much more often, showing it is a weaker method on its own [1]. When the cervix is unripe, amniotomy by itself does not make labour progress faster, while oxytocin does [2]. So it is usually combined with medications rather than used alone [1][2].

safety.positive_question: Is amniotomy alone safe for induction of labour?
safety.negative_question: Is amniotomy alone dangerous for induction of labour?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The first trial compared amniotomy alone with a prostaglandin gel in low‑risk term pregnancies with a favorable cervix. It did not report higher rates of serious complications with amniotomy, suggesting it was reasonably safe in that selected group, but women needed more oxytocin to keep labor progressing and more strong pain relief, indicating it was less comfortable and less efficient than prostaglandin induction [1]. The second study evaluated several “preparation” methods, including amniotomy, and found that only oxytocin meaningfully shortened time from induction to birth; cervical methods (including amniotomy) did not improve effectiveness when other factors were controlled [2]. Safety problems were not highlighted, but the study was small [2]. Together, these data suggest amniotomy alone can be used safely in carefully chosen women, but it is less effective than modern methods and typically requires added oxytocin. Evidence is limited, so practice usually combines amniotomy with other induction agents.

- **Full Answer**:  
In the studies summarized, amniotomy (artificially breaking the waters) used by itself for induction in low‑risk term pregnancies with a favorable cervix did not show more serious complications than prostaglandin gel, suggesting it was reasonably safe in that narrow group [1]. However, women induced with amniotomy alone were more likely to need extra oxytocin to keep labor going and more strong pain relief than those given prostaglandins, meaning the process was less efficient and often more uncomfortable [1].  

Another small study that included amniotomy as a cervical “preparation” method found that only oxytocin clearly shortened the time from starting induction to birth; cervical methods, including amniotomy, did not make labor more efficient once oxytocin use and timing of membrane rupture were controlled [2].  

Overall, these data suggest amniotomy alone appears reasonably safe in carefully selected women, but it is less effective than other options and usually needs to be combined with oxytocin or other medications [1][2].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The first study directly compared amniotomy (breaking the waters) alone with a prostaglandin gel for starting labour in low‑risk women at term with a favourable cervix [1]. Women who had amniotomy alone more often needed extra drugs to strengthen contractions (oxytocin) and more pain relief (epidural or injected opioids), and their labours tended to be a bit longer, but the summary does not report more serious complications for mother or baby in the amniotomy group [1]. The second study used amniotomy as part of different preparation methods and found that it changed the cervix but did not worsen outcomes; only oxytocin clearly shortened the time to birth [2]. Neither study describes amniotomy alone as causing dangerous outcomes; the issue is mainly effectiveness and comfort, not safety, in these low‑risk settings [1,2].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, amniotomy by itself does not appear dangerous for inducing labour in low‑risk women at term with a favourable cervix [1,2].  

When amniotomy alone was compared with a prostaglandin gel, women who had only amniotomy more often needed extra oxytocin to strengthen contractions and more pain medication, and their labour was somewhat longer [1]. However, the study summary does not report higher rates of serious problems for mothers or babies in the amniotomy group [1].  

Another study found that amniotomy changed the cervix but, like other mechanical methods, did not worsen induction outcomes when labour was otherwise well‑managed [2].  

So, in these carefully monitored hospital settings, amniotomy alone was less efficient and more uncomfortable, but not shown to be inherently dangerous [1,2].

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing amniotomy alone is good for induction of labour?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing amniotomy alone is harmful for induction of labour?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
One trial compared prostaglandin (PGE₂) vaginal gel plus later amniotomy with amniotomy started first for induction at term in low‑risk women with a favourable cervix [1]. In the group starting with amniotomy, many more women needed oxytocin to strengthen contractions, whereas starting with PGE₂ gel clearly reduced the need for oxytocin and pain relief, without worse delivery times [1]. This suggests amniotomy by itself is less effective than prostaglandin-based methods.  
Another study in women with an unfavourable cervix (low Bishop score) compared several “preparation” methods including amniotomy and oxytocin [2]. Only oxytocin shortened the time from induction to delivery; amniotomy and other cervical methods did not improve how quickly labour progressed [2].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes, there are scientific studies including amniotomy alone for induction. However, they show it is not a particularly effective standalone method. Compared with prostaglandin gel, starting induction with amniotomy led to more women needing oxytocin and stronger pain relief, with no clear benefit in time to birth [1]. In women with an unripe cervix, amniotomy did not shorten the time from induction to delivery, whereas oxytocin did [2]. Overall, these studies do not support amniotomy alone as a strong induction method.
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The first trial compared starting induction with a prostaglandin gel versus starting with artificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy) in low‑risk term pregnancies with a favorable cervix [1]. Women induced with prostaglandin needed less oxytocin and less pain relief, and their labors tended to be shorter, but there is no report of higher rates of serious problems (such as cesarean birth, infection, or poor outcomes for the baby) in the amniotomy group [1]. The second study compared several “preparation” methods, including amniotomy, in women with an unfavorable cervix [2]. Amniotomy changed the cervix but did not shorten time from induction to delivery; again, no specific harms or complications related to amniotomy alone were reported [2]. Thus, these studies suggest amniotomy alone may be less effective or require more additional interventions, but they do not show it to be directly harmful.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, amniotomy alone has not been shown to be harmful for induction of labour. In the randomized trial, women who started induction with prostaglandin gel needed less oxytocin and pain relief than those who started with amniotomy, but the study did not report more serious complications or worse outcomes in the amniotomy group [1]. This suggests amniotomy alone is less efficient and more likely to require additional interventions, but not clearly more dangerous.  

In the second study, amniotomy changed the cervix but did not shorten the induction‑to‑delivery time compared with other methods; again, no specific harms from amniotomy alone were described [2].  

Overall, these scientific studies indicate that amniotomy by itself is not proven harmful, but it may be less effective and more intervention‑intensive than some other induction methods [1][2].

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is amniotomy alone a good choice for induction of labour?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is amniotomy alone a bad choice for induction of labour?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The first study compared two ways to start labour in low‑risk women with a favourable (ripe) cervix: (1) prostaglandin gel in the vagina followed by amniotomy, versus (2) amniotomy alone. Women who had prostaglandin needed less oxytocin to keep labour going, used less strong pain relief, and tended to deliver a bit sooner, although that timing difference was not statistically firm [1]. The second study looked at women with an unfavourable (unripe) cervix. When amniotomy was used as part of a 12‑hour “preparation” phase, it did not shorten the time from starting induction to birth; only oxytocin clearly did that [2]. Together, these suggest that simply breaking the waters, especially when the cervix is not ready, is not the most effective or comfortable way to induce labour. Adding medications that stimulate contractions (like prostaglandin or oxytocin) generally makes induction more effective than amniotomy alone.

- **Full Answer**:  
On its own, amniotomy (breaking the waters) is usually not the best choice for inducing labour.  

In women with a cervix that is already favourable, starting induction with vaginal prostaglandin gel led to less need for oxytocin, less strong pain relief, and slightly shorter labours compared with amniotomy alone, suggesting amniotomy by itself is less efficient and more likely to need extra help [1].  

In women whose cervix is still unripe (low Bishop score), using amniotomy during a 12‑hour preparation phase did not shorten the time from induction to birth; only oxytocin clearly improved how quickly labour progressed [2].  

Taken together, these studies indicate that amniotomy alone is generally not the most effective or comfortable method for induction. It tends to work better when combined with labour‑stimulating medications, and prostaglandin or oxytocin‑based approaches are usually more effective than relying on amniotomy by itself [1][2].
timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Trials compare amniotomy with other induction methods. In women at term with a favourable cervix, amniotomy alone did start labour, but more women needed oxytocin and stronger pain relief than with prostaglandin gel plus later amniotomy [1]. In women with an unripe cervix, amniotomy as the only preparation did not shorten time to birth, while oxytocin did [2]. No extra harms from amniotomy alone were reported, but it was less efficient [1][2].

- **Full Answer**:  
Amniotomy alone is not shown to be unsafe, but it is a weaker way to induce labour than medicines. With amniotomy alone, more women need oxytocin and pain relief compared with starting with prostaglandin gel [1]. When the cervix is not ready, amniotomy does not shorten time from induction to birth, whereas oxytocin does [2]. So amniotomy alone is reasonable if your cervix is favourable, but you are likely to need induction drugs later [1][2].

cost.positive_question: Is amniotomy alone worth the money for induction of labour?
cost.negative_question: Is amniotomy alone not worth the money for induction of labour?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Amniotomy changes the cervix but, when studied carefully, it does not clearly shorten labour or reduce other interventions compared with standard care. In women with an unripe cervix, only oxytocin—not amniotomy—improved time from induction to birth. In women with a favourable cervix, starting with prostaglandin gel and using amniotomy later reduced the need for extra drugs and pain relief compared with immediate amniotomy. Since amniotomy alone does not improve outcomes much yet can still lead to further interventions, it is unlikely to be the best use of healthcare resources for induction.

- **Full Answer**:  
Evidence does not support amniotomy (breaking the waters) alone as a worthwhile or cost‑effective way to induce labour.

In women whose cervix was still “unripe” (low Bishop score), amniotomy as a preparation method changed the cervix but did not shorten the time from starting induction to birth once membrane rupture and oxytocin use were standardised. Only oxytocin infusion clearly improved how quickly labour progressed [2]. This means amniotomy alone did not add efficiency.

In women at term with favourable cervixes, starting with prostaglandin E2 gel and doing amniotomy later led to less need for oxytocin, less strong pain relief, and similar delivery times compared with immediate amniotomy alone [1]. This suggests amniotomy by itself is less effective and may lead to more drug use and interventions [1].

Overall, breaking the waters alone is unlikely to be the best use of resources for induction, compared with prostaglandins or oxytocin [1][2].
cost.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The first trial shows that starting induction with prostaglandin gel, then doing amniotomy, leads to less need for oxytocin and pain relief than starting with amniotomy alone, suggesting amniotomy alone is clinically less efficient. The second trial shows that when the cervix is unripe, amniotomy as a preparation method does not shorten time to birth, unlike oxytocin. Neither study reports actual cost data, so we can only infer cost‑effectiveness indirectly from resource use (e.g., extra drugs and procedures).

- **Full Answer**:  
Available studies suggest amniotomy (artificially breaking the waters) is a weak method when used by itself for inducing labour.  

In women at term with favourable cervixes, prostaglandin gel followed by amniotomy led to less need for oxytocin drip and less pain‑relief medication than starting with amniotomy alone [1]. This implies that using amniotomy as the main induction method results in more drug use and more procedures later on, which likely increases overall resource use [1].  

In women with an unripe cervix, doing amniotomy as the initial “preparation” step did change the cervix, but it did not shorten the time from starting induction to birth; only oxytocin did that [2]. So, as a stand‑alone strategy, amniotomy did not make induction more efficient [2].  

None of these trials directly measured costs, so we cannot say definitively it is “not worth the money,” but its added value over other methods appears limited [1][2].

family.positive_question: My family said amniotomy alone worked great for induction of labour. Will it work for me too?
family.negative_question: My family said amniotomy alone didn't work for induction of labour. Will it not work for me too?
family.positive_answer:

Amniotomy can trigger or strengthen labor, but its success depends heavily on how “ready” the cervix is and whether other methods (like oxytocin or prostaglandins) are used. The articles compare amniotomy alone with medication-based methods and look at women with both favorable and unfavorable cervixes. Overall, they show that amniotomy on its own often isn’t enough, especially if the cervix is not already soft and open. Individual factors (your Bishop score, medical history, baby’s status) matter more than family experience, so this choice should be personalized with your care team.

Amniotomy (breaking the waters) can help start or speed labor, but it does not work the same for everyone.  

In one study of low‑risk women at term with a soft, “favorable” cervix, using amniotomy alone usually led to a need for extra oxytocin to keep contractions going, compared with using a cervical ripening gel first [1]. Another study in women with an unripe cervix (low Bishop score) found that amniotomy by itself did not shorten the time from induction to birth; only oxytocin did that [2].  

This suggests amniotomy works best when your cervix is already favorable and when it’s combined with other methods as needed [1][2]. Whether it is a good choice for you depends on your cervix, baby’s condition, your medical history, and your preferences. Discuss with your maternity team which overall induction method (or combination) gives you the safest and most comfortable possible chance of vaginal birth.
family.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that how well amniotomy (breaking the waters) works depends a lot on how “ready” the cervix is (Bishop score) and whether medicines like oxytocin or prostaglandins are used alongside it. Your family’s experience reflects that amniotomy alone often isn’t enough, but that doesn’t mean it could never work for you—just that it’s commonly part of a combined plan rather than the only method.

Your response may be different from your family’s, but most women need amniotomy **plus** medicines (prostaglandins or oxytocin) rather than amniotomy alone [1][2]. Your provider will assess your cervix and overall situation to choose the safest, most effective approach.

friend.positive_question: My friend said amniotomy alone worked great for induction of labour. Will it work for me too?

testimonials.positive_question: I read online testimonials that amniotomy alone works well for induction of labour. Is this true?
testimonials.negative_question: I read online testimonials that amniotomy alone doesn't work for induction of labour. Is this true?
