This evidence comes from very premature newborns; whether antithrombin is appropriate in any other setting should be decided with your own doctor.

ReviewTitle: Post‐operative radiotherapy for ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: The addition of radiotherapy (RT) following breast conserving surgery (BCS) was first shown to reduce the risk of ipsilateral recurrence in the treatment of invasive breast cancer. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a pre-invasive lesion. Recurrence of ipsilateral disease following BCS can be either DCIS or invasive breast cancer. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have shown that RT can reduce the risk of recurrence, but assessment of potential long-term complications from addition of RT following BSC for DCIS has not been reported for women participating in RCTs.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To summarise the data from RCTs testing the addition of RT to BCS for treatment of DCIS to determine the balance between the benefits and harms.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Breast Cancer Group Specialised Register (2 June 2011), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (The Cochrane Library 2008, Issue 1), MEDLINE (2 June 2011), EMBASE (2 June 2011) and the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP; 2 June 2011). Reference lists of articles and handsearching of ASCO (2007), ESMO (2002 to 2007), and St Gallen (2005 to 2007) conferences were performed.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: RCTs of breast conserving surgery with and without radiotherapy in women at first diagnosis of pure ductal carcinoma in situ (no invasive disease present).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two authors independently assessed each potentially eligible trial for inclusion and its quality. Two authors also independently extracted data from published Kaplan-Meier analysis (survival curves) and reported summary statistics. Data were extracted and pooled for four trials. Data for planned subgroups were extracted and pooled for analysis.There were insufficient data to pool for long-term toxicity from radiotherapy.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Four RCTs involving 3925 women were identified and included in this review. All were high quality with minimal risk of bias. Three trials compared the addition of RT to BCS. One trial was a two by two factorial design comparing the use of RT and tamoxifen, each separately or together, in which participants were randomised in at least one arm. Analysis confirmed a statistically significant benefit from the addition of radiotherapy on all ipsilateral breast events (hazards ratio (HR) 0.49; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.58, P < 0.00001), ipsilateral invasive recurrence (HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.76, p=0.001) and ipsilateral DCIS recurrence (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.95, P = 0.03). All the subgroups analysed benefited from addition of radiotherapy. No significant long-term toxicity from radiotherapy was found. No information about short-term toxicity from radiotherapy or quality of life data were reported.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: This review confirms the benefit of adding radiotherapy to breast conserving surgery for the treatment of all women diagnosed with DCIS. No long-term toxicity from use of radiotherapy was identified.

Inputs.Title: Breast-conserving treatment with or without radiotherapy in ductal carcinoma-in-situ: ten-year results of European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer randomized phase III trial 10853--a study by the EORTC Breast Cancer Cooperative Group and EORTC Radiotherapy Group.
Inputs.Abstract:
The European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer conducted a randomized trial investigating the role of radiotherapy (RT) after local excision (LE) of ductal carcinoma-in-situ (DCIS) of the breast. We analyzed the efficacy of RT with 10 years follow-up on both the overall risk of local recurrence (LR) and related to clinical, histologic, and treatment factors.
                After complete LE, women with DCIS were randomly assigned to no further treatment or RT (50 Gy). One thousand ten women with mostly (71%) mammographically detected DCIS were included. The median follow-up was 10.5 years.
                The 10-year LR-free rate was 74% in the group treated with LE alone compared with 85% in the women treated by LE plus RT (log-rank P < .0001; hazard ratio [HR] = 0.53). The risk of DCIS and invasive LR was reduced by 48% (P = .0011) and 42% (P = .0065) respectively. Both groups had similar low risks of metastases and death. At multivariate analysis, factors significantly associated with an increased LR risk were young age (< or = 40 years; HR = 1.89), symptomatic detection (HR = 1.55), intermediately or poorly differentiated DCIS (as opposed to well-differentiated DCIS; HR = 1.85 and HR = 1.61 respectively), cribriform or solid growth pattern (as opposed to clinging/micropapillary subtypes; HR = 2.39 and HR = 2.25 respectively), doubtful margins (HR = 1.84), and treatment by LE alone (HR = 1.82). The effect of RT was homogeneous across all assessed risk factors.
                With long-term follow-up, RT after LE for DCIS continued to reduce the risk of LR, with a 47% reduction at 10 years. All patient subgroups benefited from RT.

Inputs.Title: Lumpectomy and radiation therapy for the treatment of intraductal breast cancer: findings from National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project B-17.
Inputs.Abstract:
In 1993, findings from a National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project (NSABP) trial to evaluate the worth of radiation therapy after lumpectomy concluded that the combination was more beneficial than lumpectomy alone for localized intraductal carcinoma-in-situ (DCIS). This report extends those findings.
                Women (N = 818) with localized DCIS were randomly assigned to lumpectomy or lumpectomy plus radiation (50 Gy). Tissue was removed so that resected specimen margins were histologically tumor-free. Mean follow-up time was 90 months (range, 67 to 130). Size and method of tumor detection were determined by central clinical, mammographic, and pathologic assessment. Life-table estimates of event-free survival and survival, average annual rates of occurrence for specific events, relative risks for event-specific end points, and cumulative probability of specific events comprising event-free survival are presented.
                The benefit of lumpectomy plus radiation was virtually unchanged between 5 and 8 years of follow-up and was due to a reduction in invasive and noninvasive ipsilateral breast tumors (IBTs). Incidence of locoregional and distant events remained similar in both treatment groups; deaths were only infrequently related to breast cancer. Incidence of noninvasive IBT was reduced from 13.4% to 8.2% (P = .007), and of invasive IBT, from 13.4% to 3.9% (P < .0001). All cohorts benefited from radiation regardless of clinical or mammographic tumor characteristics.
                Through 8 years of follow-up, our findings continue to indicate that lumpectomy plus radiation is more beneficial than lumpectomy alone for women with localized, mammographically detected DCIS. When evaluated according to the mammographic characteristics of their DCIS, all groups benefited from radiation.

Inputs.Title: Absolute risk reductions for local recurrence after postoperative radiotherapy after sector resection for ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast.
Inputs.Abstract:
Evaluate the effects of radiotherapy after sector resection for ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast (DCIS) in patient groups as defined by age, size of the lesion, focality, completeness of excision and mode of detection.
                A total of 1,067 women in Sweden were randomly assigned to either postoperative radiotherapy (RT) or control from 1987 to 1999, and 1,046 were followed for a mean of 8 years. The main outcome was new ipsilateral breast cancer events and distant metastasis-free survival analyzed according to intention to treat.
                There were 64 ipsilateral events in the RT arm and 141 in the control group corresponding to a risk reduction of 16.0 percentage points at 10 years (95% CI, 10.3% to 21.6%) and a relative risk of 0.40 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.54). There was no statistically significant difference in distant metastasis-free survival. There was an effect modification by age, yielding a low effect of RT in women younger than 50, but substantial protection in women older than 60 years. The age effect was not confounded by focality, lesion size, completeness of excision, or detection mode. There was no group as defined by our stratification variables that had a low risk without radiotherapy.
                Our results indicate that younger women have a low protective effect of conventional RT after sector resection. Older women benefit substantially. We caution that the age effect was seen in a subgroup analysis. Further search with conventional clinical variables for a low risk group that does not need RT does not seem fruitful.

Inputs.Title: Radiotherapy and tamoxifen in women with completely excised ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand: randomised controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract:
As a consequence of mammographic breast screening programmes, ductal carcinoma in situ is diagnosed with increasing frequency. Mastectomy for localised ductal carcinoma in situ is thought to be an over-treatment by many physicians, but there is much controversy as to whether complete local excision alone is sufficient. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of adjuvant radiotherapy and tamoxifen.
                We used a 2x2 factorial design in a randomised controlled trial. Between May, 1990, and August, 1998, 1701 patients recruited from screening programmes were randomised to both treatments in combination or singly, or to none, or to either one (eg, radiotherapy) with an elective decision to give or to withhold the other (ie, in this case tamoxifen). Patients had complete surgical excision of the lesion confirmed by specimen radiography and histology. Patients have been followed up at least once a year. Median follow-up was 52.6 (range 2.4-118.3) months. Our primary endpoint was the incidence of ipsilateral invasive disease.
                Ipsilateral invasive disease was not reduced by tamoxifen but recurrence of overall ductal carcinoma in situ was decreased (hazard ratio 0.68 [0.49-0.96]; p=0.03). Radiotherapy reduced the incidence of ipsilateral invasive disease (0.45 [0.24-0.85]; p=0.01) and ipsilateral ductal carcinoma in situ (0.36 [0.19-0.66]; p=0.0004), but there was no effect on the occurrence of contralateral disease. There was no evidence of interaction between radiotherapy and tamoxifen.
                Radiotherapy can be recommended for patients with ductal carcinoma in situ treated by complete local excision; however, there is little evidence for the use of tamoxifen in these women.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is radiotherapy for ductal carcinoma in situ?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is radiotherapy for ductal carcinoma in situ?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Randomized trials compared surgery alone with surgery plus radiotherapy for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Across several large studies, adding radiotherapy consistently cut the chance of cancer coming back in the treated breast (either as DCIS or invasive cancer) by about half, but did not change overall survival. Benefits were seen across most patient subgroups, though one study suggested younger women might gain somewhat less.

- **Full Answer**:  
Radiotherapy after surgical removal of DCIS substantially lowers the chance of the cancer returning in the same breast.

In a large European trial, adding radiotherapy after local excision improved 10‑year freedom from any local recurrence from 74% to 85%, roughly a 47–50% relative reduction in both DCIS and invasive recurrences, without affecting survival [1].  

In a U.S. trial, radiotherapy reduced new invasive tumors in the treated breast from 13.4% to 3.9% and new DCIS from 13.4% to 8.2% over about 8 years [2].  

A Swedish study found about 16% fewer same‑breast events at 10 years (relative risk 0.40) [3].  

A UK/Australasian trial showed similar roughly 55–65% relative reductions in invasive and DCIS recurrences [4].  

Overall, radiotherapy roughly halves local recurrence risk but does not clearly improve overall survival.
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks “how ineffective” radiotherapy is for DCIS, but the trial data consistently show that radiotherapy after breast‑conserving surgery is *effective* at cutting local recurrences by about half. Across four major randomized trials, radiation substantially reduced new cancers in the treated breast (both DCIS and invasive), with absolute risk reductions of roughly 10–16 percentage points over 8–10 years, but it did *not* clearly improve survival or reduce distant spread. Therefore, radiotherapy is best understood as very effective for local control, but not as a treatment that usually changes life expectancy in DCIS.

- **Full Answer**:  
Radiotherapy after breast‑conserving surgery for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is quite effective at lowering the chance that cancer returns in the treated breast, but it does not seem to change overall survival.

In a large European trial, adding radiation raised the 10‑year “no‑recurrence” rate from 74% to 85%, cutting local recurrences by about half [1]. A Swedish study found a similar 60% relative reduction and a 16% absolute drop in 10‑year risk of new cancers in the same breast [3]. In NSABP B‑17, radiation reduced invasive recurrences from 13.4% to 3.9% and non‑invasive recurrences from 13.4% to 8.2% over 8 years [2]. The UK/ANZ trial likewise showed roughly halved risks of both invasive and in‑situ recurrences [4].  

It does not clearly lower spread outside the breast or deaths, which are already uncommon in DCIS [1–4]. This is a benefit for preventing cancer returning.

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is radiotherapy a good choice for ductal carcinoma in situ?

cost.positive_question: Is radiotherapy worth the money for ductal carcinoma in situ?

cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Radiotherapy after breast‑conserving surgery for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) does not clearly help women live longer, but it substantially lowers the chance that cancer will come back in the treated breast. Across several large randomized trials, adding radiotherapy cut local recurrences (both DCIS and invasive cancer) by about half, with absolute reductions of about 10–16 extra recurrences prevented per 100 women over 8–10 years [1–4]. Invasive recurrences often require more extensive treatment, such as mastectomy or chemotherapy, which are costly and more burdensome than radiotherapy itself [2–4]. No consistent “very low‑risk” group has been reliably identified that can safely skip radiotherapy after surgery [1,3,4]. Because trials did not directly test costs, the value question is partly personal: women must weigh the up‑front cost, inconvenience, and side effects of radiotherapy against a substantially lower risk of needing more aggressive, expensive treatment if the cancer returns [1–4].

- **Full Answer**:  
Radiotherapy after surgery for DCIS roughly halves the chance of cancer returning in the treated breast, lowering 10‑year local recurrence rates by about 10–16 percentage points in randomized trials [1–3]. This benefit includes both non‑invasive DCIS recurrences and invasive breast cancers, which are more serious and usually need more intensive, costly treatment such as mastectomy or chemotherapy [1–4]. However, these studies have not shown a clear improvement in overall survival or reduction in distant metastases with radiotherapy [1–4].  

No consistently safe “low‑risk” subgroup has been identified in which the recurrence risk is low enough to confidently omit radiotherapy, although younger women may gain slightly less benefit and older women often gain more [1,3]. Cost‑effectiveness was not directly studied, but by preventing many invasive recurrences, radiotherapy likely avoids substantial future treatment costs and morbidity for many women [1–4].  

So, for most women with DCIS choosing breast‑conserving surgery, radiotherapy is generally considered “worth it,” but the decision should reflect individual recurrence risk, side‑effect tolerance, and out‑of‑pocket costs [1–4].

In one European trial, the 10‑year “no‑recurrence” rate improved from 74% with surgery alone to 85% with surgery plus radiotherapy, cutting recurrences by about half [1]. A US trial found invasive recurrences fell from 13.4% to 3.9%, and non‑invasive recurrences from 13.4% to 8.2% with radiotherapy [2]. A Swedish study showed a 16% absolute reduction in cancer events in the treated breast at 10 years and a 60% relative risk reduction [3]. A UK/Australasian trial also found radiotherapy roughly halved both invasive and DCIS recurrences in the same breast [4].

Across these studies, radiotherapy did **not** clearly improve overall survival, because DCIS already has an excellent prognosis [1–4]. So radiotherapy is effective for reducing local recurrences, but its pros and cons should be weighed with your cancer team.

ReviewTitle: Pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for body dysmorphic disorder

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a prevalent and disabling preoccupation with a slight or imagined defect in appearance. Trials have investigated the use of serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs) and cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) for BDD.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess the efficacy of pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy or a combination of both treatment modalities for body dysmorphic disorder.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Depression, Anxiety and Neurosis Trial Register (December 2007), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (The Cochrane Library Issue 4, 2007), MEDLINE (January 1966 to December 2007), and PsycINFO (1967 to December 2007). Ongoing and unpublished trials were located through searching the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, the CRISP and WHO ICTRP search portals (databases searched in December 2007), and through contacting key researchers and pharmaceutical companies. Additional studies were located through study reference lists.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of patients meeting DSM or ICD diagnostic criteria for BDD, in which the trials compare pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy or multi-modal treatment groups with active or non-active control groups. Short or long-term trials were eligible.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two review authors independently assessed RCTs for inclusion in the review, collated trial data, and assessed trial quality. Investigators were contacted to obtain missing data. Summary effect sizes for dichotomous and continuous outcomes were calculated using a random effects model and heterogeneity was assessed.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Two pharmacotherapy and three psychotherapy trials were eligible for inclusion in the review, with data from four short-term RCTs (169 participants) available for analysis. Response data from a single placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine suggested overall superiority of medication relative to placebo (relative risk (RR) 3.07, 95% CI 1.4 to 6.72, n = 67). Symptom severity was also significantly reduced in the RCTs of fluoxetine and clomipramine (relative to desipramine), as well as in the two CBT trials (WMD -44.96, 95% CI -54.43 to -35.49, n = 73). A low relapse rate (4/22) was demonstrated in one trial of CBT.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: Results from the small number of available RCTs suggest that SRIs and CBT may be useful in treating patients with BDD. The findings of these studies need to be replicated. In addition, future controlled studies in other samples, such as adolescents, and using other selective SRIs, as well as a range of psychological therapy approaches and modalities (alone and in combination), are essential in supplementing the sparse data currently available.

Inputs.Title: Body dysmorphic disorder: a preliminary evaluation of treatment and maintenance using exposure with response prevention.
Inputs.Abstract: In recent investigations, body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) has been shown to share common etiological and symptom presentation to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). When treating BDD, there have been some investigations suggesting that exposure with response prevention is effective in alleviating symptoms. Ten patients diagnosed with BDD participated in a study examining the effects of treatment and maintenance using exposure with response prevention. They received a standard behavior therapy protocol which consisted of exposure in vivo and in imagery, with response prevention. Symptom severity, depression, anxiety, and avoidance were assessed weekly during treatment. Following treatment, a 6-month maintenance program was instituted for five patients, with the other five serving as controls. Patients in the maintenance program were assessed bi-weekly with all measures and a 6-month follow-up was conducted. Patients improved for measures of avoidance, BDD symptoms, depression and anxiety when using exposure with response prevention. Although all patients remained symptom free at follow-up, those in the maintenance program continued to improve. Based on these results, BDD appears to be amenable to exposure with response prevention treatment. Additional treatment gains can be obtained when structured maintenance programs are implemented.

Inputs.Title: Body dysmorphic disorder: a cognitive behavioural model and pilot randomised controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract: A cognitive behavioural model of body image is presented with specific reference to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). We make specific hypotheses from the model for testing BDD patients in comparison with: (i) patients with "real" disfigurements who seek cosmetic surgery; (ii) subjects with "real" disfigurements who are emotionally well adjusted; and (iii) healthy controls without any defect. There have been no randomised controlled trials of treatment for BDD and therefore the model has clear implications for the development of cognitive behavioural therapy. This was evaluated in a pilot controlled trial. Nineteen patients were randomly allocated to either cognitive behaviour therapy or a waiting list control group over 12 weeks. There were no significant pre-post differences on any of the measures in the waiting list group. There were significant changes in the treated group on specific measures of BDD and depressed mood. Cognitive behaviour therapy should be further evaluated in a larger controlled trial in comparison with another psychological treatment such as interpersonal therapy and pharmacotherapy.

Inputs.Title: Cognitive-behavioral body image therapy for body dysmorphic disorder.
Inputs.Abstract: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a distressing body image disorder that involves excessive preoccupation with physical appearance in a normal appearing person. Prior case reports of behavior therapy were encouraging, but no controlled evaluation of behavior therapy or any other type of treatment had been conducted. In the present study, 54 BDD subjects were randomly assigned to cognitive behavior therapy or no treatment. Patients were treated in small groups for eight 2-hour sessions. Therapy involved modification of intrusive thoughts of body dissatisfaction and overvalued beliefs about physical appearance, exposure to avoided body image situations, and elimination of body checking. Body dysmorphic disorder symptoms were significantly decreased in therapy subjects and the disorder was eliminated in 82% of cases at posttreatment and 77% at follow-up. Overall psychological symptoms and self-esteem also improved in therapy subjects.

Inputs.Title: Clomipramine vs desipramine crossover trial in body dysmorphic disorder: selective efficacy of a serotonin reuptake inhibitor in imagined ugliness.
Inputs.Abstract:
Body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance) is a common and disabling disorder associated with high rates of delusional symptoms and suicide attempts. Although preliminary studies suggest that serotonin reuptake inhibitors may be effective for body dysmorphic disorder, to date no controlled treatment studies have been published.
                Forty patients were enrolled and 29 were randomized into a 16-week, double-blind, crossover-design study of clomipramine, a potent serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and active control desipramine, a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Outcome measures included specific ratings of body dysmorphic disorder severity, delusionality, and functional impairment.
                Clomipramine was superior to desipramine in the acute treatment of body dysmorphic disorder symptoms as measured by assessment of patients' obsessive preoccupation with perceived body defects, repetitive behaviors in response to this preoccupation, and global ratings of symptom severity. Treatment efficacy was independent of the presence or severity of comorbid diagnoses of obsessive-compulsive disorder, depression, or social phobia. Likewise, clomipramine was equally effective regardless of whether the patients had insight or held their dysmorphic misperception with delusional intensity. Clomipramine was also superior to desipramine in improving functional disability.
                Clomipramine is more effective than desipramine in the treatment of body dysmorphic disorder and is effective even among those patients who are delusional.

Inputs.Title: A randomized placebo-controlled trial of fluoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder.
Inputs.Abstract:
Research on the pharmacotherapy of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a common and often disabling disorder, is limited. Available data suggest that this disorder may respond to serotonin reuptake inhibitors. However, no placebo-controlled treatment studies of BDD have been published.
                Seventy-four patients with DSM-IV BDD or its delusional variant were enrolled and 67 were randomized into a placebo-controlled parallel-group study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoxetine hydrochloride. After 1 week of single-blind placebo treatment, patients were randomized to receive 12 weeks of double-blind treatment with fluoxetine or placebo. Outcome measures included the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Modified for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD-YBOCS) (the primary outcome measure), the Clinical Global Impressions Scale, the Brown Assessment of Beliefs Scale, and other measures.
                Results of the BDD-YBOCS indicated that fluoxetine was significantly more effective than placebo for BDD beginning at week 8 and continuing at weeks 10 and 12 (F(1,64) = 16.5; P<.001). The response rate was 18 (53%) of 34 to fluoxetine and 6 (18%) of 33 to the placebo (chi(2)(1) = 8.8; P=.003). The BDD symptoms of delusional patients were as likely as those of nondelusional patients to respond to fluoxetine, and no delusional patients responded to the placebo. In the sample as a whole, treatment response was independent of the duration and severity of BDD and the presence of major depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or a personality disorder. Fluoxetine was generally well tolerated.
                Fluoxetine is safe and more effective than placebo in delusional and nondelusional patients with BDD.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for body dysmorphic disorder?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for body dysmorphic disorder?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Psychotherapy using cognitive‑behavioral techniques (CBT), including exposure and response prevention, has shown strong benefits. In small and medium trials, CBT led to marked reductions in BDD symptoms, depression, and avoidance, with many patients no longer meeting criteria for the disorder at the end of treatment and follow‑up [1–3]. However, some studies are small, so results, while promising, need confirmation in larger trials [1–3].  

Pharmacotherapy with serotonin reuptake–enhancing antidepressants is also effective. In a crossover trial, clomipramine outperformed desipramine in reducing BDD preoccupations, rituals, and disability, regardless of depression, OCD, or delusional beliefs [4]. In a placebo‑controlled trial, fluoxetine helped about half of patients, versus fewer than one in five on placebo, with benefits seen even in very severe or delusional cases [5].  

Overall, both CBT‑based psychotherapy and serotonin reuptake–enhancing antidepressants show moderate‑to‑large benefits for many people with BDD, especially when properly delivered and monitored [1–5].

- **Full Answer**:  
Cognitive‑behavioral psychotherapy (CBT), often including exposure and response prevention, appears highly effective for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). In controlled studies, CBT significantly reduced BDD symptoms, depression, and avoidance compared with no treatment [1,2]. In a larger trial, group CBT led to BDD no longer being diagnosable in 82% of patients after treatment and 77% at follow‑up, with improved general psychological well‑being and self‑esteem [3]. Smaller studies also found that gains were maintained or improved with structured follow‑up sessions [1].  

Medications that strongly affect serotonin are also effective. In a head‑to‑head trial, clomipramine (a serotonin‑reuptake–focused drug) was clearly better than desipramine for reducing BDD obsessions, compulsive behaviors, and functional disability, regardless of comorbid depression, OCD, or delusional intensity [4]. A placebo‑controlled trial of fluoxetine found that about 53% of patients responded versus 18% on placebo, with similar benefit for delusional and non‑delusional BDD and generally good tolerability [5].  

Overall, both CBT and serotonin‑reuptake antidepressants provide meaningful relief for many people with BDD [1–5].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The articles show that both psychotherapy and medication can clearly help many people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), though they are not perfect. Cognitive‑behavioral therapies (including exposure with response prevention) reduce BDD symptoms, avoidance, anxiety, and depression, and often lead to loss of the diagnosis in most treated patients, at least in the short term [1][2][3]. Serotonin reuptake–enhancing antidepressants (like clomipramine and fluoxetine) work better than placebo or non‑serotonergic antidepressants, but only about half of patients respond in the main fluoxetine trial [4][5]. Studies are relatively small and follow‑up is limited, so long‑term effectiveness and relapse rates are less certain.

- **Full Answer**:  
Available research does not suggest that treatment is “ineffective”; both psychotherapy and medication help many—but not all—people with BDD.  

Cognitive‑behavioral approaches, including exposure with response prevention, led to marked symptom improvement, with all 10 patients in one small study symptom‑free at 6‑month follow‑up [1]. In randomized trials, CBT significantly outperformed waiting‑list controls, with about 82% no longer meeting criteria for BDD immediately after group CBT and 77% still in remission at follow‑up [2][3].  

For medication, clomipramine (a serotonin reuptake inhibitor) was clearly superior to desipramine, improving BDD symptoms and functioning [4]. Fluoxetine was more effective than placebo, with 53% responding versus 18% on placebo, meaning nearly half did not respond to medication in that trial [5].  

So, current treatments are meaningfully helpful but not universally effective, and more high‑quality, long‑term studies are needed.

efficacy.positive_question: Does pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy work for body dysmorphic disorder?
efficacy.negative_question: Does pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy not work for body dysmorphic disorder?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The summaries include several controlled studies of psychotherapy and medication for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) with techniques such as exposure and response prevention has been tested against wait‑list or no‑treatment controls and showed clear reductions in BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance [1–3]. One larger group‑CBT trial reported loss of the BDD diagnosis in most treated participants with maintained benefits [3]. On the medication side, randomized trials show that serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants (clomipramine and fluoxetine) are superior to comparison drugs or placebo, improving core BDD preoccupations and functioning, including in people with delusional intensity of beliefs and common comorbid conditions [4,5]. Sample sizes are modest, but results are consistent. Together, this supports that both CBT‑based psychotherapy and SSRI‑like pharmacotherapy are effective evidence‑based options for BDD, and they are often combined in practice.

- **Full Answer**:  
Research suggests that both psychotherapy and medication can meaningfully help many people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).

Several trials show that cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT), including exposure and response prevention, reduces BDD symptoms, anxiety, depression, and avoidance [1–3]. In one study, group CBT led to loss of the diagnosis in about 8 in 10 patients after treatment, with most benefits maintained at follow‑up [3].

Medication studies show that serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants are effective. Clomipramine worked better than desipramine for improving obsessive appearance concerns and functioning [4]. Fluoxetine was significantly more effective than placebo, helping about half of patients, including those with fixed (delusional) beliefs and those with depression or OCD [5].

Overall, CBT with exposure/response prevention and serotonin reuptake–inhibiting antidepressants both appear effective, and are often used together. However, studies are small, so more research is needed to refine who benefits most and how to maintain gains long term over time [1–5].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research shows that both medication (pharmacotherapy) and talk therapy (psychotherapy) can help many people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Several controlled trials found that specific types of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and exposure with response prevention (ERP) reduce BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, with many patients no longer meeting criteria for BDD after treatment and at follow‑up [1–3]. Medication studies show that serotonin reuptake–enhancing drugs such as clomipramine and fluoxetine work better than comparison drugs or placebo, including for people with very fixed (“delusional”) beliefs about their appearance [4–5]. This means BDD is treatable, though not every person responds, and more research is still needed.

- **Full Answer**:  
Pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy do work for many people with body dysmorphic disorder.  
Exposure with response prevention—a behavioral therapy where patients face avoided situations without performing rituals—reduced BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, with patients remaining symptom‑free at 6‑month follow‑up [1]. Cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) also led to significant improvements in BDD symptoms and mood in randomized trials, with the disorder no longer present in most treated patients and benefits maintained at follow‑up [2–3].  
Medications that strongly affect serotonin, such as clomipramine, were superior to a norepinephrine‑focused drug in reducing BDD preoccupations and improving functioning [4]. Fluoxetine was significantly more effective than placebo, with about half of patients responding, including those with delusional levels of conviction about their perceived defects [5].  
So, while not everyone improves, both CBT/ERP and serotonin‑targeting medication have solid evidence of benefit for BDD.

safety.positive_question: Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy safe for body dysmorphic disorder?
safety.negative_question: Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy dangerous for body dysmorphic disorder?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research has tested both talking therapies and medication for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Several studies of cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT), including exposure with response prevention and body‑image–focused CBT, show clear symptom improvement and lasting benefit, with no serious safety problems reported [1][2][3]. These therapies are considered low risk, though they can temporarily increase anxiety while facing feared situations.  
Medication studies show that serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants help many people with BDD. Clomipramine was more effective than desipramine for reducing BDD symptoms and disability [4]. A placebo‑controlled trial of fluoxetine found it significantly more effective than placebo, and it was “generally well tolerated,” meaning side effects were present but not usually severe [5]. As with all antidepressants, monitoring by a clinician is important.  

- **Full Answer**:  
Overall, both psychotherapy (especially CBT with exposure and response prevention) and antidepressant medication (such as fluoxetine and clomipramine) appear effective and generally safe for BDD when delivered and monitored by qualified clinicians [1][2][3][4][5].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The articles show that structured psychotherapies (like exposure with response prevention and cognitive‑behavioral therapy) improve body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) symptoms, mood, and avoidance, with no serious treatment‑related harms reported and good maintenance of gains [1][2][3]. Medication studies of clomipramine and fluoxetine (antidepressants that increase serotonin) also show significant improvement in BDD symptoms and functioning compared with other drugs or placebo [4][5]. Fluoxetine is described as “generally well tolerated,” indicating that side effects were mostly mild and manageable [5]. While all antidepressants can have side effects and require monitoring, BDD itself carries substantial distress and suicide risk [4], so effective treatment is usually safer than no treatment.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, psychotherapy and medication for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) are not considered dangerous when used under professional care.  

Behavior therapies such as exposure with response prevention and cognitive‑behavioral therapy led to clear reductions in BDD symptoms, anxiety, depression, and avoidance, with patients often remaining well at follow‑up; no serious treatment‑related harms were reported [1][2][3].  

Medications that affect serotonin, such as clomipramine and fluoxetine, improved obsessive appearance worries and functioning more than comparison drugs or placebo [4][5]. Fluoxetine was described as “generally well tolerated,” meaning side effects were mild and manageable [5].  

All antidepressants can cause side effects (for example, stomach upset, sleep or sexual problems) and rarely may worsen mood or suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment. That is why monitoring by a clinician is important.  

Given the distress and suicide risk in BDD [4], evidence‑based psychotherapy and medication are generally safer than leaving the disorder untreated.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy is good for body dysmorphic disorder?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy is harmful for body dysmorphic disorder?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The summaries include randomized and controlled trials of psychotherapy (especially cognitive‑behavioral approaches) and pharmacotherapy (serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants) for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). These studies show symptom reductions versus control or placebo, supporting both treatments as effective.

- **Full Answer**:  
There is solid scientific evidence that both psychotherapy and medication can help body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).

Several controlled studies of cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT)—which includes changing unhelpful appearance‑related thoughts, reducing checking and camouflaging, and gradual exposure to feared situations—showed large reductions in BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, with many patients no longer meeting criteria for BDD after treatment and benefits maintained at follow‑up [1][2][3].

Medication studies focusing on serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants also show benefit. In a head‑to‑head trial, clomipramine (a serotonin reuptake inhibitor) was clearly more effective than desipramine for reducing BDD obsessions, repetitive behaviors, and disability, even in patients with delusional beliefs [4]. In a randomized, placebo‑controlled trial, fluoxetine significantly outperformed placebo, with about half of patients responding versus less than one‑fifth on placebo [5].

These trials support both CBT‑based psychotherapy and serotonin‑reuptake–enhancing antidepressants as effective evidence‑based treatments for BDD.
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: The provided studies tested standard therapies and medications for BDD, reporting symptom improvement and tolerability, and did not show overall worsening or harm from these treatments.

- **Full Answer**:  
The studies summarized do not show that pharmacotherapy (medications) or psychotherapy is harmful for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Instead, they suggest these treatments are helpful for many patients. Behavioral and cognitive‑behavioral therapies, including exposure with response prevention and body image–focused CBT, led to reduced BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, with many patients no longer meeting full criteria for BDD at follow‑up [1–3]. Medication trials found that the antidepressants clomipramine and fluoxetine (serotonin reuptake inhibitors) were more effective than comparison drugs or placebo and were generally well tolerated [4,5]. These studies are relatively small and short-term, so they cannot rule out rare or long‑term side effects, but within these trials, psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy appeared beneficial rather than harmful when provided in a clinical setting [1–5].

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy a good choice for body dysmorphic disorder?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy a bad choice for body dysmorphic disorder?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research shows that certain antidepressant medicines (those that increase serotonin) and specific talking therapies clearly help many people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Medicines reduce obsessive appearance worries and related rituals, while cognitive‑behavioral therapies change unhelpful thoughts and avoidance behaviors. Studies have not directly tested using both together, but because each works on its own, using them in combination is a reasonable choice, especially for more severe or long‑lasting symptoms. Decisions should also consider side effects, your preferences, and access to qualified therapists.

- **Full Answer**:  
Structured psychotherapy, especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) with exposure and response prevention, significantly reduces BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, and many people remain improved at follow‑up [1][2][3]. In one trial, BDD was no longer present after CBT in about 8 out of 10 patients, with effects maintained over time [3].  

Serotonin‑acting antidepressants are also effective. Clomipramine worked better than another antidepressant that does not focus on serotonin [4], and fluoxetine was clearly more effective than placebo, helping about half of patients versus fewer than one in five on placebo [5]. These benefits occurred even when beliefs were very fixed or delusional [4][5].  

Although these studies tested medication and therapy separately, both have solid evidence. Using pharmacotherapy plus CBT is therefore a well‑supported and timely choice for treating BDD.
timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research shows that both specific forms of psychotherapy and certain medications can meaningfully reduce symptoms of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), including distress, avoidance, and depression, and can improve daily functioning. Cognitive‑behavioral therapies tailored to BDD and serotonin reuptake–enhancing medications have each been tested against no treatment, placebo, or comparison drugs and consistently perform better. No evidence suggests that using these treatments is a “bad choice”; rather, they are among the best‑supported options, provided they are prescribed and monitored by qualified clinicians and tailored to the individual.

- **Full Answer**:  
Pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy are not a bad choice for body dysmorphic disorder; they are actually the main evidence‑based treatments.

Cognitive‑behavioral therapies, including exposure with response prevention and body‑image–focused CBT, significantly reduce BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance, with many patients becoming symptom‑free and maintaining gains over time [1–3].

Medications that strongly affect serotonin (such as clomipramine and fluoxetine) are clearly more effective than comparison drugs or placebo for reducing BDD obsessions, compulsive behaviors, and impairment, even when symptoms are very severe or delusional, and are generally well tolerated [4–5].

These studies do not show that medication or psychotherapy is harmful; rather, they support them as effective options. The “best” approach (therapy, medication, or both) should be decided with a mental health professional who can explain benefits, side effects, and your personal preferences.

cost.positive_question: Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy worth the money for body dysmorphic disorder?
cost.negative_question: Is pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy not worth the money for body dysmorphic disorder?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research shows both psychological therapy and medication clearly work better than no treatment or placebo for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Exposure‑based and cognitive‑behavioural therapies reduce BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance; many patients no longer meet criteria for BDD after treatment, and benefits can continue or even increase with a structured maintenance program [1][2][3]. Medications that boost serotonin, such as clomipramine and fluoxetine, outperform comparison drugs and placebo, reduce obsessive appearance worries and related behaviours, and improve day‑to‑day functioning, even in very severe or delusional cases, with generally tolerable side effects [4][5]. Because BDD often causes major distress, disability, and suicide risk, these consistent, meaningful improvements are likely to be worth the financial cost for many people.

- **Full Answer**:  
Overall, yes. Good studies show that structured cognitive‑behavioural talk therapies and exposure with response prevention usually produce large, lasting improvements in BDD symptoms, mood, and daily functioning compared with no treatment [1][2][3]. Serotonin‑based medications like clomipramine and fluoxetine clearly beat placebo or other antidepressants and also help very severe or delusional patients [4][5]. Given how disabling BDD can be, these benefits generally justify the money spent.
cost.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is about value for money. None of the studies directly measured treatment cost or cost‑effectiveness. However, several randomized controlled trials show that both psychotherapy (especially cognitive‑behavioral approaches with exposure/response prevention) and serotonin‑targeting medications significantly reduce BDD symptoms, improve mood and functioning, and often lead to remission [1][2][3][4][5]. Because BDD is disabling and linked to high suicide risk, meaningful symptom relief and recovery are typically of very high value to patients, suggesting these treatments are generally “worth it,” especially when lower‑cost options are used.

- **Full Answer**:  
Available research suggests that both psychotherapy and medication are usually worth the cost for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Behavioral and cognitive‑behavioral therapies that include exposure, response prevention, and changing unhelpful appearance beliefs led to large and lasting improvements in BDD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and avoidance; many patients became essentially symptom‑free and stayed well at follow‑up [1][2][3]. Medications that strongly affect serotonin, such as clomipramine and fluoxetine, clearly outperformed comparison drugs and placebo, cutting obsessive appearance worries and related behaviors and improving daily functioning in about half of patients, including those with very fixed, “delusional” beliefs [4][5]. The studies did not directly measure cost‑effectiveness, but BDD is common, very disabling, and linked to high suicide risk [4][5]. Given the substantial chance of getting much better with treatment, the potential benefits usually outweigh the financial cost, especially when lower‑cost options (group therapy, generics, public services) are available [1][3][5] in many healthcare settings.

family.positive_question: My family said pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy worked great for body dysmorphic disorder. Will it work for me too?
family.negative_question: My family said pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy didn't work for body dysmorphic disorder. Will it not work for me too?
family.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that specific psychotherapies (especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy and exposure with response prevention) and certain medications that act on serotonin (like fluoxetine and clomipramine) often reduce body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) symptoms and improve functioning [1][2][3][4][5]. Many participants no longer met full BDD criteria after treatment, and results were similar even for people with severe or delusional beliefs and other mental health diagnoses [3][4][5]. However, not every person responds, and the research cannot guarantee results for any one individual.

- **Full Answer**:  
Research suggests that both medication and psychotherapy can help many people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), but no treatment works for everyone.

Cognitive‑behavioral therapies that include changing unhelpful appearance beliefs, reducing body checking, and gradual exposure to feared situations significantly reduced BDD symptoms, with most treated people no longer meeting full criteria after therapy and maintaining gains over time [2][3]. Exposure with response prevention also led to lasting improvement when followed by structured maintenance sessions [1].

Medications that strongly affect serotonin, such as clomipramine and fluoxetine, improved BDD symptoms more than comparison drugs or placebo, including in people with very severe or delusional symptoms, and benefits did not depend on other diagnoses like depression or OCD [4][5].

Because individuals differ, you might need to try different treatments or combinations. A mental health professional can assess your specific situation and help you decide on psychotherapy, medication, or both for you personally.
family.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Evidence from several controlled studies shows that both psychotherapy (especially cognitive‑behavioral approaches) and certain antidepressants help many people with body dysmorphic disorder, even when symptoms are severe, long‑lasting, or accompanied by depression, OCD, or delusional beliefs. Treatment response varies person to person, and a family member’s poor response does not mean you will respond the same way. It often takes finding the right therapist, method, medication, and dose, and sticking with treatment long enough, sometimes with maintenance sessions, to see full benefit.

- **Full Answer**:  
Your relatives’ experiences don’t determine how you will respond. High‑quality studies show that both psychotherapy and medication can help many people with body dysmorphic disorder.

ReviewTitle: Transcranial magnetic stimulation for the treatment of obsessive‐compulsive disorder

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) was introduced as a neurophysiological technique in 1985 when Anthony Barker and his team developed a compact machine that permitted non-invasive stimulation of the cerebral cortex (Barker 1985). Since its introduction, TMS has been used to evaluate the motor system, to study the function of several cerebral regions, and for the pathophysiology of several neuropsychiatric illnesses. In addition, it has been suggested that TMS might have therapeutic potential.
Some controlled studies have evaluated the effects of repetitive TMS (rTMS) in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Greenberg (Greenberg 1997) observed that a single session of right prefrontal cortex stimulation produced a significant decrease in compulsive urges in OCD patients lasting over eight hours. Other studies have reported transitory improvements in mood but there are no observations for changes in anxiety or obsessions.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To develop a systematic review on the clinical efficacy and safety of transcranial magnetic stimulation from randomised controlled trials in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: An electronic search was performed including the Cochrane Collaboration Depression, Anxiety and Neurosis Review Group trials register (last searched June, 2002), the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (Issue 2, 2002), MEDLINE (1966-2002), EMBASE (1974-2002), PsycLIT (1980-2002), and bibliographies from reviewed articles.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials assessing the therapeutic efficacy and safety of transcranial magnetic stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: All reviewers independently extracted the information and verified it by cross-checking. Disagreements were resolved through discussion.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Three trials were included in the review and only two contained data in a suitable form for quantitative analysis. It was not possible to pool any results for a meta-analysis. No difference was seen between rTMS and sham TMS using the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale or the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale for all time periods analysed.

Inputs.Title: Right versus left prefrontal transcranial magnetic stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder: a preliminary investigation.
Inputs.Abstract:
There is preliminary evidence that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) may be useful for the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but no definitive study has been published, and the effect of laterality of stimulation is uncertain.
                Subjects (N = 12) with resistant OCD were allocated randomly to either right or left prefrontal rTMS daily for 2 weeks and were assessed by an independent rater at 1 and 2 weeks and 1 month later.
                Subjects had an overall significant improvement in the obsessions (p < .01), compulsions (p < .01), and total (p < .01) scores on the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) after 2 weeks and at 1-month follow-up. This improvement was significant for obsessions (p < .05) and tended to significance for total Y-BOCS scores (p = .06) after correction for changes in depression scores on the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale. There was no significant difference between right- and left-sided rTMS on any of the parameters examined. Two subjects (33%) in each group showed a clinically significant improvement that persisted at I month but with relapse later in I subject.
                A proportion (about one quarter) of patients with resistant OCD appear to respond to rTMS to either prefrontal lobe, although in the absence of a sham treatment group in this study, we cannot rule out the possibility of this being a placebo response. This treatment warrants further investigation to better establish its efficacy and examine the best parameters for response.

Inputs.Title: Effect of prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder: a preliminary study.
Inputs.Abstract:
Prefrontal mechanisms are implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The authors investigated whether prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation influenced obsessive-compulsive disorder symptoms.
                Twelve patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder were given repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (80% motor threshold, 20 Hz/2 seconds per minute for 20 minutes) to a right lateral prefrontal, a left lateral prefrontal, and a midoccipital (control) site on separate days, randomized. The patients' symptoms and mood were rated for 8 hours afterward.
                Compulsive urges decreased significantly for 8 hours after right lateral prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, but there were nonsignificant increases in compulsive urges after repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of the midoccipital site. A shorter-lasting (30 minutes), modest, and nonsignificant reduction in compulsive urges occurred after left lateral prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. Mood improved during and 30 minutes after right lateral prefrontal stimulation.
                These preliminary results suggest that right prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation might affect prefrontal mechanisms involved in obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Inputs.Title: Right prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
Inputs.Abstract:
The efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) of the right prefrontal cortex for patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) was studied under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions.
                Patients were randomly assigned to 18 sessions of real (N=10) or sham (N=8) rTMS. Treatments lasted 20 minutes, and the frequency was 1 Hz for both conditions, but the intensity was 110% of motor threshold for real rTMS and 20% for the sham condition.
                No significant changes in OCD were detected in either group after treatment. Two patients who received real rTMS, with checking compulsions, and one receiving sham treatment, with sexual/religious obsessions, were considered responders.
                Low-frequency rTMS of the right prefrontal cortex failed to produce significant improvement of OCD and was not significantly different from sham treatment. Further studies are indicated to assess the efficacy of rTMS in OCD and to clarify the optimal stimulation characteristics.

ReviewTitle: Pedicle screw fixation for traumatic fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Spine fractures are common. The treatment of traumatic fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine remains controversial but surgery involving pedicle screw fixation has become a popular option.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess the effects (benefits and harms) of pedicle screw fixation for traumatic fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register (March 2011), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; The Cochrane Library, 2011 Issue 1), MEDLINE (1948 to March 2011), EMBASE (1980 to 2011 Week 11), the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM Database) (1978 to March 2011), the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (March 2011), reference lists of articles and conference proceedings.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomised controlled trials comparing pedicle screw fixation and other methods of surgical treatment, or different methods of pedicle screw fixation, for treating traumatic fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Three review authors independently performed study selection, risk of bias assessment and data extraction. Limited meta-analysis was performed.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text:
Pedicle screw fixation versus other methods of surgery that do not involve pedicle screw fixation was not looked at in any of the identified trials. Studies that were identified investigated different methods of pedicle fixation.
Five randomised and three quasi-randomised controlled trials were included. All were at high or unclear risk of various biases, including selection, performance and detection bias. A total of 448 patients with thoracic and lumbar spine fractures were included in the review. Participants were restricted to individuals without neurological impairment in five trials. The mean ages of study populations of the eight trials ranged from 33 to 41 years, and participants had generally experienced traumatic injury. Mean follow-up for trial participants in the eight trials ranged from 28 to 72 months.
Five comparisons were tested.
Two trials compared short-segment instrumentation versus long-segment instrumentation. These studies found no significant differences between the two groups in self-reported function and quality of life at final follow-up. Aside from one participant, who sustained partial neurological deterioration that was resolved by further surgery (group not known), no neurological deterioration was noted in these trials.
One trial comparing short-segment instrumentation with transpedicular bone grafting versus short-segment ﬁxation alone found no significant difference between the two groups related to patient-perceived function and pain at final follow-up. All participants had normal findings on neurological examination at final follow-up.
Two trials compared posterior instrumentation with fracture level screw incorporation ('including' group) versus posterior instrumentation alone ('bridging' group). Investigators reported no differences between the two groups in patient-reported function, quality of life, or pain at final follow-up. One trial confirmed that all participants had normal findings on neurological examination at final follow-up.
One trial comparing monosegmental pedicle screw instrumentation versus short-segment pedicle instrumentation found no significant differences between the two groups in Oswestry Disability Index results or in pain scores at final follow-up. No neurological deterioration was reported.
Three trials compared posterior instrumentation with fusion versus posterior instrumentation without fusion. Researchers found no differences between the two groups in function and quality of life or pain. No participants showed a decline in neurological status in any of the three trials, and no significant difference was reported between groups in the numbers whose status had improved at final follow-up. Two trials stated that patients in the fusion group frequently had donor site pain. Other reported complications included deep vein thrombosis and superficial infection.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: This review included only eight small trials and five different comparisons of methods of pedicle fixation in various participants while looking at a variety of outcomes at different time points. Overall, evidence is insufficient to inform the selection of different methods of pedicle screw fixation or the combined use of fusion. However, in the absence of robust evidence to support fusion, it is important to factor the risk of long-term donor site pain related to bone harvesting into the decision of whether to use this intervention. Further research involving high-quality randomised trials is needed.

Inputs.Title: The use of screw at the fracture level in the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures.
Inputs.Abstract:
In this prospective randomized study, the results of treating unstable thoracolumbar burst fractures by pedicle instrumentation with and without fracture level screw combination were given.
                Our aim was to evaluate the efficacy of fracture level screw combination in achieving and maintaining correction in the treatment of unstable thoracolumbar burst fractures.
                Most authors reported that intraoperative correction of sagittal deformity is important for the maintenance of fracture reduction and is one of the most consistent predictor of satisfactory functional outcome.
                Seventy-two patients with unstable thoracolumbar burst fractures were randomized into 4 groups with equal number of patients. In group 1, patients were treated by segmental posterior instrumentation with 2 levels above and 2 levels below the fracture level fixation, in group 2 they were treated as in group 1 with fracture level screw incorporation. In group 3, patients were treated by short-segment posterior instrumentation with 1 level above and 1 level below, in group 4 they were treated by short-segment posterior instrumentation with fracture level screw incorporation. Clinical and radiologic parameters were evaluated before surgery, after surgery, and at follow-up.
                The average follow-up was 50 months. Fracture level screw combination provided better intraoperative correction and maintenance in the treatment of unstable thoracolumbar burst fractures, which was more prevalent in short-segment fixation group.
                Reinforcement with fracture level screw combination can help to provide better kyphosis correction and offers immediate spinal stability in patients with thoracolumbar burst fracture.

Inputs.Title: Long segment instrumentation of thoracolumbar burst fracture: fusion versus nonfusion.
Inputs.Abstract:
The treatment of thoracolumbar burst fracture is a controversial issue. Although spinal fusion has been a touchstone of spinal fixation, nonfusion technique have become raising its popularity recently. Some studies suggested that nonfusion had several advantages over fusion. The aim of this prospective study was to compare long segment posterior instrumentation with fusion versus long-segment posterior instrumentation without fusion.
                For this purpose, 42 consecutive patients were assigned to two groups. Group 1 included 21 patients treated by long segment instrumentation with fusion (WF), whereas Group 2 included 21 patients treated by long segment instrumentation without fusion (WOF). Long segment instrumentation was hook fixation (claw hooks attached to second upper vertebra and infralaminar hooks attached to first upper vertebra) above and pedicle fixation (pedicle screws attached to first and second lower vertebrae) below the fractured vertebra.
                Measurements of local kyphosis, sagittal index and anterior vertebral height compression showed that both group had similar outcome at final follow-up. Moreover, there was no difference between the two groups according to low back outcome score. Also, implant failure rate (4.7%) was quite low in both groups. However, WF group had prolonged operative time, increased blood loss and donor site morbidity.
                Radiological and clinical parameters demonstrated that spinal fusion is not necessary in long segment posterior instrumentation for the management of thoracolumbar burst fractures.

Inputs.Title: Posterior fixation of thoracolumbar burst fracture: short-segment pedicle fixation versus long-segment instrumentation.
Inputs.Abstract:
The treatment of thoracolumbar burst fracture is a controversial issue. Short-segment (SS) pedicle fixation has become a popular treatment option. However, there are several studies regarding the high rate of failure. The aim of this prospective study was to compare SS versus long-segment (LS) instrumentation.
                For this purpose, 18 consecutive patients were assigned to two groups. Group 1 included nine patients treated by SS pedicle fixation, whereas group 2 included nine patients treated by LS instrumentation. SS instrumentation was pedicle fixation one level above and below the fractured vertebra. LS instrumentation was hook fixation (claw hooks attached to second upper vertebra and infralaminar hooks attached to first upper vertebra) above and pedicle fixation (pedicle screws attached to first and second lower vertebrae) below the fractured vertebra.
                As a result, measurements of local kyphosis, sagittal index, and anterior vertebral height compression showed that the LS group had a better outcome at final follow-up (P < 0.05). Also, the SS group had a 55% failure rate, whereas the LS group had prolonged operative time and increased blood loss. However, there was no difference between the two groups according to Low Back Outcome Score.
                In conclusion, radiographic parameters demonstrated that LS instrumentation is a more effective management of thoracolumbar burst fractures. Nevertheless, clinical outcome was the same between the two groups. However, our conclusions were based on posterior-only surgery. Anterior column support would negate the need for LS fixation. Also, SS would have been more successful if two above and two below pedicle screws were used.

Inputs.Title: Is fusion necessary for surgically treated burst fractures of the thoracolumbar and lumbar spine?: a prospective, randomized study.
Inputs.Abstract:
A prospective clinical trial was conducted.
                To compare the results of fusion versus nonfusion for surgically treated burst fractures of the thoracolumbar and lumbar spine.
                The operative results of surgically treated burst fractures with short segmental fixation have been well documented. There is no report comparing the results of fusion and nonfusion.
                Fifty-eight patients were included in this study, with the inclusion criteria as follows: neurologically intact spine with a kyphotic angle > or = 20 degrees, decreased vertebral body height > or = 50% or a canal compromise > or = 50%, incomplete neurologic deficit with a canal compromise 50%, complete neurologic deficit, and multilevel spinal injury or multiple traumas. All patients were randomly assigned to fusion or nonfusion groups, and operative treatment with posterior reduction and instrumentation was carried out. Posterior fusion with autogenous bone graft was performed for the fusion group (n = 30), and no fusion procedure was done for the nonfusion group (n = 28). The average follow-up period was 41 months (range, 24-71 months).
                The average loss of kyphotic angle was not statistically significant between these 2 groups. The radiographic parameters were statistically significantly better in the nonfusion group, including angular change in the flexion-extension lateral view (4.8 degrees vs. 1.0 degrees), lost correction of decreased vertebral body height (3.6% vs. 8.3%), intraoperative estimated blood loss (303 mL vs. 572 mL), and operative time (162 minutes vs. 224 minutes). The scores on the low back outcome scale were not statistically significant for these 2 groups.
                The short-term results of short segmental fixation without fusion for surgically treated burst fractures of the thoracolumbar spine were satisfactory. The advantages of instrumentation without fusion are the elimination of donor site complications, saving more motion segments, and reducing blood loss and operative time.

Inputs.Title: Short-segment pedicle instrumentation of thoracolumbar burst fractures: does transpedicular intracorporeal grafting prevent early failure?
Inputs.Abstract:
A prospective, randomized study comparing two treatment methods for thoracolumbar burst fractures: short-segment instrumentation with transpedicular grafting and the same procedure without transpedicular grafting.
                To evaluate the efficacy of transpedicular grafting in preventing failure of short-segment fixation for the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures.
                Short-segment pedicle instrumentation for thoracolumbar burst fractures is known to fail early because of the absence of anterior support. Additional transpedicular grafting has been offered as an alternative to prevent this failure. However, there is controversy about the results of transpedicular grafting.
                Twenty patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures were included in the study. The inclusion criterion was the presence of fractures through the T11-L3 vertebrae without neurologic compromise. The patients were randomized by a simple method into two groups. Group 1 patients were treated using short-segment instrumentation with transpedicular grafting (TPG) (n = 10), and Group 2 patients were treated by short-segment fixation alone (NTPG) (n = 10). Clinical (Likert's questionnaire) and radiologic (sagittal index, percentage of anterior body height compression, and local kyphosis) outcomes were analyzed.
                The two groups were similar in age, follow-up period, and severity of the deformity and fracture. The postoperative and follow-up sagittal index, percentage of anterior body height compression, and average correction loss in local kyphosis in both groups were not significantly different. The failure rate, defined as an increase of 10 degrees or more in local kyphosis and/or screw breakage, was also not significantly different (TPG = 50%, NTPG = 40%, P = 0.99).
                Short-segment transpedicular instrumentation of thoracolumbar burst fractures is associated with a high rate of failure that cannot be decreased by additional transpedicular intracorporeal grafting.

Inputs.Title: Transpedicular fixation in management of thoracolumbar burst fractures: monosegmental fixation versus short-segment instrumentation.
Inputs.Abstract:
A prospective clinical trial was conducted.
                To compare the clinical and radiologic late results of monosegmental transpedicular fixation versus short-segment pedicle instrumentation (SSPI) in management of thoracolumbar burst fractures and evaluate the efficacy of monosegmental transpedicular fixation.
                SSPI (1 level above and 1 below the fracture level) are accepted by many surgeons as an accepted technique for the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures. To preserve more motion segments, some authors have advocated monosegmental pedicle instrumentation (MSPI). The recent developments showed that MSPI yielded good clinical results; however, there were no report about comparison of clinical outcome between monosegmental and biosegmental transpedicular fixation in management of thoracolumbar burst fractures.
                Eighty-five patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures fulfilling the inclusion criteria were included in the study. The patients were randomized by a simple method into 2 groups. Group 1 were treated with monosegmental transpedicular fixation (n = 47), and group 2 were treated with biosegmental transpedicular fixation (n = 38). Clinical (Low Back Outcome Score and Oswestry Disability Index) and radiologic (load-sharing classification index, sagittal index, and percentage of anterior body height compression) outcomes were analyzed.
                The 2 groups were similar in age, follow-up period, and severity of the deformity and fracture. The postoperative and follow-up sagittal index, local kyphosis, percentage of anterior body height compression, and average correction loss in local kyphosis in both groups were not significantly different. The failure rate between the 2 surgical approaches was also not significantly different (group 1 = 6.38% and group 2 = 5.26%). Oswestry Disability Index improved in both groups by >25 points in a similar amount (P = 0.23). The average follow-up Low Back Outcome Score was 74.9 and 60.2 for group 1 and group 2, respectively (P = 0.033).
                In conclusion, radiologic parameters demonstrated that both MSPI and SSPI are the effective and reliable operative techniques for selected thoracolumbar burst fractures. MSPI shortened the operative time and decreased the amount of blood loss significantly and, thus, offered better clinical results. Nevertheless, long-term studies are supposed to be performed to support the outcomes.

Inputs.Title: Posterior short-segment fixation with or without fusion for thoracolumbar burst fractures. a five to seven-year prospective randomized study.
Inputs.Abstract:
The impact of fusion as a supplement to short-segment instrumentation for the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures is unclear. We conducted a controlled clinical trial to define the effect of fusion on lumbar spine and patient-related functional outcomes.
                From 2000 to 2002, seventy-three consecutive patients with a single-level Denis type-B burst fracture involving the thoracolumbar spine and a load-sharing score of <or=6 were managed with posterior pedicle screw instrumentation. The patients were followed for at least five years after surgery and were assessed with regard to clinical and radiographic outcomes. Radiographic outcomes were assessed on the basis of the local kyphosis angle and loss of kyphosis correction.
