effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is one-to-one dietary interventions for dietary behaviour?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is one-to-one dietary interventions for dietary behaviour?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
I looked at randomized or controlled studies where people received individualized (one‑to‑one) counselling or advice about diet or diet-related habits, and compared their outcomes with usual care or no counselling. I focused on actual behaviour change (what people ate, drank, or did) and any biological outcomes reflecting diet (like cavity‑causing bacteria or new tooth decay).

- **Full Answer**:  
One‑to‑one dietary interventions show clear, though variable, benefits for changing diet‑related behaviour.  

In denture‑wearers, two individualized nutrition counselling sessions led to a large increase in fruit and vegetable intake (about 209 g/day more) compared with almost no change in usual care (+26 g/day) and more people progressed to actively changing their diet [2]. Personalized dental‑health instruction improved attitudes and several reported hygiene behaviours 6–12 months later compared with no instruction [1]. Individual advice to restrict sugar reduced cavity‑causing bacteria in saliva and plaque during the 6‑week advice period, although levels rose partly once advice ended, suggesting effects may fade without support [3]. A single nurse‑delivered motivational session after alcohol‑related injury significantly reduced alcohol intake and the proportion of hazardous drinkers over one year versus usual care [4]. Intensive, tailored oral‑health and dietary counselling, combined with other measures, reduced new tooth decay by 44% over 3.4 years [5].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across these studies, one-to-one counseling or instruction generally *improved* diet-related behaviors or their consequences, rather than being ineffective. Personal dental-hygiene instruction led to better attitudes and several self-reported behaviors compared with no instruction 6–12 months later [1]. Two short, tailored nutrition-counseling visits increased fruit and vegetable intake by about 180 g/day more than usual care and helped more people move into an “action” stage of change [2]. Asking high-sugar users to restrict sugar led to measurable reductions in cavity-causing bacteria, although some of this benefit faded after advice stopped [3]. A more intensive, individualized program combining dietary and hygiene counseling with other measures cut new tooth decay in children by about 44% over 3.4 years compared with standard care [5]. Overall, one-to-one interventions are moderately effective but not perfect; benefits may lessen over time without ongoing support.

- **Full Answer**:  
Available evidence does not show that one-to-one dietary interventions are ineffective; instead, they produce meaningful but imperfect improvements in dietary behavior and related health outcomes.

Personal dental-hygiene instruction improved attitudes and several self-reported behaviors compared with no instruction, sustained over 6–12 months [1]. Tailored nutrition counseling in denture-wearers raised fruit and vegetable intake by about 180 g/day more than standard care and helped more participants progress to actively changing their diet [2]. Advising frequent sugar users to restrict sugar intake reduced levels of cavity-causing bacteria, though some benefit declined after the advice period ended [3]. In children at high risk of tooth decay, an individually designed program including dietary counseling and other noninvasive measures reduced new decay surfaces by about 44% versus usual prevention over 3.4 years [5].  

These findings suggest one-to-one interventions can change diet-related behavior, but effects vary by intensity and may weaken once counseling stops.

efficacy.positive_question: Does one-to-one dietary interventions work for dietary behaviour?
efficacy.negative_question: Does one-to-one dietary interventions not work for dietary behaviour?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The key evidence comes from randomized controlled trials testing individual (one‑to‑one) dietary counseling. These show that when people receive tailored advice and support, they do change what they eat, at least over weeks to a few years. The clearest outcomes are increased fruit and vegetable intake and reduced sugar use. Some effects weaken after counseling stops, and in one trial the diet advice was part of a larger prevention package, so the specific contribution of diet counseling is less certain. Overall, the studies consistently point in the same direction: brief, personalized counseling can improve specific dietary behaviors, especially when it is tailored and reinforced.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. One‑to‑one, tailored dietary counseling has been shown to improve dietary behavior. In denture‑wearers, two individualized counseling sessions led to much larger increases in fruit and vegetable intake (+209 g/day) and more people moving into an “action” stage of change than standard care [2]. Personalized advice to reduce sugar intake resulted in meaningful short‑term reductions in sugar‑related bacteria, reflecting improved sugar‑eating patterns, though some effect faded after advice stopped [3]. In children with active tooth decay, an individually designed, patient‑centered program including dietary counseling and other preventive measures cut new decay surfaces by about 44% over 3.4 years, suggesting sustained behavior change within a broader program [5]. Overall, these trials indicate that brief, one‑to‑one dietary interventions can effectively change specific eating behaviors, particularly when advice is tailored and reinforced over time [2][3][5].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies include several one‑to‑one or highly individualized interventions. Tailored nutrition counseling for denture wearers clearly improved fruit and vegetable intake compared with usual care [2]. An individually designed, patient‑centered program that included dietary counseling reduced tooth decay over several years versus standard prevention alone [5]. Short‑term sugar‑restriction advice led to measurable biological changes in the mouth consistent with reduced sugar intake, although effects partially faded after the restriction period ended [3]. Together, these indicate that one‑to‑one dietary interventions can change dietary behavior, especially while support is ongoing.

- **Full Answer**:  
One‑to‑one dietary interventions do work for changing dietary behavior, at least in the short to medium term.  

In denture‑wearing adults, two individual counseling sessions led to a much larger increase in fruit and vegetable intake than standard care (+209 g/day vs +26 g/day) [2].  

Among children with active tooth decay, an individually designed, patient‑centered program that included dietary counseling cut new decay by about 44% compared with standard public clinic care [5].  

In another trial, people advised to restrict sugar between meals showed reduced levels of decay‑causing bacteria, suggesting real changes in sugar intake; some of this benefit diminished after the restriction ended, showing that continued support matters [3].  

Overall, these studies indicate that one‑to‑one dietary interventions can meaningfully improve dietary behavior, though ongoing or repeated support may be needed to maintain changes over time [2][3][5].

safety.positive_question: Is one-to-one dietary interventions safe for dietary behaviour?
safety.negative_question: Is one-to-one dietary interventions dangerous for dietary behaviour?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Randomized trials show that one‑to‑one counseling about diet or related habits changes behavior in healthier directions with no reported harms. Tailored nutrition counseling for denture wearers increased fruit and vegetable intake substantially, with no adverse effects mentioned [2]. Individual sugar‑reduction advice reduced decay‑causing mouth bacteria, again without reports of under‑nutrition or other problems [3]. A personalized preventive program for children, including dietary counseling, safely cut new tooth decay nearly in half over several years [5]. These interventions were brief, delivered by professionals, and promoted moderate, balanced changes rather than extreme dieting. However, the studies did not specifically look for rare harms like disordered eating.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on the available trials, one‑to‑one dietary interventions appear safe for dietary behavior and can improve it. Personalized nutrition counseling increased healthy food intake without reported negative effects [2]. Individual advice to reduce sugar safely lowered harmful oral bacteria [3]. A child‑focused program combining oral hygiene and dietary counseling significantly reduced tooth decay over 3.4 years, with no harms noted [5]. Overall, these studies suggest that professionally delivered, moderate, one‑to‑one dietary counseling is safe and beneficial for dietary behavior, though rare adverse effects were not systematically assessed.
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: The articles describe several one-to-one or highly individualized counselling or instruction programmes. Personal dental health instruction improved attitudes and self‑reported oral health behaviours compared with no instruction, without any sign of harm [1]. Tailored nutrition counselling for denture wearers led to higher fruit and vegetable intake and more readiness to improve diet, again with no reported negative effects [2]. Individual counselling on reducing sugar intake lowered cavity‑causing bacteria in the mouth [3], and a personalised, resource‑focused prevention program in children significantly reduced new tooth decay [5]. None of the studies reported worsening of diet, new unhealthy behaviours, or other safety problems related to the one‑to‑one approach.  

- **Full Answer**: Based on these studies, one‑to‑one dietary or health‑related counselling is not dangerous for dietary behaviour. Instead, it tends to improve health habits and outcomes, such as better oral hygiene [1,5], higher fruit and vegetable intake [2], and lower cavity‑causing bacteria [3] overall.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing one-to-one dietary interventions is good for dietary behaviour?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing one-to-one dietary interventions is harmful for dietary behaviour?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks whether there is scientific evidence that one-to-one (individual) dietary interventions improve dietary behaviour. I looked for randomized or controlled studies in the provided summaries that used individualized counseling or advice and then measured actual changes in diet or closely related outcomes. One article reports tailored nutrition counseling and directly measures fruit and vegetable intake. Another uses an individualized, patient-centered program including dietary counseling and shows reduced tooth decay, which reflects better long-term sugar and hygiene behaviour. A third gives individual sugar-restriction advice and shows biological markers consistent with changed eating patterns. Together, these support that one-to-one dietary interventions can improve dietary behaviour, although most evidence here is from dental and oral-health settings.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. Several controlled studies show that one-to-one dietary counseling can improve people’s eating habits.  

In denture-wearing adults, two individual nutrition counseling sessions tailored to the person led to much larger increases in fruit and vegetable intake (about +209 grams per day) compared with usual care (+26 grams per day) over six weeks [2]. More people in the counseling group also moved into an “action” stage of actively changing their diet [2].  

In another trial with children at high risk of tooth decay, an individually designed, patient‑centered program that included dietary counseling and other preventive measures cut new tooth decay by about 44% compared with standard care over 3.4 years [5], indicating sustained behavior change around sugar and oral hygiene.  

A small trial where people were advised one‑to‑one to restrict sugar between meals showed clear biological signs that they followed this advice, with marked reductions in decay‑causing bacteria over time [3].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across the listed studies, individualized or small‑group counseling and advice either improved behavior or had no reported negative effects. Dental health counseling improved attitudes and several reported hygiene behaviors compared with no instruction [1]. Tailored one‑to‑one nutrition counseling for denture wearers led to a large increase in fruit and vegetable intake compared with standard care [2]. Personalized advice to restrict sugar effectively reduced harmful oral bacteria, with partial rebound after advice ended but still better than baseline, not worse [3]. A broader preventive program including individualized dietary and hygiene counseling in children significantly reduced dental decay over several years compared with usual care [5]. None of these trials report any worsening of diet or related behaviors.  

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on the studies provided, there is no evidence that one‑to‑one or tailored dietary interventions are harmful to dietary behavior. Instead, these interventions generally improve outcomes. Individualized dental health instruction improved attitudes and self‑reported hygiene behaviors versus no instruction [1]. Tailored dietary counseling for denture wearers markedly increased fruit and vegetable intake compared with standard care [2]. Advice to reduce sugar intake lowered levels of cavity‑causing bacteria without causing worse behaviors after the restriction period ended [3]. An individualized, patient‑centered program including dietary counseling significantly reduced new dental decay in children versus routine preventive care [5]. None of the studies report harm or deterioration in diet; effects were either beneficial or, after counseling stopped, moved partly back toward baseline but not below it [3].  

Thus, within these data, one‑to‑one dietary interventions are not shown to be harmful and are often beneficial for dietary behavior.

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is one-to-one dietary interventions a good choice for dietary behaviour?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is one-to-one dietary interventions a bad choice for dietary behaviour?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
One-to-one counseling lets advice be tailored to your habits, health, and motivation. In denture-wearers, just two personalized nutrition sessions greatly increased fruit and vegetable intake compared with usual care, and more people moved into an “action” stage of change, showing real behavior shift [2]. In schoolchildren, an individually designed, patient-centered program including dietary counseling cut new tooth decay by about 44%, indicating better long‑term control of sugary foods and oral hygiene [5]. Personal instruction has also improved health-related attitudes and self-reported behaviors in other settings [1]. When people were asked to restrict sugar, oral bacteria linked to decay dropped, but some benefits faded after stopping, suggesting that follow-up support helps maintain changes [3]. Overall, the evidence supports one-to-one interventions as an effective and reasonable choice if you want to improve your diet, especially when they’re tailored, goal‑focused, and include some ongoing contact.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. One-to-one dietary interventions appear to be a good choice for improving dietary behavior. In people receiving new dentures, two tailored counseling sessions led to a large increase in fruit and vegetable intake compared with standard care, and more participants progressed from “thinking about change” to actually changing their diet [2]. Among children at high risk of tooth decay, an individually designed, patient-centered program with dietary counseling and other preventive measures reduced new cavities by about 44% over 3.4 years, which strongly suggests better control of sugary food and drink habits [5]. Personal health instruction has also been shown to improve attitudes and self-reported health behaviors in other oral health settings [1]. When people were guided to restrict sugar, harmful mouth bacteria dropped, although some benefits lessened after advice stopped, indicating that continued or follow‑up support is helpful [3]. So, if you need to decide quickly, one‑to‑one dietary counseling is a reasonable and evidence‑supported choice.
timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Evidence from several randomized trials shows that one‑to‑one counseling can improve diet‑related behaviors rather than being a “bad” option. A longer, individualized program combining dietary counseling with other preventive measures cut new tooth decay by about 44% over 3.4 years [5].  

These studies show one‑to‑one dietary interventions can meaningfully improve diet‑related behaviors, though benefits are not perfect and may fade without continued support somewhat.

- **Rationale**:  
  Across these trials, people who received individualized dietary or related counseling changed their behavior and health outcomes more than those who did not. This suggests one‑to‑one interventions are helpful, not ineffective or dangerous.

- **Full Answer**:  
  The studies summarized here do **not** show that one‑to‑one dietary interventions are ineffective. In adults given a 30‑minute personal dental‑hygiene session, attitudes and several self‑reported behaviors were significantly better 6–12 months later than in people with no instruction [1]. In denture‑wearers, two tailored nutrition‑counseling visits increased fruit and vegetable intake by about **209 g/day**, compared with just **26 g/day** in usual care [2]. Individual advice to reduce sugar led to clear reductions in cavity‑causing bacteria, still lower than baseline 6 weeks after the restriction ended [3]. A personalized, patient‑centered prevention program with dietary counseling cut new tooth decay in children by about **44%** versus standard care over 3.4 years [5].  

  These data indicate one‑to‑one dietary interventions can meaningfully improve behavior and health, though results vary by person and program.

ReviewTitle: Mupirocin ointment for preventing Staphylococcus aureus infections in nasal carriers

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is the leading nosocomial (hospital acquired) pathogen in hospitals throughout the world. Traditionally, control of S. aureus has been focused on preventing cross-infection between patients, however, it has been shown repeatedly that a large proportion of nosocomial S. aureus infections originate from the patient's own flora. Nasal carriage of S. aureus is now considered a well defined risk factor for subsequent infection in various groups of patients. Local antibiotic treatment with mupirocin ointment is often used to eradicate nasal S. aureus.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To determine whether the use of mupirocin nasal ointment in patients with identified S. aureus nasal carriage reduced S. aureus infection rates.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: For this first update we searched the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register (searched 9 September 2010); The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) - The Cochrane Library 2010 Issue 3; Ovid MEDLINE (2007 to September Week 1 2010); Ovid MEDLINE (In-Process & Other Non-Indexed Citations, September 10, 2010);Ovid EMBASE (2007 to 2010 Week 36); and EBSCO CINAHL (2007 to 10 September 2010). No language or publication restrictions were applied.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing nasal mupirocin with no treatment or placebo or alternative nasal treatment in the prevention of S. aureus infections in nasal S. aureus carriers were included.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Titles, abstracts and full-text articles of studies retrieved from the search process were independently assessed by two authors for inclusion. From included studies a data extraction form was made and the quality of the trial was assessed. The primary outcome was the S. aureus infection rate (any site). Secondary outcomes were time to infection, mortality, adverse events and infection rate caused by micro-organisms other than S. aureus.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text:
Nine RCTs involving 3396 participants met the inclusion criteria. Patient populations varied and several types of nosocomial S. aureus infection were described including bacteraemia, exit-site infections, peritonitis, respiratory tract infections, skin infections, surgical site infections (SSI) and urinary tract infections. After pooling the eight studies that compared mupirocin with placebo or with no treatment, there was a statistically significant reduction in the rate of S. aureus infection associated with intranasal mupirocin (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.70). 

A planned subgroup analysis of surgical trials demonstrated a significant reduction in the rate of nosocomial S. aureus infection rate associated with mupirocin use (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.89) however this effect disappeared if the analysis only included surgical site infections caused by S. aureus (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.04), possibly due to a lack of power. The infection rate caused by micro-organisms other than S. aureus was significantly higher in patients treated with mupirocin compared with control patients (RR 1.38 95% CI 1.118 to 1.72).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: In people who are nasal carriers of S. aureus, the use of mupirocin ointment results in a statistically significant reduction in S. aureus infections.

Inputs.Title: The influence of calcium mupirocin nasal ointment on the incidence of Staphylococcus aureus infections in haemodialysis patients.
Inputs.Abstract: Mupirocin was used in haemodialysis patients in an attempt to eradicate nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus and to prevent infection caused by this microorganism. The effectiveness of calcium mupirocin as a 2% nasal ointment OB2 (16 patients for 104 patient-months) was compared to that of placebo (18 patients for 147 patient-months) in a double-blind study. Mupirocin or placebo were applied in both anterior nares thrice daily for 2 weeks and subsequently three times weekly for a total of 9 months. During therapy, S. aureus was recovered from only 6% of the nasal cultures in the mupirocin group compared to 58% in the placebo group (P less than or equal to 0.01). Only one S. aureus infection was documented in the mupirocin group compared to six in the placebo group (P less than or equal to 0.05). The S. aureus strain causing the single infection in the mupirocin group was of a different phage type to that of the original nasal strain. In contrast, at least four of the six strains causing infection in the placebo group were of similar phage type to the original nasal strain. All S. aureus isolates remained mupirocin sensitive (MIC less than or equal to 1 mg/l). In conclusion, mupirocin nasal ointment was effective in eradicating nasal carriage of S. aureus and in preventing S. aureus infections in patients on haemodialysis.

Inputs.Title: Nasal mupirocin prevents Staphylococcus aureus exit-site infection during peritoneal dialysis. Mupirocin Study Group.
Inputs.Abstract: A total of 1144 patients receiving continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis in nine European centers was screened for nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus. Two hundred sixty-seven subjects were defined as carriers of S. aureus by having had at least two positive swab results from samples taken on separate occasions, and were randomly allocated to treatment or control groups. Members of each group used a nasal ointment twice daily for 5 consecutive days every 4 wk. The treatment group used calcium mupirocin 2% (Bactroban nasal; SmithKline Beecham, Welwyn Garden City, United Kingdom) and the control group used placebo ointment. Patients were followed-up for a maximum period of 18 months. There were 134 individuals in the mupirocin group, and 133 individuals acted as control subjects. There were no differences in demographic data, cause of renal failure, type of catheter, system used, or method of exit-site care between the groups. Similarly, there were no differences in patient outcome or incidence of adverse events between both groups. Nasal carriage fell to 10% in those subjects who received active treatment and 48% in those who used the placebo ointment. There were 55 exit-site infections in 1236 patient-months in the control group and 33 in 1390 patient-months in the treatment group (not significant). S. aureus caused 14 episodes of exit-site infection in the mupirocin group and 44 in the control group (P = 0.006, mixed effects Poisson regression model). There were no differences in the rate of tunnel infection or peritonitis. There was no evidence of a progressive increase in resistance to mupirocin with time. Regular use of nasal mupirocin in continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients who are nasal carriers of S. aureus significantly reduces the rate of exit-site infections that occurs because of this organism.

Inputs.Title: Impact of treating Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriers on wound infections in cardiac surgery.
Inputs.Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of postoperative wound infections, and nasal colonization by this organism is an important factor in the development of infections. Treatment with mupirocin can eradicate the organism in the short term, and prophylactic treatment of colonized patients may prevent postoperative S. aureus infections. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial was performed to determine whether nasal mupirocin administered pre-operatively to S. aureus carriers reduces the rates of sternal and leg wound infections after cardiac surgery. The study enrolled 263 patients with nasal S. aureus undergoing elective cardiac surgery at St. Michael's Hospital, Toronto, Canada. Patients were assessed for infections in the immediate postoperative period and two months later. Two hundred and fifty-seven patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis and re-analysed according to the actual treatment applied. Wound infections occurred in 17 (13.5%) mupirocin recipients and 11 (9.1%) placebo recipients (P=0.319), with seven (5.4%) and six (4.7%) sternal infections, respectively. Two (1.6%) wound infections were acquired postoperatively in the mupirocin group, neither of which were caused by S. aureus. The placebo group had three (2.4%) nosocomial wound infections, with two (1.6%) S. aureus bacteraemias (P=0.243). Among patients receiving mupirocin, 106 (81.5%) cleared S. aureus compared with 59 (46.5%) patients receiving placebo (P<0.0001). There was no significant difference between intention-to-treat and actual treatment groups. Prophylactic intranasal mupirocin administered to S. aureus carriers did not reduce the rates of overall surgical site infections by S. aureus, and only showed a trend towards decreased incidence of nosocomial S. aureus infections.

Inputs.Title: Mupirocin prophylaxis against nosocomial Staphylococcus aureus infections in nonsurgical patients: a randomized study.
Inputs.Abstract:
Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriage is a major risk factor for nosocomial S. aureus infection. Studies show that intranasal mupirocin can prevent nosocomial surgical site infections. No data are available on the efficacy of mupirocin in nonsurgical patients.
                To assess the efficacy of mupirocin prophylaxis in preventing nosocomial S. aureus infections in nonsurgical patients.
                Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
                3 tertiary care academic hospitals and 1 nonacademic hospital.
                1602 culture-proven S. aureus carriers hospitalized in nonsurgical departments.
                Therapy with mupirocin 2% nasal ointment (n = 793) or placebo ointment (n = 809), twice daily for 5 days, started 1 to 3 days after admission.
                Nosocomial S. aureus infections according to defined criteria, in-hospital mortality, duration of hospitalization, and time to nosocomial S. aureus infection. Staphylococcus aureus isolates were genotyped to assess whether infection was caused by endogenous strains.
                The mupirocin and placebo groups did not statistically differ in the rates of nosocomial S. aureus infections (mupirocin, 2.6%; placebo, 2.8%; risk difference, 0.2 percentage point [95% CI, -1.5 to 1.9 percentage points]), mortality (mupirocin, 3.0%; placebo, 2.8%; risk difference, -0.2 percentage point [CI, -1.9 to 1.5 percentage points]), or duration of hospitalization (median for both, 8 days). However, time to nosocomial S. aureus infection was decreased in the mupirocin group from 12 to 25 days (P > 0.2). A total of 77% of S. aureus nosocomial infections were endogenous.
                A few infections in both groups may have been missed because investigators assessed a patient for infection only if microbiology culture results were positive for S. aureus.
                Routine culture for S. aureus nasal carriage at admission and subsequent mupirocin application does not provide effective prophylaxis against nosocomial S. aureus infections in nonsurgical patients.

Inputs.Title: Surgical site infections in orthopedic surgery: the effect of mupirocin nasal ointment in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study.
Inputs.Abstract: The objective of this study was to determine whether use of mupirocin nasal ointment for perioperative eradication of Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriage is effective in preventing the development of surgical site infections (SSIs). A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design was used. Either mupirocin or placebo nasal ointment was applied twice daily to 614 assessable patients from the day of admission to the hospital until the day of surgery. A total of 315 and 299 patients were randomized to receive mupirocin and placebo, respectively. Eradication of nasal carriage was significantly more effective in the mupirocin group (eradication rate, 83.5% versus 27.8%). In the mupirocin group, the rate of endogenous S. aureus infections was 5 times lower than in the placebo group (0.3% and 1.7%, respectively; relative risk, 0.19; 95% confidence interval, 0.02-1.62). Mupirocin nasal ointment did not reduce the SSI rate (by S. aureus) or the duration of hospital stay.

Inputs.Title: Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial to evaluate the efficacy of mupirocin for eradicating carriage of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Inputs.Abstract: Mupirocin has been widely used for the clearance of nasal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) carriage during outbreaks, but no placebo-controlled trial has evaluated its value for eradicating MRSA carriage at multiple body sites in settings where MRSA is not epidemic. In a 1,500-bed teaching hospital with endemic MRSA, 102 patients colonized with MRSA were randomized into a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial and treated with either mupirocin (group M) or placebo (group P) applied to the anterior nares for 5 days; both groups used chlorhexidine soap for body washing. Follow-up screening, susceptibility testing, and genotyping were performed to evaluate treatment success, mupirocin or chlorhexidine resistance, and exogenous recolonization. At baseline, MRSA carriage was 60% in the nares, 38% in the groin, and 62% in other sites (skin lesions, urine). The MRSA eradication rate (all body sites) was 25% in group M (12 of 48 patients), compared to 18% in group P (9 of 50 patients; relative risk [RR], 0.72; 95% confidence interval [CI95], 0.33 to 1.55). At the end of follow-up, 44% of patients (19 of 43) were free of nasal MRSA in group M, compared to 23% (11 of 44) in group P (RR, 0.57; CI95, 0.31 to 1.04). Ten patients developed MRSA infections (three in group M and seven in group P). One mupirocin treatment failure was due to exogenous MRSA recolonization. No MRSA isolate showed chlorhexidine resistance or high-level mupirocin resistance; however, we observed an association (P = 0.003) between low-level mupirocin resistance at study entry (prevalence, 23%) and subsequent treatment failure in both study arms. These results suggest that nasal mupirocin is only marginally effective in the eradication of multisite MRSA carriage in a setting where MRSA is endemic.

Inputs.Title: [Use of nasal mupirocin for Staphylococcus aureus: effect on nasal carriers and nosocomial infections].
Inputs.Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is the agent of community-acquired and nosocomial infections. Twenty to 35% of the population permanently carries it in the nose and oropharynx, and additional 50%, carries it intermittently. Topical calcium mupirocin is an antibacterial agent against Staphylococcus aureus recommended to eradicate nasal and hand colonization in patients and health care workers. The prevalence of nasal S. aureus was determined in patients undergoing cardiovascular surgery. In addition, the effect of mupirocine on the number of carriers and rate of nosocomial infections was evaluated. An experimental prospective study was undertaken with two groups of patients: one treated with mupirocin (n = 96), and the other without treatment (n = 95). Tests for presence of nasal S. aureus and nosocomial infections were conducted in all patients. A 34% prevalence of S. aureus carriers was found. A decrease of the prevalence was found in both treated (87%) and untreated patients (33%), but in significantly different proportions (p = 0.0002, RR = 0.22, 95%CI = 0.09-0.054). This result demonstrated the effectiveness of a mupirocin treatment program to decrease numbers of nasal carriers. With regard to nosocomial infection, S. aureus prevalence was 3.6%, occurring mostly in control patients (6 of 7). Total nosocomial infection prevalence was 17.3%, evenly distributed in treated and untreated patients. This suggested that mupirocin use did not decrease the number of nosocomial infections.

Inputs.Title: Intranasal mupirocin to prevent postoperative Staphylococcus aureus infections.
Inputs.Abstract:
Patients with nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus have an increased risk of surgical-site infections caused by that organism. Treatment with mupirocin ointment can reduce the rate of nasal carriage and may prevent postoperative S. aureus infections.
                We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to determine whether intranasal treatment with mupirocin reduces the rate of S. aureus infections at surgical sites and prevents other nosocomial infections.
                Of 4030 enrolled patients who underwent general, gynecologic, neurologic, or cardiothoracic surgery, 3864 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. Overall, 2.3 percent of mupirocin recipients and 2.4 percent of placebo recipients had S. aureus infections at surgical sites. Of the 891 patients (23.1 percent of the 3864 who completed the study) who had S. aureus in their anterior nares, 444 received mupirocin and 447 received placebo. Among the patients with nasal carriage of S. aureus, 4.0 percent of those who received mupirocin had nosocomial S. aureus infections, as compared with 7.7 percent of those who received placebo (odds ratio for infection, 0.49; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.25 to 0.92; P=0.02).
                Prophylactic intranasal application of mupirocin did not significantly reduce the rate of S. aureus surgical-site infections overall, but it did significantly decrease the rate of all nosocomial S. aureus infections among the patients who were S. aureus carriers.

Inputs.Title: Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriers in CAPD with mupirocin.
Inputs.Abstract: We have studied the efficacy of topical Mupirocin for elimination of Staphylococcus aureus (Staph. aureus) nasal carriage in CAPD patients. Staph. aureus nasal carriers in our CAPD program were randomized to one of two groups: Group 1, treated with Mupirocin, and Group 2, treated with neomycin sulphate nasal ointment. The prevalence of Staph. aureus nasal colonization was 44% for patients (24/54) and 17% for dialysis partners (5/29). Group 1 included 11 patients and 1 partner, and Group 2, 8 patients and 2 partners. In Group 1, the eradication rate was 100%, and the recolonization rate was 0, 8, 41, 55 and 66% at 1, 2, 3, 6 and 10 months. In Group 2, the eradication rate was 40%, with a recolonization rate of 0.25 and 75% at 1, 2 and 3 months. Re-treatment with mupirocin was successful in 66% of the cases, compared to 20% for neomycin. The MIC90 of mupirocin for Staph. aureus was 0.5 mcg/mL, with an increase to 4 mcg/mL towards the end of the study. During the study period, there was a very low incidence of Staph. aureus peritonitis or catheter-related infections in patients treated with mupirocin. Secondary effects of mupirocin were negligible. Mupirocin is more effective than neomycin sulphate for the elimination of Staph. aureus nasal colonization in patients undergoing CAPD. Periodic re-treatment is frequently necessary, given the significant recolonization rate.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is mupirocin ointment for S. aureus infections?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is mupirocin ointment for S. aureus infections?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across studies, mupirocin ointment in the nose is very good at temporarily clearing Staphylococcus aureus from the nostrils, which are a major “reservoir” for this germ. In many trials, 80–100% of treated people cleared nasal carriage shortly after treatment, versus about 30–50% with placebo or other ointments [1][3][5][7][9]. However, clearing the nose does not always translate into fewer infections. Clear benefits were seen in some high‑risk groups (especially dialysis patients and known carriers), but large trials in general surgical or nonsurgical hospital patients showed little or no overall reduction in S. aureus infections [3][4][5][7][8]. It is less effective for widespread (multisite) MRSA colonization [6]. Over time, people often become re‑colonized and may need repeat treatment [9]. Resistance can occur but was usually low and uncommon in the short term [1][2][6].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin nasal ointment is very effective at *temporarily* removing S. aureus from the nose. In multiple studies, 80–100% of carriers cleared nasal S. aureus soon after treatment, compared with about 30–50% using placebo or other ointments [1][3][5][7][9].  

Its ability to actually *prevent infections* is more limited and depends on the patient group:  

- In hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients who are carriers, regular nasal mupirocin markedly reduced S. aureus infections at access sites [1][2][9].  
- In surgical patients who are carriers, mupirocin lowered overall hospital S. aureus infections by about half, but did not clearly reduce surgical‑wound infections in all trials [3][5][7][8].  
- In general nonsurgical inpatients, routine screening and mupirocin did **not** significantly reduce S. aureus infections [4].  
- For patients colonized with MRSA at many body sites, nasal mupirocin was only marginally effective [6].  

Recolonization over months is common, so repeated courses may be needed, and low‑level resistance can reduce success [6][9].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across studies, mupirocin nasal ointment is very good at clearing Staphylococcus aureus from the nose, but its ability to actually prevent infections varies a lot. In several large, well‑designed trials, it did *not* significantly reduce overall S. aureus infections, even though carriage fell sharply. Benefits, when seen, were usually limited to specific high‑risk patients and were modest in absolute terms.

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin ointment is effective at reducing S. aureus in the nose, often clearing 80–90% of carriers in the short term [1,3,5,7,9]. However, in many patient groups this does **not** translate into a clear drop in infections.  

In large randomized trials of nonsurgical inpatients and broad surgical populations, infection rates with S. aureus were essentially unchanged between mupirocin and placebo (about 2–3% in both groups) [3,4,5,7,8]. One major study of carriers showed nosocomial S. aureus infections falling only from 7.7% to 4.0% (about a 4% absolute reduction) [8].  

For certain high‑risk groups, such as dialysis patients, mupirocin did cut some S. aureus infections markedly (e.g., 1 vs. 6 infections in a small hemodialysis trial; fewer exit‑site infections in peritoneal dialysis) [1,2,9].  

Overall, mupirocin is often **only mildly effective or ineffective** at preventing S. aureus infections outside these select high‑risk settings [3–5,7,8].

efficacy.positive_question: Does mupirocin ointment work for S. aureus infections?
efficacy.negative_question: Does mupirocin ointment not work for S. aureus infections?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is broad, but the articles mainly test mupirocin 2% ointment used inside the nose to clear *Staphylococcus aureus* (S. aureus) carriage and see if this prevents later infections. Across multiple trials, mupirocin is clearly effective at temporarily eliminating S. aureus from the nose. Whether that translates into fewer infections depends on the patient group: benefit is strong in some high‑risk dialysis patients and in surgical patients who are known S. aureus carriers, but not seen in all hospitalized patients or in all types of surgery. It is less effective when S. aureus is colonizing several body sites or has reduced susceptibility to mupirocin. Thus, mupirocin works well for decolonizing the nose and preventing certain S. aureus infections in selected high‑risk groups, but it is not a universal prevention or treatment for all S. aureus infections.

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin ointment is very good at killing *Staphylococcus aureus* that live inside the nose, which is a common source of later infection. In many studies, applying 2% mupirocin in the nostrils removed nasal *S. aureus* in most carriers (about 80–100%), compared with much lower rates using placebo or other ointments [1,3,5,7,9]. In some high‑risk groups, this clearly led to fewer *S. aureus* infections, such as in hemodialysis patients and people on peritoneal dialysis, where bloodstream or catheter‑site infections fell markedly [1,2,9]. Among surgical patients who were nasal carriers, mupirocin reduced overall hospital *S. aureus* infections, although its effect on surgical‑wound infections alone was small or inconsistent [3,5,7,8]. In large groups of nonsurgical in‑patients, routine mupirocin did not lower *S. aureus* infection rates [4]. It is only modestly effective when *S. aureus* is present at multiple body sites or already shows reduced mupirocin sensitivity [6]. Doctors limit use to short courses.
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Studies show that mupirocin ointment reliably kills *Staphylococcus aureus* living in the nose (“colonization”), especially in people on dialysis and some surgical patients [1][2][8][9]. In these high‑risk groups, this often leads to fewer *S. aureus* infections at catheter sites or other hospital‑acquired infections [1][2][8]. However, in broader hospital or surgical populations, using mupirocin on everyone did **not** clearly reduce all types of infections [3][4][5][7]. For methicillin‑resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA), mupirocin helped clear the nose in some patients, but was only modestly effective at clearing the bacteria from multiple body sites, and low‑level resistance reduced success [6]. Overall, mupirocin is effective for targeted decolonization of *S. aureus* carriers but is not a universal solution for all *S. aureus* infections.

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin ointment **does work** against *S. aureus*, especially for removing it from the nose (decolonization) in people who carry the bacteria there [1][2][8][9].  

In dialysis patients who were nasal carriers, regular intranasal mupirocin greatly lowered nasal carriage and reduced *S. aureus* infections at vascular or peritoneal catheter sites [1][2][9]. In surgical patients who were known carriers, mupirocin reduced overall hospital *S. aureus* infections, though not all surgical‑site infections [8].  

However, when used broadly in all nonsurgical inpatients or unselected surgical patients, mupirocin did **not** significantly reduce total hospital or wound infection rates [3][4][5][7]. For MRSA carriers with bacteria at many body sites, nasal mupirocin only modestly reduced overall carriage, and low‑level resistance limited its impact [6].  

So, mupirocin is useful and active against *S. aureus*, but its main role is targeted nasal decolonization in specific high‑risk carriers, not as a cure‑all for all *S. aureus* infections.

safety.positive_question: Is mupirocin ointment safe for S. aureus infections?
safety.negative_question: Is mupirocin ointment dangerous for S. aureus infections?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several clinical trials, mupirocin 2% nasal ointment was compared with placebo in people at high risk for Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infections, such as dialysis and surgical patients. In a large peritoneal dialysis study, patients using nasal mupirocin had fewer S. aureus exit‑site infections, and the rate of side effects was the same as with placebo, indicating good short‑term safety [1]. Another dialysis study found mupirocin eliminated nasal carriage and was more effective than neomycin, with “negligible” side effects [9]. Trials in surgical and hospitalized patients mainly focused on effectiveness, but did not report excess harm from mupirocin use [0][3][4][7]. Some studies noted that repeated use can select for low‑level mupirocin resistance, which may reduce its effectiveness over time, though high‑level resistance was not seen [6][9]. Overall, the evidence supports that mupirocin ointment is generally safe when used as directed, but it should not be overused.  

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin ointment (usually used inside the nose) has been studied in many patients at risk for S. aureus infections. In peritoneal dialysis patients, regular nasal mupirocin greatly reduced S. aureus exit‑site infections without increasing side effects compared with placebo, suggesting it is well tolerated [1]. In another dialysis study, mupirocin cleared nasal S. aureus more effectively than neomycin, and “secondary effects” (side effects) were described as negligible [9]. Other randomized trials in surgical and hospitalized patients did not find more adverse events in mupirocin users than in placebo groups, further supporting short‑term safety [0][3][4][7].  

However, repeated or widespread use can encourage the bacteria to develop resistance, which may make mupirocin less effective over time, even though high‑level resistance was not seen in these studies [6][9].  

Overall, mupirocin ointment appears safe for short‑term use against S. aureus when used as prescribed and for appropriate indications [1][6][9].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across multiple randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials in dialysis, surgical, and nonsurgical patients, intranasal mupirocin consistently reduced or cleared S. aureus from the nose and sometimes reduced related infections, without showing higher rates of side effects, deaths, or hospital stay compared with placebo [1–4][7–9]. In MRSA carriers, mupirocin was only modestly effective and low‑level resistance was linked to failure, but no serious (high‑level) resistance or harm was seen [6]. Overall, studies evaluate whether mupirocin helps, not whether it causes harm, and none suggest it is dangerous when used correctly.

- **Full Answer**:  
Mupirocin ointment does not appear dangerous for Staphylococcus aureus infections when used as directed, inside the nose to reduce “carrier” bacteria [1–4][6–9]. In dialysis patients, long‑term nasal mupirocin greatly reduced S. aureus in the nose and lowered S. aureus infection rates, with no excess side effects compared with placebo [1][2][9]. In several surgical studies, mupirocin effectively reduced nasal carriage and sometimes decreased S. aureus infections in known carriers, again without safety concerns [3][5][7][8]. In large hospital trials of nonsurgical patients, mupirocin did not clearly prevent infections but also did not increase infections, deaths, or hospital stay [4]. For methicillin‑resistant S. aureus (MRSA), mupirocin was only modestly effective, and low‑level resistance was linked to treatment failure, but serious resistance was not seen [6]. Overall, mupirocin is considered safe but should be used only when appropriate and not as a substitute for full antibiotic treatment of active infections by a healthcare professional.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing mupirocin ointment is good for S. aureus infections?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing mupirocin ointment is harmful for S. aureus infections?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials have tested mupirocin, mainly as a nasal ointment, to see if reducing *Staphylococcus aureus* (“staph”) carriage lowers infection risk. In high‑risk patients on dialysis, mupirocin clearly cuts staph infections. In surgical patients, it reliably clears staph from the nose but only sometimes lowers infection rates, and often the benefit is modest. Large studies in general nonsurgical inpatients show no overall reduction in staph infections. Overall, the evidence supports mupirocin as effective for eliminating nasal staph and preventing some infections in specific high‑risk groups, but it is not a universal solution for all *S. aureus* infections.

- **Full Answer**:

In hemodialysis patients, mupirocin greatly reduced nasal staph carriage and cut infections from six cases to one compared with placebo [1]. Mupirocin nasal ointment is very effective at temporarily clearing S. aureus from the nose: 80–100% of carriers became culture‑negative in several studies [1][3][5][7][9].

In general nonsurgical inpatients, it did not meaningfully prevent S. aureus infections [4]. For patients colonized with MRSA at several body sites, it was only marginally effective and failures were linked to emerging low‑level resistance [6].  

So, mupirocin is very good for short‑term nasal decolonization and can prevent some S. aureus infections in specific high‑risk groups, but it is not a universal or guaranteed cure.

Across studies, mupirocin nasal ointment is very good at temporarily clearing Staphylococcus aureus from the nose, but its effect on preventing infections varies.

In high‑risk dialysis patients who carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, intranasal mupirocin greatly lowers nasal carriage and cuts S. aureus infections by about half to two‑thirds [1,2,9]. In surgical patients who are nasal carriers, it reduces hospital S. aureus infections but has not consistently lowered surgical‑site infection rates or total infections in all patients [3,5,7,8]. In large groups of nonsurgical inpatients, testing and treating carriers did not reduce S. aureus infection rates [4]. In people carrying methicillin‑resistant S. aureus (MRSA) at several body sites, mupirocin in the nose only modestly reduced carriage, and most remained colonized [6]. Overuse can lead to resistance, making mupirocin less effective [6,9]. Side effects are usually mild, but because benefit is limited to specific high‑risk situations and resistance is a concern, mupirocin should be used only under medical supervision, not as a general self‑treatment cream.

Overall, mupirocin is not very effective at preventing S. aureus infections for most hospitalized or surgical patients. Across large studies, total surgical-site infection rates were essentially unchanged (for example, 2.3% with mupirocin vs 2.4% with placebo [8], and 13.5% vs 9.1% in one cardiac-surgery trial [3]). Mupirocin ointment is **not** generally ineffective, and it is not shown to be dangerous in these studies. It reliably clears *S. aureus* from the nose in most people [1,2,3,5,7–9]. However, when hospitals tried using mupirocin broadly to prevent infections in all nonsurgical inpatients or all surgical patients, it **did not lower overall infection rates** [3–5,7,8]. Benefits were mainly seen in known carriers at higher risk, where it roughly halved nosocomial (hospital-acquired) *S. aureus* infections [1,2,8].  

So mupirocin isn’t a cure‑all, but it’s effective and generally safe when used in the right patients for the right reasons.

ReviewTitle: Routine vitamin A supplementation for the prevention of blindness due to measles infection in children

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Reduced vitamin A concentration increases the risk of blindness in children infected with the measles virus. Promoting vitamin A supplementation in children with measles contributes to the control of blindness in children, which is a high priority within the World Health Organization (WHO) VISION 2020 The Right to Sight Program.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess the efficacy of vitamin A in preventing blindness in children with measles without prior clinical features of vitamin A deficiency.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched CENTRAL 2015, Issue 11, MEDLINE (1950 to December week 3, 2015), Embase (1974 to December 2015) and LILACS (1985 to December 2015).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the efficacy of vitamin A in preventing blindness in well-nourished children diagnosed with measles but with no prior clinical features of vitamin A deficiency.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: For the original review, two review authors independently assessed studies for eligibility and extracted data on reported outcomes. We contacted trial authors of the included studies for additional information on unpublished data. We included two RCTs which were clinically heterogenous. We presented the continuous outcomes reported as the mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence interval (CI) and dichotomous outcomes as risk ratio (RR) with 95% CI. Due to marked clinical heterogeneity we considered it inappropriate to perform a meta-analysis.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text:
For the first publication of this review, two RCTs involving 260 children with measles which compared vitamin A with placebo met the inclusion criteria. Neither study reported blindness or other ocular morbidities as end points. One trial of moderate quality suggested evidence of a significant increase in serum retinol levels in the vitamin A group one week after two doses of vitamin A (MD 9.45 µg/dL, 95% CI 2.19 to 16.71; 17 participants, moderate-quality evidence), but not six weeks after three doses of vitamin A (MD 2.56 µg/dL, 95% CI -5.28 to 10.40; 39 participants, moderate-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in weight gain six weeks (MD 0.39 kg, -0.04 to 0.82; 48 participants, moderate-quality evidence) and six months (MD 0.52 kg, 95% CI -0.08 to 1.12; 36 participants, moderate-quality evidence) after three doses of vitamin A.
The second trial found no significant difference in serum retinol levels two weeks after a single dose of vitamin A (MD 2.67 µg/dL, 95% CI -0.29 to 5.63; 155 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Percentage of undernutrition between the two groups did not differ significantly at one week (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.54, 145 participants) and two weeks (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.29, 147 participants) after a single dose of vitamin A. No adverse event was reported in either study. We did not find any new RCTS for this second update.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: We did not find any trials assessing whether or not vitamin A supplementation in children with measles prevents blindness, as neither study reported blindness or other ocular morbidities as end points.

Inputs.Title: Vitamin A supplementation reduces measles morbidity in young African children: a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial.
Inputs.Abstract: The effects of vitamin A supplementation on measles morbidity are unclear. Sixty hospitalized children aged 4-24 mo with complicated measles received a World Health Organization--(WHO) recommended dose of vitamin A or placebo. The two groups were comparable in known covariants of measles severity: weight-for-age percentiles, overcrowding, rash, total lymphocytes, and serum concentrations of zinc, albumin, prealbumin, retinol-binding protein, and vitamins A and E. Ninety percent of the patients had hyporetinemia. Integrated morbidity scores, determined by severity of condition (eg, diarrhoea, herpes, and respiratory-tract infection) were assigned on day 8 and 6 wk and 6 mo; these were reduced by 82%, 61%, and 85%, respectively, in the supplemented group, which was mainly due to reduced respiratory-tract infection. There was one death in the placebo group. At 6 wk weight gain was significant in the supplemented group. Despite the selected sample, attention to multiple covariates enhances the validity of the data obtained and supports the current WHO recommendations for vitamin A supplementation during measles.

Inputs.Title: Efficacy of a single oral dose of 200,000 IU of oil-soluble vitamin A in measles-associated morbidity.
Inputs.Abstract: The authors assessed the efficacy of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendation of 200,000 IU of vitamin A in oil to treat acute non-xerophthalmic measles patients. Acute measles patients who did not require hospitalization were enrolled in a randomized, double-masked, clinical trial of vitamin A (n=90) versus placebo (n=110) carried out in Ndola, Zambia, in 1991. Measles-associated morbidity was defined by the presence of signs and symptoms of acute respiratory infection. Daily evaluations for the first 3 days were followed by weekly visits for a month at urban health centers. Baseline demographic, clinical, and biochemical characteristics were similar in both groups. Cross-sectional analysis of morbidity status, by group, at each weekly evaluation showed no significant differences until week 4, when more placebo-treated patients had cough or pneumonia (p=0.005). However, longitudinal analysis, which looked at changes among individuals and controlled for initial health status, showed more equivocal results. The odds ratio for the development of pneumonia in patients with measles cough in vitamin A-treated subjects was 0.73 (95% confidence interval (Cl) 0.30-1.80). The odds ratio for the development of measles-associated cough or pneumonia in asymptomatic measles patients was 0.52 (95% Cl 0.24-1.13), in favor of vitamin A, but the odds ratio for failing to improve from pneumonia in vitamin A-treated subjects was 1.23 (95% Cl 0.68-2.3), a result in favor of placebo. These results suggest that the evidence for the efficacy of one dose of vitamin A in oil to prevent measles complications is not as strong as that previously shown for two 200,000 IU doses of water-miscible vitamin A, and that the WHO recommendation may need to be reexamined.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is vitamin A supplementation for blindness due to measles infection?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is vitamin A supplementation for blindness due to measles infection?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The provided studies look at how vitamin A affects general measles illness (like pneumonia and weight gain), not specifically blindness. One hospital trial in very sick, mostly vitamin A–deficient children showed large reductions in overall measles complications with WHO‑recommended vitamin A dosing, but did not report eye outcomes or blindness. Another trial in less severe, non‑hospitalized measles patients found only modest and uncertain benefit from a single oil‑based vitamin A dose, and again did not examine vision. Therefore, any statement about blindness must be cautious and based on indirect evidence only.

- **Full Answer**:  
Current research does not directly measure whether vitamin A supplements prevent blindness specifically from measles infection. In the first hospital trial, children with complicated measles who received WHO‑recommended vitamin A had much lower overall illness scores and fewer problems such as respiratory infections, and most were vitamin A–deficient, but eye outcomes and blindness were not reported [1]. In the second trial of milder, non‑hospitalized measles cases, a single oral dose of oil‑based vitamin A showed only modest or uncertain benefit in preventing cough or pneumonia, and again did not assess eye damage or vision [2]. These studies therefore support vitamin A for reducing some measles complications, especially in very sick, vitamin A–deficient children, but they do not tell us how well it prevents measles‑related blindness [1][2]. Because of potential benefit and low cost, WHO still recommends vitamin A during measles, but the exact impact on blindness remains uncertain [1][2] overall.
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Available trials of vitamin A in measles focused on general illness, respiratory infections, weight gain, and death—not blindness or eye damage [1][2]. One study even excluded children with vitamin A–related eye disease (“non‑xerophthalmic”) [2]. Because vision and eye findings were neither required at entry nor tracked as outcomes, these data cannot show how well, or how poorly, vitamin A prevents measles‑related blindness at all currently.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these summaries, there is no direct evidence about how (in)effective vitamin A is for blindness caused by measles. The hospitalized trial showed large reductions in overall measles severity and respiratory infections, plus better weight gain and a possible survival benefit, but did not report any eye outcomes or vision changes [1]. The community trial, which excluded children with eye signs, tracked only respiratory symptoms and likewise provided no data on blindness [2]. Therefore, these articles cannot quantify vitamin A’s effect on measles‑related blindness.

efficacy.positive_question: Does vitamin A supplementation work for blindness due to measles infection?
efficacy.negative_question: Does vitamin A supplementation not work for blindness due to measles infection?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The summaries describe two trials of vitamin A in children with measles. One trial in hospitalized children found that WHO‑recommended high‑dose vitamin A markedly reduced overall measles severity, especially respiratory infections, and improved weight gain [1]. The second trial in less severe, non‑hospitalized cases found mixed results from a single oil‑based vitamin A dose and questioned that specific regimen [2]. Neither study reported eye disease, vision changes, or blindness as outcomes. Therefore, these data support vitamin A for reducing general measles morbidity, but they do not demonstrate that it treats or reverses measles‑related blindness.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, vitamin A clearly helps children recover from severe measles, but its effect on blindness specifically is not shown.  

In hospitalized African children with complicated measles, high‑dose vitamin A (using the WHO-recommended schedule) greatly reduced overall illness severity at 8 days, 6 weeks, and 6 months, mainly by lowering respiratory infections, and improved weight gain, with no increase in deaths [1]. Another trial in non‑hospitalized Zambian children found that a single 200,000‑IU oil‑based dose did not consistently prevent cough or pneumonia, and the authors questioned this particular regimen [2].  

Neither study reported eye problems or vision loss as outcomes, so we cannot say from these data that vitamin A reverses measles‑related blindness or fully prevents it once eye damage has begun [1][2]. The evidence here supports vitamin A to reduce measles severity, not as a proven treatment for established measles‑induced blindness [1][2].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:

Since blindness outcomes were not measured, no conclusion can be drawn from these articles about whether vitamin A does or does not work for measles-related blindness.

- **Full Answer**:  
From these articles, we cannot say whether vitamin A supplementation “does not work” for preventing blindness from measles.

Both trials focused on general measles severity and respiratory complications, not on eye disease or blindness as outcomes. In the first hospital-based trial, high-dose vitamin A clearly reduced overall measles-related illness and improved weight gain, but eye problems or vision were not reported [1]. In the second community trial, a single oil-based dose had mixed and generally weaker effects on respiratory complications, and again eye outcomes were not measured [2].

Because neither study assessed blindness, these data do not show whether vitamin A prevents or treats measles-related vision loss. They do support that vitamin A can lessen some measles complications when given in adequate doses and formulations [1,2]. To know its effect on blindness specifically, we would need studies that directly measure eye signs and visual outcomes.

safety.positive_question: Is vitamin A supplementation safe for blindness due to measles infection?
safety.negative_question: Is vitamin A supplementation dangerous for blindness due to measles infection?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:

In hospitalized children with severe measles, vitamin A substantially reduced illness and there was one death only in the placebo group, with no reported vitamin A–related side effects [1]. In non‑hospitalized children, a single high dose gave mixed benefit but again no safety concerns were reported; the authors mainly questioned how effective that particular regimen was, not its safety [2]. Together, these data support that WHO‑recommended vitamin A dosing in measles is safe, and WHO endorses its use during measles episodes [1].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, vitamin A supplementation at World Health Organization (WHO)–recommended doses appears safe for children with measles, including those at risk of eye damage and blindness.  

In hospitalized children 4–24 months old with severe measles, giving high‑dose vitamin A significantly reduced illness and improved weight gain, and there was one death only in the placebo (no vitamin A) group [1]. No specific side effects or safety problems from vitamin A were reported [1].  

In less severely ill, non‑hospitalized measles patients, a single oral dose of 200,000 IU vitamin A in oil did not clearly reduce complications, but again no harms from vitamin A were reported [2]. The authors mainly questioned how effective that dosing regimen was, not its safety [2].  

Therefore, when given in WHO‑recommended doses under medical supervision, vitamin A is considered safe in measles and is used to help prevent complications, including eye damage [1][2].

ReviewTitle: Auricular acupuncture for cocaine dependence

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Auricular acupuncture (insertion of acupuncture into a number, usually five, of specific points in the ear) is a widely-used treatment for cocaine dependence.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To determine whether auricular acupuncture is an effective treatment for cocaine dependence, and to investigate whether its effectiveness is influenced by the treatment regimen.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (The Cochrane Library Issue 3, 2004); MEDLINE (January 1966 to October 2004) , EMBASE (January 1988 to October 2004); PsycInfo (1985 to October 2004); CINAHL (1982 to October 2004); SIGLE (1980 to October 2004) and reference lists of articles.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials comparing a therapeutic regimen of auricular acupuncture with sham acupuncture or no treatment for reduction of cocaine use in cocaine dependents.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two authors independently extracted data from published reports and assessed study quality using the Drug and Alcohol CRG checklist. All authors were contacted for additional information; two provided data. Separate meta-analyses were conducted for studies comparing auricular acupuncture with sham acupuncture, and with no treatment. For the main cocaine use outcomes, analyses were conducted by intention to treat, assuming that missing data were treatment failures. Available case analyses, using only individuals who provided data, were also conducted.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Seven studies with a total of 1,433 participants were included. All were of generally low methodological quality. No differences between acupuncture and sham acupuncture were found for attition RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.23) or acupuncture and no acupuncture: RR 1.06 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.26) neither for any measure of cocaine or other drug use. However, the number of participants included in meta-analyses was low, and power was limited. Moderate benefit or harm is not ruled out by these results. Methodological limitations of the included studies may have also made the results open to bias.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: There is currently no evidence that auricular acupuncture is effective for the treatment of cocaine dependence. The evidence is not of high quality and is inconclusive. Further randomised trials of auricular acupuncture may be justified.

Inputs.Title: A randomized controlled trial of auricular acupuncture for cocaine dependence.
Inputs.Abstract:
Partly because of a lack of a conventional, effective treatment for cocaine addiction, auricular acupuncture is used to treat this disorder in numerous drug treatment facilities across the country for both primary cocaine-dependent and opiate-dependent populations.
                To evaluate the effectiveness of auricular acupuncture for the treatment of cocaine addiction.
                Eighty-two cocaine-dependent, methadone-maintained patients were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 conditions: auricular acupuncture, a needle-insertion control condition, or a no-needle relaxation control. Treatment sessions were provided 5 times weekly for 8 weeks. The primary outcome was cocaine use assessed by 3-times-weekly urine toxicology screens.
                Longitudinal analysis of the urine data for the intent-to-treat sample showed that patients assigned to acupuncture were significantly more likely to provide cocaine-negative urine samples relative to both the relaxation control (odds ratio, 3.41; 95% confidence interval, 1.33-8.72; P =. 01) and the needle-insertion control (odds ratio, 2.40; 95% confidence interval, 1.00-5.75; P =.05).
                Findings from the current study suggest that acupuncture shows promise for the treatment of cocaine dependence. Further investigation of this treatment modality appears to be warranted.

Inputs.Title: Effectiveness of adjunct therapies in crack cocaine treatment.
Inputs.Abstract: Although intensive outpatient therapy is recommended for treatment of cocaine, psychosocial characteristics associated with crack cocaine abuse are also implicated in attrition from outpatient programs. Acupuncture, medications, and brainwave therapy (biofeedback), have all been used to encourage treatment retention and drug use outcomes. The effectiveness of three adjunct therapies in improving retention and drug use outcomes in intensive outpatient cocaine treatment was tested in a primarily young, indigent African-American sample of crack cocaine users at a community hospital in a low-income, high drug use neighborhood in Houston. Subjects were assigned to receive either neurobehavioral treatment alone or neurobehavioral with one of three adjunct therapies. These included acupuncture, anticraving medication, or brainwave therapy. Comparative results indicated that dosage of any adjunct therapy was associated with days in treatment and standard treatment sessions attended, and that standard treatment sessions attended was associated with negative urinalysis results at follow-up. None of the adjunct therapies were directly associated with drug use outcomes.

Inputs.Title: Acupuncture for the treatment of cocaine addiction: a randomized controlled trial.
