ReviewTitle: Topical capsaicin (low concentration) for chronic neuropathic pain in adults

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Topical creams with capsaicin are used to treat pain from a wide range of chronic conditions including neuropathic pain. Following application to the skin capsaicin causes enhanced sensitivity to noxious stimuli, followed by a period with reduced sensitivity and, after repeated applications, persistent desensitisation. There is uncertainty about the efficacy and tolerability of capsaicin for treating painful chronic neuropathies. This is an update of an earlier review of topical capsaicin for chronic neuropathic pain in adults that looked at all doses and formulations of capsaicin. The original review has now been split: here we consider only formulations using a low concentration of capsaicin (< 1%) applied several times daily over several weeks, while another review will consider a single application of capsaicin at a high concentration.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To review the evidence from controlled trials on the efficacy and tolerability of topically applied low-concentration (< 1%) capsaicin in chronic neuropathic pain in adults.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: Cochrane CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE and Oxford Pain Relief Database, searched to July 2012.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies of at least six weeks' duration, using low-concentration (< 1%) topical capsaicin to treat neuropathic pain.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two review authors independently assessed study quality and validity, and extracted data. Information was extracted on numbers of participants with pain relief (clinical improvement) after at least six weeks, and with local skin reactions, and used to calculate relative risk (or risk ratio, RR) and numbers needed to treat to benefit (NNT) and harm (NNH). Details of definition of pain relief and specific adverse events were sought.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: No additional studies were identified for this update of low concentration capsaicin. Included studies were published before 1996. Six studies (389 participants in total) compared regular application of low dose (0.075%) capsaicin cream with placebo cream. There was substantial heterogeneity in results, probably as a result of the small number of studies each with small numbers of participants, as well as the different pain conditions studied and different definitions of "clinical success" reported. Only two studies reported data for the preferred primary outcome of at least 50% pain relief, and there were too few data for pooled analysis. Local skin reactions were more common with capsaicin, usually tolerable, and attenuated with time; the NNH for repeated low-dose application was 2.5 (95% confidence interval (CI) 2.1 to 3.1). All studies satisfied minimum criteria for quality and validity, but maintenance of blinding remains a potential problem.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: There were insufficient data to draw any conclusions about the efficacy of low-concentration capsaicin cream in the treatment of neuropathic pain. The information we have suggests that low-concentration topical capsaicin is without meaningful effect beyond that found in placebo creams; given the potential for bias from small study size, this makes it unlikely that low-concentration topical capsaicin has any meaningful use in clinical practice. Local skin irritation, which was often mild and transient but may lead to withdrawal, was common. Systemic adverse effects were rare.

Inputs.Title: Effect of treatment with capsaicin on daily activities of patients with painful diabetic neuropathy. Capsaicin Study Group.
Inputs.Abstract:
To establish the effects of topically applied capsaicin on daily activities in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy.
                Investigators at 12 sites enrolled 277 men and women with painful peripheral polyneuropathy and/or radiculopathy in an 8-wk double-blind vehicle-controlled study with parallel randomized treatment assignments. Participants were unresponsive or intolerant to conventional therapy and were experiencing pain that interfered with functional activities and/or sleep. Either 0.075% capsaicin cream or vehicle cream was applied to the painful areas 4 times/day. A visual analogue scale of pain intensity and baseline measurements of the pain's interference with the ability to walk, work, participate in recreational activities, use shoes and socks, sleep, and eat were recorded at onset and at 2-wk intervals. A physician's global evaluation scale assessed changes in pain status from baseline.
                Statistically significant differences are percentage of patients with improvement in favor of capsaicin versus vehicle: 69.5 vs 53.4% with clinical improvement in pain status (P = 0.012), 26.1 vs. 14.6% with improvement in walking (P = 0.029), 18.3 vs. 9.2% with improvement in working (P = 0.019), 29.5 vs. 20.3% with improvement in sleeping (P = 0.036), and 22.8 vs. 12.1% with improvement in participating in recreational activities (P = 0.037).
                The results from this study suggest that topical 0.075% capsaicin is effective for reducing pain in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy with subsequent improvement in daily activities, enhancing the quality of the patient's life.

Inputs.Title: Topical capsaicin treatment of chronic postherpetic neuralgia.
Inputs.Abstract: Uncontrolled studies have indicated that topically applied capsaicin may be a safe and effective treatment for postherpetic neuralgia. In a double-blind study 32 elderly patients with chronic postherpetic neuralgia were treated with either capsaicin cream or its vehicle for a 6-week period. Response to treatment was evaluated by visual analogue scales of pain and of pain relief, together with changes in a categoric pain scale and in a physician's global evaluation. Significantly greater relief in the capsaicin-treated group compared with vehicle was observed for all efficacy variables. After 6 weeks almost 80% of capsaicin-treated patients experienced some relief from their pain. Because capsaicin avoids problems with drug interactions and systemic toxicity, we suggest that topical capsaicin be considered for initial management of postherpetic neuralgia.

Inputs.Title: Double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the application of capsaicin cream in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy.
Inputs.Abstract: We have completed a 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized study on the efficacy of the application of capsaicin (CAPS) cream (0.075%) in the treatment of chronic distal painful polyneuropathy. Forty patients were enrolled and 39 completed the study. The 2 limbs were randomly assigned to CAPS or placebo (PLAC). The cream was applied 4 times a day. The first tube contained the active PLAC, methyl nicotinate. In the final 4 weeks (single-blind wash-out phase), PLAC was administered bilaterally. Efficacy was evaluated using the following scales: (1) investigator global, (2) patient global, (3) visual analog (VAS) of pain severity, (4) VAS of pain relief, (5) activities of daily living, and (6) allodynia. Patients were examined at onset and at monthly intervals using a neurologic disability scale, nerve conduction studies, computer-assisted sensory examination for vibration and thermal cooling and warming, QSART (quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test) and quantitative flare response. There was no statistical evidence of efficacy of CAPS cream over PLAC for any of the pain indices. At early time points (1-4 weeks), there were a small number of indices that favored the PLAC. The percent of limbs that improved on the investigator's global scale were 51.3 vs. 53.8 at 4 weeks, 56.4 vs. 64.1 at 8 weeks and 59 vs. 66.7 at 12 weeks for CAPS vs. PLAC; no statistically significant difference was found. All the safety indices showed no difference between sides. We interpret the early hyperalgesia on the CAPS side as being responsible for the better performance of PLAC at early time points. The large percentage of limbs that improved may be a pronounced PLAC response.

Inputs.Title: A double-blind comparison of topical capsaicin and oral amitriptyline in painful diabetic neuropathy.
Inputs.Abstract: An 8-week double-blind, multicenter, parallel study compared the safety and efficacy of topical capsaicin and oral amitriptyline in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy involving the feet. Two hundred thirty-five patients were randomized to treatment with either capsaicin cream or amitriptyline capsules. Capsaicin-treated patients received inactive capsules, and amitriptyline-treated patients applied vehicle cream. A visual analogue scale of pain intensity and measurements of interference by pain with functional activities were recorded at onset and at 2-week intervals. A visual analogue scale of pain relief and physicians' global evaluation assessed changes in pain status from baseline. Topical capsaicin and oral amitriptyline produced equal and statistically significant improvements in pain over the course of the study. By the end of week 8, 76% of patients in each group experienced less pain, with a mean reduction in intensity of more than 40%. By the end of the study, the interference with daily activities by pain had diminished significantly (P = .001) in both groups, including improvements in sleeping and walking. No systemic side effects were observed in patients treated with topical capsaicin. Most patients receiving amitriptyline experienced at least one systemic side effect, ranging from somnolence (46%) to neuromuscular (23%) and cardiovascular (9%) adverse effects. Topically applied capsaicin is an equally effective but considerably safer alternative to amitriptyline for relief of the pain of diabetic neuropathy.

Inputs.Title: A randomized vehicle-controlled trial of topical capsaicin in the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia.
Inputs.Abstract: A large double-blind, vehicle-controlled study of 143 patients with chronic postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) was performed to evaluate the degree of efficacy of topically applied capsaicin 0.075% cream. In addition, the safety and efficacy of long-term application of topical capsaicin in PHN was assessed by following patients in an open-label study for up to 2 years. In the double-blind phase, 143 patients with PHN of 6 months' duration or longer were enrolled. Since epidemiologic studies of patients who receive no treatment have shown that only 10% to 25% of those with PHN after 1 month will still have pain at 1 year, two separate efficacy analyses were performed: one with all evaluable patients (n = 131) and the other with 93 patients whose PHN lasted for longer than 12 months prior to study startup. All efficacy variables, including the physician's global evaluation of reduction in PHN pain, changes in pain severity on the categoric scale, visual analogue scale for pain severity, visual analogue scale for pain relief, and functional capacity scale, showed significant improvement at nearly all time points throughout the study for both patient groups, based on duration of PHN pain. In contrast, the group receiving vehicle cream remained essentially unchanged. Data from the long-term, open-label phase (up to 2 years, n = 77), which immediately followed the 6-week blinded phase, showed that the clinical benefit in patients treated for a short (6-week) period with topical capsaicin could be maintained or amplified in most patients (86%) during prolonged therapy. There were no serious adverse effects observed or reported throughout the trial; in fact, the only side effect associated with capsaicin treatment was the burning or stinging at local sites of application (in 9% of patients) during exposures of up to 2 years (long-term phase). On the basis of these data, we conclude that capsaicin 0.075% cream is a safe and effective treatment for the pain of postherpetic neuralgia and should be considered for initial management of patients with this condition.

Inputs.Title: The postmastectomy pain syndrome and topical capsaicin: a randomized trial.
Inputs.Abstract: This paper describes a randomized parallel trial of topical 0.075% capsaicin versus vehicle (placebo) in the postmastectomy pain syndrome (PMPS). The study was double-blind in design; however, this was compromised by the burning sensation induced by capsaicin. We could not demonstrate a significant difference in the visual analogue scale (VAS) for steady pain although a trend was present. A significant difference was found, however, in the VAS for jabbing pain, in category pain severity scales, and in overall pain relief scales in favour of capsaicin. Five of 13 patients on capsaicin were categorized as good-to-excellent responses with 8 (62%) having 50% or greater improvement. Only 1 of 10 cases had a good response to vehicle with 3 rated as 50% or better.

Inputs.Title: Phase III placebo-controlled trial of capsaicin cream in the management of surgical neuropathic pain in cancer patients.
Inputs.Abstract:
A minority of cancer survivors develops long-term postsurgical neuropathic pain. Based on evidence that capsaicin, the pungent ingredient in hot chili peppers, might be useful for treating neuropathic pain, we developed the present clinical trial.
                Ninety-nine assessable patients with postsurgical neuropathic pain were entered onto this study. After stratification, patients were to receive 8 weeks of a 0.075% capsaicin cream followed by 8 weeks of an identical-appearing placebo cream, or vice versa. A capsaicin/placebo cream was to be applied to the painful site four times daily. Treatment evaluation was performed by patient-completed weekly questionnaires.
                During the first 8-week study period, the capsaicin-cream arm was associated with substantially more skin burning, skin redness, and coughing (P < .0001 for each). Nonetheless, treatment was stopped for patient refusal or toxicity just as often while patients were receiving the placebo as compared with the capsaicin. The capsaicin cream arm had substantially more pain relief (P = .01) after the first 8 weeks, with an average pain reduction of 53% versus 17%. On completion of the 16-week study period, patients were asked which treatment period was most beneficial. Of the responding patients, 60% chose the capsaicin arm, 18% chose the placebo arm, and 22% chose neither (P = .001).
                A topical capsaicin cream decreases postsurgical neuropathic pain and, despite some toxicities, is preferred by patients over a placebo by a three-to-one margin among those expressing a preference.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is topical capsaicin for chronic neuropathic pain?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is topical capsaicin for chronic neuropathic pain?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Trials of 0.075% capsaicin cream in several chronic neuropathic pain conditions generally show modest but meaningful benefit versus placebo (vehicle cream), though one study in distal polyneuropathy was negative [1][2][3][4][5][6][7]. In painful diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia, most patients reported some degree of pain reduction and better daily functioning, with improvements similar to those from oral amitriptyline but without systemic drug side effects [1][2][4][5]. Studies in postmastectomy and postsurgical neuropathic pain also show about half or more patients achieving substantial relief [6][7]. The main drawback is local burning or stinging at the application site; serious complications were not seen [4][5][7]. Overall, topical capsaicin appears moderately effective and relatively safe, but not all patients or neuropathic conditions respond [3].

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin 0.075% cream provides modest but real relief for many people with chronic neuropathic pain. In painful diabetic neuropathy, about 70–76% of patients had pain improvement, with pain intensity falling by more than 40% and better sleep, walking, work, and recreation compared with placebo cream [1][4]. In postherpetic neuralgia, around 80% reported at least some relief, and benefits were clearly greater than vehicle cream and maintained for up to 2 years of continued use [2][5]. Capsaicin also reduced postsurgical and postmastectomy neuropathic pain; roughly 50–60% of patients had at least 50% pain reduction and preferred capsaicin over placebo [6][7]. One trial in distal polyneuropathy found no benefit over placebo, showing that not everyone responds [3]. Compared with oral amitriptyline, capsaicin worked equally well but caused no systemic side effects; the main problem is local burning or stinging where it is applied [4][5][7].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is framed around “how ineffective” capsaicin is, so the key issue is the size and consistency of benefit over placebo. Across the summaries, several randomized, placebo‑controlled trials show capsaicin cream giving modest but real extra pain relief in different chronic nerve pain conditions: diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, postsurgical neuropathic pain, and postmastectomy pain [1][2][4][5][6][7]. One well‑done trial in distal painful polyneuropathy found no difference from placebo, highlighting that results are not uniform and placebo responses can be large [3]. The degree of benefit is generally in the “somewhat better” range (around 40–50% average pain reduction in responders), not dramatic, and some patients get little or no help. Side effects are mostly local burning or stinging, without systemic toxicity [1][4][5][7]. So the fairest lay explanation is that capsaicin is not “very ineffective,” but a modest, condition‑dependent option.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across several studies of chronic neuropathic pain, capsaicin cream was usually a little better than placebo but far from a cure. In painful diabetic neuropathy, about 70–76% of patients using capsaicin reported improvement, versus 53% on inactive cream, with average pain intensity falling by a bit over 40% [1][4]. In postherpetic neuralgia, nearly 80% had some relief, and benefits clearly exceeded vehicle cream and persisted with long‑term use [2][5]. After surgery‑related nerve pain in cancer, average pain fell 53% with capsaicin versus 17% with placebo [7]. In contrast, one trial of distal painful polyneuropathy found no meaningful difference between capsaicin and placebo on any pain measure, likely reflecting a strong placebo response and early capsaicin‑induced burning [3]. Overall, capsaicin cream seems modestly effective for many, clearly ineffective for some, and generally safer than systemic drugs, so it is not “very ineffective” but offers limited, condition‑specific benefit for many patients [1][2][3][4][5][7].

efficacy.positive_question: Does topical capsaicin work for chronic neuropathic pain?
efficacy.negative_question: Does topical capsaicin not work for chronic neuropathic pain?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several good-quality trials, 0.075% capsaicin cream applied several times daily gave better pain relief than placebo for postherpetic neuralgia, painful diabetic neuropathy, postmastectomy pain, and postsurgical neuropathic pain, often improving sleep and daily activities [1,2,4–7]. In one trial of chronic distal painful polyneuropathy, capsaicin did not outperform placebo, suggesting it does not work for everyone or every neuropathic pain type [3]. In diabetic neuropathy, capsaicin was about as effective as the oral drug amitriptyline but caused fewer whole‑body side effects [4]. The main side effect is local burning or stinging at the application site, which many patients tolerate and which tends to lessen over time [5,7]. Long-term use up to two years appeared safe [5]. Overall, capsaicin offers modest but real benefit for many people with chronic neuropathic pain and is a reasonable option, especially when standard pills are not tolerated.

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin has been shown to reduce chronic neuropathic pain in several conditions, though its benefit is modest and not universal.

In painful diabetic neuropathy, 0.075% capsaicin cream four times daily reduced pain and improved walking, sleep, work, and recreation compared with placebo [1]. In another study, capsaicin worked about as well as the oral drug amitriptyline, with similar pain reduction but far fewer systemic side effects [4].

For postherpetic neuralgia, both small and large placebo-controlled trials found capsaicin provided significantly greater pain relief and better daily function; benefits could be maintained or increased with long-term use up to two years, with no serious safety issues [2,5].

Capsaicin also helped in postmastectomy pain and postsurgical neuropathic pain in cancer patients, giving about 50% average pain reduction and being preferred over placebo [6,7].

However, one trial in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy found no advantage over placebo [3].

The main side effect is local burning or stinging at the application site, which is usually manageable [5,7].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: Evidence is mixed but generally supportive. Multiple good-quality trials show topical capsaicin reduces pain and improves function in several chronic neuropathic pain conditions, though one study found no benefit in a specific type of polyneuropathy. So it works for many, but not all, patients and pain types.

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin is not useless, but it is not a guaranteed fix for all chronic neuropathic pain.  

In painful diabetic neuropathy, several randomized trials show capsaicin cream reduces pain and improves sleep, walking, and daily activities, performing as well as the oral drug amitriptyline but with fewer systemic side effects [1][4]. In postherpetic neuralgia, capsaicin gives significantly more pain relief than placebo, and many patients maintain or deepen the benefit with long‑term use [2][5]. It can also lessen postmastectomy and other postsurgical neuropathic pain, with a substantial proportion of patients preferring it over placebo [6][7].  

However, one 12‑week study in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy found no clear benefit over placebo, suggesting a strong placebo effect and that capsaicin may not help all neuropathic pain types [3].  

Overall, topical capsaicin can help many people with chronic neuropathic pain, especially when pills cause side effects, but individual responses vary.

safety.positive_question: Is topical capsaicin safe for chronic neuropathic pain?
safety.negative_question: Is topical capsaicin dangerous for chronic neuropathic pain?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: Trials in diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, postsurgical neuropathic pain, and polyneuropathy show topical capsaicin causes mainly local burning or redness, with no serious or systemic harms reported, even with up to two years of treatment, and fewer systemic side effects than oral amitriptyline [2–5,7].

- **Full Answer**: Overall, topical capsaicin appears safe for treatment of chronic neuropathic pain when used on intact skin. In painful diabetic neuropathy, it reduced pain as much as oral amitriptyline but caused no systemic side effects, unlike amitriptyline, which often led to drowsiness or heart problems [4]. In postherpetic and postsurgical neuropathic pain, capsaicin gave greater pain relief than placebo; the main side effect, over two years, was local burning or stinging in some patients [2,5,7]. Objective testing in polyneuropathy showed no evidence of nerve damage or other safety concerns [3]. Thus, for most adults, the key limitation is local discomfort rather than serious risk.
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several clinical trials in different types of chronic neuropathic pain, topical capsaicin (0.075% cream) did not cause serious or lasting harm. The main side effects were local burning, stinging, redness, or cough, especially when treatment started, and sometimes a short‑term increase in pain. These effects rarely led people to stop treatment and often improved with continued use. No meaningful nerve damage, systemic (whole‑body) toxicity, or dangerous drug interactions were reported, even with use up to 2 years. Compared with an oral drug (amitriptyline), capsaicin provided similar pain relief with far fewer systemic side effects. Overall, it appears uncomfortable for some but not dangerous for most patients when used as directed.

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin creams have been tested for painful diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, postmastectomy pain, and postsurgical neuropathic pain. Studies consistently report local burning or stinging, redness, or cough as the main side effects, especially early on, but no serious adverse events or systemic toxicity [2][3][5][7].  

Long‑term follow‑up (up to 2 years) in postherpetic neuralgia found only local burning in about 9% of patients and no serious complications [5]. In a head‑to‑head trial with oral amitriptyline for diabetic neuropathy, capsaicin provided similar pain relief but caused no systemic side effects, while most amitriptyline users had drowsiness, neuromuscular, or heart‑related side effects [4].  

One neuropathy trial showed no clear benefit over placebo but also found no safety differences between treated and untreated limbs [3].  

Overall, for chronic neuropathic pain, topical capsaicin is generally not considered dangerous, though it can cause bothersome local burning and a temporary pain increase when starting treatment [1][2][5][7].

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing topical capsaicin is good for chronic neuropathic pain?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing topical capsaicin is harmful for chronic neuropathic pain?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Multiple randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trials show that 0.075% capsaicin cream can reduce chronic neuropathic pain in several conditions. In painful diabetic neuropathy, capsaicin was superior to placebo and as effective as amitriptyline, with fewer systemic side effects [1,4]. In postherpetic neuralgia (nerve pain after shingles), two controlled trials, including a large one with long‑term follow‑up, showed significantly better pain relief and function than placebo, with benefits maintained up to 2 years in many patients [2,5]. Trials also reported benefit in postmastectomy pain and postsurgical neuropathic pain in cancer patients [6,7]. However, one study in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy did not find capsaicin better than placebo [3], showing that results are not uniformly positive. The main side effect across studies is a local burning or stinging sensation at the application site, without serious systemic toxicity [1–7].

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. Clinical trials have tested capsaicin cream for nerve pain.  

In painful diabetic neuropathy, 0.075% capsaicin cream used four times daily for 8 weeks reduced pain and improved sleep, walking, work, and recreation compared with placebo [1], and worked about as well as the oral drug amitriptyline but with fewer whole‑body side effects [4].  

In postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain), randomized, placebo‑controlled studies found greater pain relief and better function with capsaicin; nearly 80% had some relief after 6 weeks, and benefits could continue for up to 2 years with ongoing use [2,5].  

Randomized trials also showed pain reductions in postmastectomy pain syndrome and postsurgical neuropathic pain in cancer patients [6,7].  

However, one study in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy did not find benefit over placebo [3].  

Overall, evidence suggests topical capsaicin can help chronic neuropathic pain for people, with burning at the application site as the main side effect [1–7].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several randomized, placebo-controlled trials in different types of chronic neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, postmastectomy pain, and postsurgical cancer pain), topical capsaicin either reduced pain or was no better than placebo, but did not make pain or nerve function worse overall. One study found early extra sensitivity to pain (hyperalgesia), yet detailed nerve tests and long‑term outcomes showed no evidence of nerve damage or lasting harm compared with placebo [3]. Long‑term follow‑up up to 2 years in postherpetic neuralgia also showed no serious adverse effects, only local burning or stinging in a minority of patients [5]. Other trials reported more local burning and redness with capsaicin than placebo, but similar dropout rates and clear pain improvement [1,2,4,6,7].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Published clinical trials do not show that topical capsaicin is harmful for chronic neuropathic pain.  

In painful diabetic neuropathy, capsaicin improved pain and daily activities, with no systemic side effects reported [1,4].  

In postherpetic neuralgia, capsaicin significantly reduced pain compared with placebo, and up to 2 years of treatment caused no serious adverse effects—only local burning or stinging in some patients [2,5].

The question asks “how ineffective” capsaicin is, so the key is the proportion of people who do not benefit and how often it is no better than placebo. I reviewed randomized, controlled trials of topical capsaicin for different chronic neuropathic pains, focusing on: (1) the percentage who improved, (2) the difference versus placebo, and (3) any trials showing no benefit. Across conditions, many patients improved, but a consistent minority did not, and one high‑quality study found no advantage over placebo. I summarized these non‑response rates in simple percentages.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across studies, topical capsaicin helps many but not all people with chronic neuropathic pain. In painful diabetic neuropathy, about 70–76% of patients improved, meaning roughly one in four got little or no benefit [1][4]. In post‑herpetic neuralgia and post‑mastectomy or other postsurgical neuropathic pain, 60–86% had some relief, but 14–40% did not, or preferred placebo or neither treatment [2][5][6][7]. The extra benefit over placebo is modest: in several trials, capsaicin increased the proportion of patients who improved by only about 10–20 percentage points [1][5][6][7]. One well‑designed study in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy found no meaningful difference between capsaicin and placebo on any pain measure, despite more burning discomfort early with capsaicin [3]. Overall, a substantial minority of patients—around 20–40%, and possibly more for some neuropathies—are unlikely to get worthwhile relief, and at least one neuropathic pain type showed no clear advantage over placebo [1][3][4][5][7].

- **Rationale**:  
Online testimonials often come from people for whom a treatment did not work or caused side effects, so they can sound more negative than the overall evidence. Controlled clinical trials give a clearer picture of average benefit and how many people improve.

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin is **not clearly ineffective**, but its benefit is **modest and inconsistent** across people and conditions.

In painful diabetic neuropathy, about 70–76% of patients using capsaicin had pain improvement, with pain intensity dropping by over 40%, similar to oral amitriptyline [1][4]. In postherpetic neuralgia, roughly 80% reported some relief, and capsaicin worked better than placebo cream [2][5]. In postmastectomy and postsurgical neuropathic pain, around half or more had at least 50% pain reduction, clearly better than placebo [6][7].

However, one well-done study in chronic distal painful polyneuropathy found **no advantage over placebo** [3].

Common issues are burning at the application site and the need to apply it several times daily for weeks before judging benefit [3][5].

The trials provided are mostly randomized, controlled studies in several chronic neuropathic pain conditions. Most show capsaicin is modestly to moderately effective for many patients, with one clearly negative trial. Across studies, systemic safety is good; the main downside is local burning or stinging. So the answer should explain that it often helps but not everyone, and that it is generally safe, addressing both effectiveness and safety in plain language.

Online reviews can be misleading because people who don’t get relief are more likely to post. High‑quality trials show topical capsaicin helps many, but not all, people with chronic neuropathic pain.

In painful diabetic neuropathy, about 70–76% of patients using capsaicin reported pain improvement, with average pain intensity dropping by more than 40%, similar to the benefit from oral amitriptyline but without its systemic side effects [1][4]. In postherpetic neuralgia and other nerve pains (post‑shingles, postmastectomy, postsurgical), 53–80% of patients had meaningful pain reduction, and capsaicin clearly outperformed placebo creams [2][5][6][7]. One study in a specific type of distal polyneuropathy did not find benefit over placebo, suggesting it won’t work for everyone [3].

Safety: across studies up to two years, no serious systemic harms were seen. The main problem is local burning or stinging at the application site, usually mild to moderate and temporary [4][5][7]. It is generally not dangerous.

- **Rationale**:  
Research in several kinds of chronic neuropathic pain shows that topical capsaicin helps many, but not all, patients. One good-quality trial in distal polyneuropathy found no benefit over placebo, so it clearly does not work for everyone [3]. However, multiple other randomized trials in diabetic nerve pain, postherpetic neuralgia, postmastectomy pain, and postsurgical neuropathic pain found meaningful average pain reductions with capsaicin, often around 40–50%, and more responders than with placebo [1][2][4][5][6][7]. Side effects were mostly local burning or stinging, with no serious systemic toxicity reported [1][4][5][7]. So it is not “dangerous” for most people, just sometimes uncomfortable and not universally effective.

- **Full Answer**:  
Topical capsaicin is **not strongly ineffective**, but its benefits are **modest and variable**:

- In one trial of distal painful polyneuropathy, capsaicin was **no better than placebo** on any pain measure [3].  
- In contrast, trials in diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia found more patients improving with capsaicin, with around 40–50% average pain reduction and better sleep and function than controls [1][2][4][5].  
- Postmastectomy and postsurgical neuropathic pain trials also showed about half or more patients had substantial pain relief, clearly better than placebo [6][7].  

Across studies, many people do **not** respond, and burning at the application site is common, but **serious harms were not seen** [1][4][5][7].  

So capsaicin is **safe for most and modestly helpful for some**, but far from a guaranteed or dramatic fix.

ReviewTitle: Adjuvant (post‐surgery) chemotherapy for early stage epithelial ovarian cancer

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: This is the second update of the review first published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2009, Issue 1. Epithelial ovarian cancer is diagnosed in over 200,000 women worldwide each year. Ten to 20% of women are diagnosed early, when there is still a good possibility of cure. The treatment of early-stage (stage I and IIa) disease involves surgery to remove the disease, often followed by chemotherapy (adjuvant chemotherapy). The largest clinical trials of adjuvant chemotherapy show an overall survival (OS) advantage with platinum-based chemotherapy; however the precise role and type of this treatment in subgroups of women with differing prognoses needs to be defined.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To undertake a systematic review of the evidence for adjuvant chemotherapy in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer to determine whether chemotherapy following surgery offers a survival advantage over the policy of observation following surgery (with chemotherapy reserved for treatment of disease recurrence); and to determine if clinical subgroups of women with differing prognoses, based on histological subtype or completeness of surgical staging, have more or less to gain from adjuvant chemotherapy.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: We performed an electronic search using the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Specialized Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL 2015, Issue 3), MEDLINE (1948 to March week 5, 2015), and EMBASE (1980 to week 14, 2015). We developed the search strategy using free-text and medical subject headings (MeSH). We also searched registers of clinical trials and citation lists of included studies for potentially relevant studies.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: We included randomised clinical trials (RCTs) of women with early stage (I/IIa) epithelial ovarian cancer staged at laparotomy.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two review authors independently extracted data and assessed study quality of included RCTs. We resolved any disagreements by discussion with a third review author. We used random-effects methods for all meta-analyses, including subgroup analyses.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text:
The original version of this Cochrane review included five RCTs involving 1277 women. In this 2015 update, no new studies met the inclusion criteria but we included an additional paper with mature data (10-year follow-up) relating to a previously included study (ICON1).
We included four studies in the meta-analyses and considered them to be at a low risk of bias. Most study participants (> 95%) had stage I ovarian cancer. Meta-analysis of five-year data from three studies indicated that women who received adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy had better overall survival (OS) than those who did not (Hazard ratio (HR) 0.71, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.53 to 0.93; 1008 women; 3 studies; I² statistic = 0%; high quality evidence). Likewise, meta-analysis of five-year data from four studies indicated that women who received adjuvant chemotherapy had better progression-free survival (PFS) than those who did not (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.84; 1170 women, 4 studies; I² statistic = 0%; high quality evidence). These findings were robust over time, with 10-year HR estimates of 0.72 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.92; 925 women, 2 studies) and 0.67 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.83; 925 women, 2 studies) for OS and PFS, respectively (high quality evidence). The risk of death at 10 years follow-up favoured the adjuvant chemotherapy arm (0.76, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; 923 women, 2 studies; I² statistic = 0%), as did the findings for risk of progression at 10 years (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.87; 925 women, 2 studies; I² statistic = 0%). Low quality evidence suggested that women with high-risk disease may have the most to gain from adjuvant chemotherapy. However, subgroup analyses could neither confirm nor exclude survival benefits in lower risk disease or in optimally staged disease. We found insufficient data to compare adverse events and long term risks between chemotherapy and observation groups.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: High-quality evidence indicates that adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy is effective in prolonging survival in women with early stage (FIGO stage I/IIa) epithelial ovarian cancer. It remains uncertain whether women with low- and intermediate-risk early stage disease will benefit as much from adjuvant chemotherapy as women with high-risk disease. Decisions to use adjuvant chemotherapy (AC) in these women should be mindful of this uncertainty, and the uncertainty regarding adverse events. Treatment of women with lower risk disease should be individualised to take into account individual factors.

Inputs.Title: Adjuvant treatment for early epithelial ovarian cancer: results of two randomised clinical trials comparing cisplatin to no further treatment or chromic phosphate (32P). G.I.C.O.G.: Gruppo Interregionale Collaborativo in Ginecologia Oncologica.
Inputs.Abstract:
From 1983 to 1990, 271 consecutive patients with stage I ovarian cancer entered two randomised trials, aimed at assessing the role of adjuvant chemotherapy after radical surgery in early stages of ovarian cancer. Trial I compared cisplatin (50 mg/m2 with repeated courses every 28 days for 6 cycles) to no further therapy in F.I.G.O. stage Ia & b Grade II-III patients; trial II compared cisplatin (same dose and schedule) to 32P in Iaii & bii and Ic patients.
                Both studies were multicentric and centrally randomized. Treatment was allocated by phone and stratified by center. All patients satisfying major eligibility criteria (histological and grade, no previous neoplasms) were analysed according to treatment allocated by randomisation.
                With a median observation time of 76 months, cisplatin significantly reduced the relapse rate by 65% (HR = 0.35; 95% CI = 0.14-0.89, p = 0.028; Cox Model) in trial I and 61% (HR = 0.39; 95% CI = 0.19-0.77, p = 0.007; Cox Model) in trial II. Survival was not significantly different (trial I - Kaplan-Meier overall 5-year survival: cisplatin = 88%, control = 82%, HR = 1.15; 95% CI = 0.44-2.98; p = 0.773; Cox Model); trial II - overall 5-year survival: cisplatin = 81%, 32P = 79%, HR = 0.72; 95% CI = 0.37-1.43; p = 0.354; Cox model). In both studies the risk of dying after relapse increased for patients originally randomized to the cisplatin arms: in trial I, 6 of 7 patients in the cisplatin relapsed arm and died of tumor compared with 8 of 14 patients in the control arm. In trial II 11 of 12 patients on cisplatin, and 18 of 26 on 32P succumbed to tumor recurrence.
                Adjuvant cisplatin treatment in early ovarian cancer significantly prevents relapse in comparison to 32P in stage IC patients or to no immediate treatment in earlier stage women. The impact of cisplatin adjuvant treatment on survival remains, however, unclear.

Inputs.Title: Adjuvant therapy in stage I and stage II epithelial ovarian cancer. Results of two prospective randomized trials.
Inputs.Abstract: About a third of patients with ovarian cancer present with localized disease; despite surgical resection, up to half the tumors recur. Since it has not been established whether adjuvant treatment can benefit such patients, we conducted two prospective, randomized national cooperative trials of adjuvant therapy in patients with localized ovarian carcinoma (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics Stages Ia to IIc). All patients underwent surgical resection plus comprehensive staging and, 18 months later, surgical re-exploration. In the first trial, 81 patients with well-differentiated or moderately well differentiated cancers confined to the ovaries (Stages Iai and Ibi) were assigned to receive either no chemotherapy or melphalan (0.2 mg per kilogram of body weight per day for five days, repeated every four to six weeks for up to 12 cycles). After a median follow-up of more than six years, there were no significant differences between the patients given no chemotherapy and those treated with melphalan with respect to either five-year disease-free survival (91 vs. 98 percent; P = 0.41) or overall survival (94 vs. 98 percent; P = 0.43). In the second trial, 141 patients with poorly differentiated Stage I tumors or with cancer outside the ovaries but limited to the pelvis (Stage II) were randomly assigned to treatment with either melphalan (in the same regimen as above) or a single intraperitoneal dose of 32P (15 mCi) at the time of surgery. In this trial (median follow-up, greater than 6 years) the outcomes for the two treatment groups were similar with respect to five-year disease-free survival (80 percent in both groups) and overall survival (81 percent with melphalan vs. 78 percent with 32P; P = 0.48). We conclude that in patients with localized ovarian cancer, comprehensive staging at the time of surgical resection can serve to identify those patients (as defined by the first trial) who can be followed without adjuvant chemotherapy. The remaining patients with localized ovarian cancer should receive adjuvant therapy, and with adjuvant melphalan or intraperitoneal 32P should have a five-year disease-free survival of about 80 percent.

Inputs.Title: Understanding the problem of inadequately staging early ovarian cancer.
Inputs.Abstract:
Early ovarian cancer patients are often incompletely staged during initial surgery.(1-3) This omission can have serious adverse consequences for the prognosis of patients as the completeness of surgical staging has been identified as an independent prognostic parameter for survival.(4,5) The reasons for the problem of inadequate staging of early ovarian cancer are largely unknown. We have analysed the data of a large randomised trial in early ovarian cancer in which detailed information of the surgical staging procedure was monitored.(5)
                Data of the EORTC Adjuvant ChemoTherapy In Ovarian Neoplasm (ACTION) Trial were used in which 448 early ovarian cancer patients were randomised between postoperative chemotherapy in one arm and observation following surgery in the other. In this trial strict criteria for surgical staging were advised but optimal, complete staging was performed in only 1/3 of patients. Staging characteristics of the incompletely staged patients were analysed and factors that could explain the failure to perform a complete staging were studied.
                Sampling of para-aortic nodes was omitted in 78% of the incompletely staged patients, while 52% of these patients had no pelvic lymph node dissection. Taking blind biopsies from different peritoneal sites was not performed in more than 1/3 of the incompletely staged group. Omission of the staging steps ranged from 3% (infracolic omentectomy) to 55% (biopsy of the right hemi-diaphragm). A significant difference (p=0.04) between the fraction of completely staged patients was found when comparing institutes who entered less than 5 patients (21%) versus those who included more than 20 patients (37%) in the trial.
                Even in a randomised trial in which comprehensive surgical staging was strongly advised in the study protocol the majority of patients (66%) were incompletely staged. Factors relating to a lack of surgical skills attributed most to the number of incompletely staged patients, but insufficient knowledge of the tumour behaviour and routes of spread of ovarian cancer also contributed substantially to this problem. Multicentre trials recruiting patients from many institutes with small volume contribution to the study, run the risk of inadequate adherence to the study protocol.

Inputs.Title: International Collaborative Ovarian Neoplasm trial 1: a randomized trial of adjuvant chemotherapy in women with early-stage ovarian cancer.
Inputs.Abstract:
The question of whether platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy can improve outcomes in patients with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer is an important one. We carried out a multicenter, open randomized trial to determine whether adjuvant chemotherapy would improve overall survival and prolong recurrence-free survival in women with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer.
                Between August 1991 and January 2000, 477 patients in 84 centers in five countries were randomly assigned to receive either adjuvant chemotherapy immediately following surgery (n = 241) or no adjuvant chemotherapy until clinically indicated (n = 236). Kaplan-Meier curves of overall survival and recurrence-free survival were compared using the Mantel-Cox version of the log-rank test. All statistical tests were two-sided.
                Women who received adjuvant chemotherapy had better overall survival than women who did not (hazard ratio [HR] of 0.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.45 to 0.97; P =.03). These results translate into 5-year survival figures of 70% for women who did not receive adjuvant chemotherapy and 79% for women who did receive adjuvant chemotherapy, a difference of 9% (95% CI = 1% to 15%). Adjuvant chemotherapy also improved recurrence-free survival (HR = 0.65; 95% CI = 0.46 to 0.91; P =.01). These results translate into 5-year recurrence-free survival figures of 62% for women who did not receive adjuvant chemotherapy and 73% for women who did receive adjuvant chemotherapy, a difference of 11% (95% CI = 3% to 18%).
                These results suggest that platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy improves survival and delays recurrence in patients with early-stage ovarian cancer.

Inputs.Title: Randomized study on adjuvant chemotherapy in stage I high-risk ovarian cancer with evaluation of DNA-ploidy as prognostic instrument.
Inputs.Abstract:
Adjuvant chemotherapy versus observation and chemotherapy at progression was evaluated in 162 patients in a prospective randomized multicenter study. We also evaluated DNA-measurements as an additional prognostic factor.
                Patients received adjuvant carboplatin AUC 7 every 28 days for six courses (n = 81) or no adjuvant treatment (n = 81). Eligibility included surgically staged and treated patients with FIGO stage I disease, grade 1 aneuploid or grade 2 or 3 non-clear cell carcinomas or clear cell carcinomas. Disease-free (DFS) and disease-specific (DSS) survival were end-points.
                Median follow-up time was 46 months and progression was observed in 20 patients in the treatment group and 19 in the control group. Estimated five-year DFS and DSS were 70% and 86% in the treatment group and 71% and 85% in the control group. The hazard ratio was 0.98 (95% confidence interval (95% CI): 0.52-1.83) regarding DFS and 0.94 (95% CI: 0.37-2.36) regarding DSS. No significant differences in DFS or DSS could be seen when the log-rank test was stratified for prognostic variables. Therefore, data from both groups were pooled for the analysis of prognostic factors. DNA-ploidy (P = 0.003), extracapsular growth (P = 0.005), tumor rupture (P = 0.04), and WHO histologic grade (P = 0.04) were significant independent prognostic factors for DFS with P < 0.0001 for the model in the multivariate Cox analysis. FIGO substage (P = 0.01), DNA ploidy (P < 0.05), and histologic grade (P = 0.05) were prognostic for DSS with a P-value for the model < 0.0001.
                Due to the small number of patients the study was inconclusive as regards the question of adjuvant chemotherapy. The survival curves were superimposable, but with wide confidence intervals. DNA-ploidy adds objective independent prognostic information regarding both DFS and DSS in early ovarian cancer.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is adjuvant chemotherapy for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is adjuvant chemotherapy for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across trials, benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer is modest and depends on risk and quality of surgical staging. Cisplatin after surgery cut the chance of the cancer coming back by about 60–65%, but did not clearly lengthen overall survival in small studies [1]. An older drug, melphalan, did not improve survival in very low‑risk, well‑staged stage I patients compared with careful follow‑up alone [2]. For higher‑risk or stage II patients, melphalan and intraperitoneal radiation (32P) gave similar 5‑year disease‑free survival of about 80% [2]. A large modern trial showed that platinum‑based chemotherapy improved 5‑year survival from 70% to 79% and reduced recurrences from 38% to 27% [4]. One carboplatin study in high‑risk stage I was too small to show a clear difference [5]. Many early‑stage patients are not fully staged, which affects prognosis and may influence who benefits most from chemotherapy [3].

- **Full Answer**:  
Adjuvant (post‑surgery) chemotherapy can reduce recurrences and modestly improve survival in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer, but its benefit varies by risk level.

In older trials, cisplatin given after surgery cut the risk of the cancer returning by about 60–65%, but did not clearly prolong overall survival, possibly because the studies were small [1]. In well‑staged, low‑risk stage I patients, melphalan chemotherapy did not improve 5‑year survival compared with observation alone; both groups had survival around 95% [2]. For higher‑risk stage I or stage II disease, melphalan or intraperitoneal 32P produced similar 5‑year disease‑free survival of about 80% [2].

A larger, modern trial using platinum‑based chemotherapy found clearer benefits: 5‑year overall survival improved from 70% to 79%, and the chance of remaining free of recurrence improved from 62% to 73% [4]. Another carboplatin trial in high‑risk stage I was inconclusive, with nearly identical outcomes between groups [5].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across trials, adjuvant chemotherapy for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer shows mixed results. Some older studies using melphalan or radioactive phosphorus found no clear survival advantage compared with careful follow‑up alone; 5‑year disease‑free and overall survival were already high (around 80–98%) without chemotherapy, so extra treatment added little benefit in these low‑ and intermediate‑risk groups [2]. A small carboplatin trial also showed almost identical survival between chemotherapy and observation, but it was too small to be conclusive [5].  

However, other studies using platinum drugs (cisplatin) found chemotherapy cut relapses by about 60–65%, although this did not clearly translate into better overall survival in those trials [1]. A larger international trial (ICON1) showed a modest but real benefit: 5‑year overall survival improved from 70% without chemotherapy to 79% with it, and recurrence‑free survival from 62% to 73% [4]. Incomplete surgical staging complicates judging who truly needs chemotherapy [3].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Adjuvant chemotherapy is not completely ineffective, but its benefit in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer is modest and depends on risk level.  

In some well-staged, low‑risk patients, adding older chemotherapy drugs like melphalan did not improve already excellent 5‑year disease‑free (91–98%) or overall survival (94–98%) compared with no chemotherapy [2]. A small trial of carboplatin also found virtually identical survival with or without adjuvant treatment, though it was too small to give a firm answer [5].  

Other studies with cisplatin showed chemotherapy reduced the chance of cancer coming back by about 60–65%, but these trials did not clearly show people lived longer overall [1]. The largest modern trial (ICON1) found a modest survival gain: 5‑year overall survival rose from 70% without chemotherapy to 79% with it, and recurrence‑free survival from 62% to 73% [4].  

Because many patients are not fully staged surgically, some “early-stage” women may actually be higher‑risk, making the true benefit of chemotherapy harder to judge [3].

efficacy.positive_question: Does adjuvant chemotherapy work for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
efficacy.negative_question: Does adjuvant chemotherapy not work for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Randomized trials of older drugs (melphalan or radioactive phosphorus) in well-staged, low‑risk women (earlier stage, well/moderately differentiated tumors) found no clear survival advantage from adjuvant chemotherapy compared with careful follow‑up, with 5‑year survival already above 90% [2]. In higher‑risk early stages, cisplatin reduced relapses by about 60% but did not clearly improve overall survival in smaller trials [1]. A larger international trial (ICON1) using modern platinum‑based chemotherapy showed better overall survival (about 9% absolute improvement at 5 years) and fewer recurrences (about 11% improvement) versus no immediate chemotherapy [4]. Another smaller carboplatin trial in high‑risk stage I showed no difference, but confidence intervals were wide and the study was underpowered, so results were inconclusive [5]. Quality of surgical staging strongly affects prognosis and who truly needs chemotherapy [3]. Overall, benefits are modest and greatest in higher‑risk early‑stage patients.

- **Full Answer**:  
Adjuvant chemotherapy can help some women with early‑stage epithelial ovarian cancer, but its benefit depends on risk level and quality of surgery.

In fully staged, low‑risk patients (very early stage, well or moderately differentiated tumors), long‑term survival is already excellent, and older chemotherapy (melphalan) did not clearly improve outcomes compared with observation alone [2].  

In higher‑risk early‑stage disease, platinum drugs such as cisplatin and carboplatin substantially reduce the chance of the cancer coming back [1,4]. The largest trial (ICON1) found that platinum‑based adjuvant chemotherapy improved both overall survival (about 70% to 79% at 5 years) and recurrence‑free survival (about 62% to 73%) compared with waiting to treat until relapse [4].  

A smaller modern carboplatin study did not show a clear benefit, but it included too few patients to be definitive [5]. Proper, comprehensive surgical staging is crucial to identify who can safely skip chemotherapy and who is likely to benefit [3].
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Several randomized trials have tested adjuvant chemotherapy in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer. Older, non‑platinum drugs (like melphalan) did *not* improve survival in carefully staged, very low‑risk stage I patients, suggesting this group can safely skip chemotherapy [2]. Platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin/carboplatin) clearly lowers the chance of the cancer coming back [1,4]. In a large international trial, platinum chemotherapy also improved overall survival by about 9% at 5 years and reduced recurrences by about 11% [4]. One smaller high‑risk stage I trial with carboplatin was underpowered and therefore inconclusive, with overlapping survival curves but wide confidence intervals [5]. In practice, many “early-stage” patients are not completely staged surgically, which increases risk and makes adjuvant chemotherapy more important [3].

- **Full Answer**:  
Adjuvant chemotherapy *does* work for many women with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer, but the benefit depends on risk level and surgical staging.  

In well-staged, low‑risk stage I disease, older chemotherapy (melphalan) did not improve survival compared with close follow‑up alone [2].  

By contrast, platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin/carboplatin) substantially reduces recurrences [1,4]. A large international trial showed platinum chemotherapy improved 5‑year overall survival (79% vs 70%) and recurrence‑free survival (73% vs 62%) compared with no immediate chemotherapy [4].  

A smaller high‑risk stage I trial using carboplatin found no clear survival difference, but it was too small to give a firm answer [5].  

Because many “early-stage” patients are incompletely staged, their true risk is often higher, and adjuvant chemotherapy is more likely to be beneficial in these cases [3].

safety.positive_question: Is adjuvant chemotherapy safe for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
safety.negative_question: Is adjuvant chemotherapy dangerous for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is about safety, not just benefit. Several randomized trials compared adjuvant chemotherapy with observation or alternative treatments in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer. Platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin) reduced recurrences and, in one large trial, improved survival without showing more treatment-related deaths, suggesting an acceptable safety profile [1][4]. Other regimens (melphalan, intraperitoneal 32P) showed similar survival to observation, again without evidence of excess harm [2][5]. One cisplatin study found that women who relapsed after cisplatin were more likely to die of their recurrence, but they relapsed less often overall [1]. Very low‑risk, well‑staged patients can safely skip chemotherapy and be followed [2][3][5].  

- **Full Answer**:  
Across multiple randomized trials, adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery for early‑stage epithelial ovarian cancer did not increase death rates and was generally considered tolerable. Platinum‑based regimens (cisplatin or carboplatin) reduced recurrences and, in one large trial, improved 5‑year survival from about 70% to 79% without evidence of excess treatment‑related deaths [1][4]. Other drugs (melphalan) and intraperitoneal radiation (32P) produced similar survival to observation, again with no signal of harm from adding treatment [2][5]. One cisplatin study suggested that, among women who later relapsed, those previously given cisplatin were more likely to die of their recurrence, but overall relapse rates were much lower in the chemotherapy group [1]. These trials support that adjuvant chemotherapy is reasonably safe and can provide net benefit, particularly for higher‑risk stage I–II disease [1][2][4][5]. Women with very low‑risk, well‑staged cancers may safely avoid chemotherapy and be monitored instead, in discussion with their gynecologic oncologist and team [2][3][5].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies focus on whether adjuvant chemotherapy helps people with early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer live longer and avoid relapse. They do not show that chemotherapy is more dangerous than observation in terms of overall survival. Some drugs clearly reduce the risk of the cancer coming back and, in at least one large trial, improve survival. In low‑risk, well‑staged patients, surgery alone can be enough. In higher‑risk or incompletely staged patients, chemotherapy is usually advised, with a trade‑off between side effects and better cancer control.

- **Full Answer**:  
Adjuvant chemotherapy is not generally considered “dangerous” for early‑stage epithelial ovarian cancer, but it is not always necessary.

Several randomized trials show that adding platinum‑based chemotherapy after surgery lowers the chance the cancer comes back and may improve survival. Cisplatin cut relapse rates by about 60–65% compared with no treatment or 32P, although the overall survival benefit was small and uncertain [1]. A larger international trial found that platinum‑based adjuvant chemotherapy improved 5‑year overall survival from about 70% to 79% and reduced recurrences from 62% to 73% [4]. Another carboplatin trial showed no clear survival difference, but chemotherapy did not worsen survival [5].

Some low‑risk patients (small, well‑differentiated tumors confined to the ovaries and fully staged) did well without chemotherapy, with 5‑year survival above 90% [2]. Therefore, chemotherapy is usually reserved for higher‑risk or incompletely staged patients [2,3]. Side effects and individual risks should be weighed carefully with an oncologist.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing adjuvant chemotherapy is good for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing adjuvant chemotherapy is harmful for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The user asks whether scientific studies show a benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy in early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer. The summaries include multiple randomized trials comparing adjuvant chemotherapy with observation or other treatments, and one large international trial shows a clear survival advantage with platinum-based chemotherapy. Others show reduced relapse but unclear survival benefit, or are inconclusive. I will synthesize these findings into a lay-friendly, 150‑word answer.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. Several randomized clinical trials have tested chemotherapy given after surgery (adjuvant chemotherapy) in early‑stage epithelial ovarian cancer. In two Italian trials, adding cisplatin after surgery reduced the chance of the cancer coming back by about 60–65% compared with no treatment or radioactive phosphorus, although an overall survival advantage was not clearly shown [1]. A large international trial (ICON1) found that platinum‑based adjuvant chemotherapy improved both survival and time before recurrence: 5‑year overall survival was 79% with chemotherapy versus 70% without, and recurrence‑free survival 73% versus 62% [4]. Some showed fewer recurrences and a small survival benefit, especially when platinum drugs were used, but others showed no clear survival gain, particularly in very low‑risk, well‑staged cancers. Benefit appears to depend strongly on stage, tumor grade, and how thoroughly surgery and staging were done. Because chemotherapy also has important side effects, it is not automatically “safe” or necessary for everyone. I can summarize evidence, but I cannot tell you personally to proceed or not; that decision should be made with your oncologist, who knows your exact stage, pathology, and overall health.

- **Full Answer**:  
Research shows that adjuvant chemotherapy for early-stage epithelial ovarian cancer offers modest benefits, not a guaranteed large effect for everyone. In one large trial, adding platinum-based chemotherapy after surgery improved 5‑year survival from about 70% to 79% and reduced recurrences from 38% to 27% [4]. Earlier trials with cisplatin also cut the risk of relapse by about 60%, but did not clearly increase overall survival [1]. Other studies found that, in very low‑risk, well‑staged stage I cancers, chemotherapy did not improve already excellent 5‑year survival (around 94%–98%) compared with careful follow‑up alone [2]. A trial in higher‑risk stage I disease using carboplatin similarly showed no clear survival advantage, although it was too small to be definitive [5]. Overall, chemo seems most helpful for patients with higher‑risk or incompletely staged disease [3][4]. It also carries side effects, so the decision should be individualized with your oncology team.
