ReviewTitle: Oral steroids for long‐term use in cystic fibrosis

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: In cystic fibrosis (CF) airway obstruction and recurrent respiratory infection lead to inflammation, long-term lung damage, respiratory failure and death. Anti-inflammatory agents, e.g. oral corticosteroids are used since inflammation occurs early in disease. This is an update of a previously published review.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess the effectiveness of oral corticosteroids in respiratory complications in CF, particularly lung function and adverse events. We examined long-term use (over 30 days) only.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text:
We searched the Cochrane CF and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register comprising references identified from comprehensive electronic database searches and handsearches of relevant journals and abstract books of conference proceedings.
Most recent search: 28 August 2015.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised trials comparing oral corticosteroids given for more than 30 days with placebo or no additional therapy in people with CF.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two authors independently assessed study eligibility and quality.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text:
Of eleven studies identified, three (354 participants) were included: two with four-year follow up and one with 12-weeks follow up. Data were lacking on predefined outcomes; common outcomes were examined at different time-points and presented differently. Meta-analyses were not possible.
In one study, oral corticosteroids at prednisolone-equivalent dose of 1 mg/kg alternate days slowed progression of lung disease; at two and four years, % predicted FEV1 in the 1 mg/kg group changed significantly more than in the placebo group (P < 0.02). During the first two years, the 2 mg/kg group was not significantly different from the placebo group. Linear growth retardation was observed from six months in the 2 mg/kg alternate days prednisolone group and from 24 months in the 1 mg/kg alternate days prednisolone group.
Adverse events terminated one four-year study early. Year 10 follow up showed catch-up growth started two years after treatment ceased. Alternate-day treatment with oral corticosteroids may have impaired growth until adulthood in boys.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: Oral corticosteroids at prednisolone-equivalent dose of 1 to 2 mg/kg alternate days appear to slow progression of lung disease in CF; benefit should be weighed against occurrence of adverse events. Risk-benefit analysis of low-dose alternate days corticosteroids is important. No further trials of this intervention are anticipated, and hence the review will no longer be regularly updated. However, if any new data are published, these will be incorporate when available.

Inputs.Title: Alternate-day prednisone reduces morbidity and improves pulmonary function in cystic fibrosis.
Inputs.Abstract: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study examined the effects of alternate-day prednisone therapy on morbidity and progression of lung disease in cystic fibrosis (CF). At baseline the patients (aged 1-12 years) had mild to moderate lung disease, and the prednisone group did not differ significantly from the placebo group for any values measured. After 4 years, the prednisone-treated group had significant advantages over the placebo group for height, weight, vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in 1 s, peak flow rate, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum IgG. The prednisone-treated group required 9 admissions to hospital for CF-related pulmonary disease compared with 35 for the placebo group. There were no steroid-induced side-effects. To rule out bias in case selection, 69 CF clinic patients comparable in age and clinical status but not included in the study were compared with the placebo group at 4 years; no significant differences between the groups were found.

Inputs.Title: Interleukin-1 alpha, soluble interleukin-2 receptor, and IgG concentrations in cystic fibrosis treated with prednisolone.
Inputs.Abstract: The cytokines interleukin-1 and interleukin-2 participate in the inflammatory response, and may contribute to hypergammaglobulinaemia G and the development of lung injury in cystic fibrosis. Anti-inflammatory treatment with corticosteroids may attenuate this response. The effect of a 12 week course of oral prednisolone on spirometry and serum concentrations of interleukin-1 alpha (IL-1 alpha), soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R), and IgG was investigated in 24 children with cystic fibrosis. Prednisolone was administered, in a double blind and placebo controlled manner, at an initial dose of 2 mg/kg daily for 14 days and tapered to 1 mg/kg on alternate days for 10 weeks. The treated group (n = 12) experienced an increase in forced expiratory volume in one second and forced vital capacity at 14 days, however, these changes were smaller at 12 weeks. In the treated group, change in pulmonary function was associated with decreased serum IgG and cytokine concentrations. Prednisolone suppresses serum concentrations of these cytokines, which may participate in the inflammatory response, the excessive synthesis of IgG, and airflow obstruction observed in cystic fibrosis patients.

Inputs.Title: A multicenter study of alternate-day prednisone therapy in patients with cystic fibrosis. Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Prednisone Trial Group.
Inputs.Abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of alternate-day prednisone therapy in treating patients with mild-to-moderate cystic fibrosis during a 4-year period. In 15 North American cystic fibrosis centers, we screened 320 patients and enrolled 285 patients from April 1986 to December 1987. Patients were randomly assigned to take prednisone, 1 mg/kg per dose or 2 mg/kg per dose, or a matching placebo given on alternate days. Lung function, clinical status, hospitalizations, growth, and steroid side effects were monitored. During the first 24 months the percentage of the predicted forced vital capacity was greater in the 1 mg/kg group (p < 0.0001) and the 2 mg/kg group (p < 0.01) when each was compared with placebo. Patients in the 1 mg/kg group had a higher percentage of predicted forced vital capacity than placebo patients during the entire 48 months (p < 0.0025), but only in the group of patients who were colonized with Pseudomonas aeruginosa at baseline. For 48 months, the 1 mg/kg group had a higher percentage of predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second than patients given placebo (p < 0.02). The prednisone-treated groups had a reduction in serum IgG concentrations (1 mg/kg vs placebo, p < 0.007; 2 mg/kg vs placebo, p < 0.003). From 6 months onward, height z scores fell in the 2 mg/kg group compared with those given placebo (p < 0.001). For the 1 mg/kg group, height z scores were lower from 24 months. An excess of abnormalities in glucose metabolism was seen in the 2 mg/kg group compared with the placebo group (p < 0.005). Our findings suggest a role for alternate-day prednisone therapy at a dose of 1 mg/kg in patients with mild to moderate cystic fibrosis. The benefit of improved lung function appears to outweigh the potential for adverse effects when the treatment period is less than 24 months.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is oral corticosteroids for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is oral corticosteroids for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The articles describe randomized, placebo‑controlled trials of oral corticosteroids in children with mild–moderate cystic fibrosis lung disease. They report consistent, though modest, improvements in lung function and reduced hospital use, but also important long‑term side effects, particularly with higher doses and longer treatment. I combined these findings to explain both benefits and risks in everyday language, emphasizing that side effects limit routine, long‑term use.

- **Full Answer**:  
Oral corticosteroids such as prednisone or prednisolone can modestly improve lung function and reduce respiratory complications in some people with cystic fibrosis, but benefits come with important risks.  

In small and large trials, alternate‑day prednisone (about 1–2 mg/kg) in children with mild to moderate lung disease improved measures like forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second over months to years compared with placebo, and reduced hospitalizations for lung problems [1][3]. Short‑term prednisolone also led to temporary gains in lung function and lowered inflammatory markers thought to contribute to airway damage [2]. However, longer‑term use, especially at higher doses (2 mg/kg), caused slowed growth and more abnormalities in blood sugar control [3]. Even 1 mg/kg was linked to reduced growth after about two years [3]. Overall, oral corticosteroids can help respiratory outcomes, but because of side effects, they are generally reserved for selected patients and limited durations [1][2][3].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks how *ineffective* oral corticosteroids are for cystic fibrosis (CF) lung problems. The three trials summarized here are all randomized, placebo‑controlled studies and consistently show that prednisone/prednisolone improves lung function and reduces some complications, at least in the short to medium term. However, the benefits are modest and partly fade over time, and longer or higher‑dose treatment causes important side effects, especially poor growth and abnormal blood sugar. So they are not “ineffective,” but their usefulness is limited by harms.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across these studies, oral corticosteroids were not completely ineffective for lung problems in cystic fibrosis, but their benefits were modest and came with important risks.

In one 4‑year trial of children with mild–moderate disease, alternate‑day prednisone improved lung function tests and reduced hospitalizations for chest infections (9 vs 35 admissions) compared with placebo [1]. Another 12‑week study of prednisolone showed a short‑term rise in breathing tests at 2 weeks, but this improvement became smaller by 12 weeks [2]. A large multicenter trial found that alternate‑day prednisone (1–2 mg/kg) improved lung capacity and airflow over 2–4 years, especially at 1 mg/kg [3]. However, longer use—particularly at 2 mg/kg—caused growth delay and more abnormal blood sugar results [3].

Overall, oral corticosteroids can help breathing somewhat, but the effects are limited and may fade over time, while side effects increase with dose and duration [1–3].

efficacy.positive_question: Does oral corticosteroids work for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
efficacy.negative_question: Does oral corticosteroids not work for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Three randomized, placebo-controlled trials in children with cystic fibrosis tested oral corticosteroids (prednisone or prednisolone) for lung disease. All showed some improvement in lung function and markers of inflammation, and one showed fewer hospitalizations for chest problems with alternate‑day prednisone. However, the largest, long‑term study also found important side effects at higher doses and with prolonged use, including reduced growth and abnormal glucose metabolism. Benefits were clearest in patients with mild–moderate disease, especially those already infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and mainly over shorter periods. Overall, oral corticosteroids can help respiratory outcomes but their risks limit routine, long‑term use, so they are used selectively rather than as standard daily treatment.

- **Full Answer**:  
Overall, oral corticosteroids can improve some respiratory outcomes in cystic fibrosis, but benefits are modest and must be weighed against side effects.  

In one 4‑year trial of children with mild–moderate lung disease, alternate‑day prednisone led to better lung function tests (vital capacity, FEV1, peak flow) and far fewer hospital admissions for chest problems (9 vs 35) than placebo, with no major steroid side effects reported in that small study [1]. A second trial using prednisolone for 12 weeks showed short‑term improvements in FEV1 and forced vital capacity and reductions in blood markers of inflammation [2]. A large multicenter trial found that alternate‑day prednisone 1 mg/kg improved lung function over up to 4 years, especially in patients already infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa [3]. However, longer or higher‑dose treatment caused growth delay and abnormal glucose metabolism, limiting routine long‑term use [3]. Doctors therefore use them selectively, not as standard everyday therapy today.
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across several controlled trials, oral corticosteroids (prednisone/prednisolone) improved lung function and reduced inflammation in people with cystic fibrosis, but longer‑term use caused important side effects, especially at higher doses and beyond about two years. This means they *do* work for respiratory complications, but their risks limit routine long‑term use.

- **Full Answer**:  
Oral corticosteroids are not useless in cystic fibrosis; they can improve breathing and reduce complications, but safety is a concern. In children with mild–moderate lung disease, alternate‑day prednisone over 4 years improved lung function (vital capacity, FEV₁, peak flow), growth measures, and reduced hospital admissions for lung problems, without clear steroid side effects in that small study [1]. Another trial of prednisolone for 12 weeks showed short‑term improvement in lung function and reduced inflammatory markers (IgG and cytokines), which are linked to airway damage [2]. A large multicenter study found that 1 mg/kg prednisone on alternate days improved FVC and FEV₁ for up to 4 years and lowered IgG [3]. However, higher doses and longer treatment led to growth suppression and abnormal glucose metabolism [3]. Thus, oral corticosteroids can work, but long‑term routine use is limited by side effects.

safety.positive_question: Is oral corticosteroids safe for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
safety.negative_question: Is oral corticosteroids dangerous for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that oral corticosteroids (like prednisone/prednisolone) can improve lung function, reduce inflammation, and lower hospitalizations in children with mild to moderate cystic fibrosis. However, safety depends strongly on dose and duration. Lower-dose, alternate‑day regimens for limited periods (up to about 2 years) showed benefits that may outweigh risks in selected patients, but higher doses and longer use led to important side effects, including growth delay and abnormal blood sugar. Therefore, oral corticosteroids are not universally “safe,” but can be used cautiously, short term, and under close medical supervision.

- **Full Answer**:  
Oral corticosteroids can improve lung function and reduce hospitalizations in some children with mild to moderate cystic fibrosis, but they are not risk‑free and are usually not used long term today. In early studies, alternate‑day prednisone for up to 4 years improved growth, lung tests, and reduced hospital admissions without clear steroid side‑effects in a small group of children [1]. A larger trial confirmed better lung function and lower IgG levels, especially with 1 mg/kg on alternate days, and suggested benefits outweigh harms if treatment is kept under about 2 years [3]. However, higher doses and longer use caused growth delay and more problems with blood sugar control, especially at 2 mg/kg [3]. Shorter 12‑week courses of prednisolone also improved breathing tests and reduced inflammation markers [2]. Overall, oral corticosteroids may be reasonably safe for carefully selected patients, at the lowest effective dose and limited duration, with close monitoring [2][3].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks if oral corticosteroids are dangerous for respiratory (lung) complications in cystic fibrosis (CF). The three trials provided all evaluated oral prednisone/prednisolone in children with mild to moderate CF over weeks to years. All show either improved or stabilised lung function and fewer pulmonary hospitalizations, with no signal that steroids worsened breathing outcomes [1–3]. However, the large multicenter trial clearly shows important non-respiratory harms (growth suppression, glucose problems), especially at higher doses or longer duration [3]. Therefore, the respiratory safety looks acceptable or even beneficial, but overall use is limited by systemic side effects and must be carefully supervised.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, oral corticosteroids do not appear dangerous for lung complications in cystic fibrosis when used carefully; in fact, they can modestly help. In one four‑year trial, children taking alternate‑day prednisone had better lung function and far fewer hospital admissions for chest problems than those on placebo, with no steroid‑related side effects reported in that group [1]. A 12‑week prednisolone course briefly improved breathing tests and reduced blood markers of inflammation, without evidence of worsened respiratory disease [2]. In a larger multicenter study, alternate‑day prednisone (especially 1 mg/kg) improved lung function over several years compared with placebo [3]. However, longer‑term use, particularly at higher doses, caused important whole‑body side effects such as slowed growth and abnormal blood sugar [3]. Overall, oral corticosteroids are not shown to worsen respiratory outcomes in cystic fibrosis, but any potential lung benefit must be weighed against systemic risks, and they should be specialist‑guided.

Yes. Multiple scientific studies show that oral corticosteroids can improve respiratory outcomes in cystic fibrosis, at least in the short to medium term.

An early randomized, placebo-controlled trial of alternate-day prednisone in children with mild–moderate CF found better lung function (vital capacity, FEV₁, peak flow) and fewer hospital admissions for lung problems in the steroid group, with no clear steroid side effects over 4 years [1].

A large multicenter trial of alternate‑day prednisone (1 mg/kg) showed better FEV₁ and FVC over up to 4 years, especially in patients with Pseudomonas infection, but also growth delay and glucose metabolism problems, particularly at higher doses or longer use [3].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:

All reported either improved or temporarily improved lung function and, in one study, fewer hospitalizations for lung problems. None showed that oral corticosteroids worsened respiratory outcomes. However, the largest, long‑term study did find significant non‑lung side effects (growth suppression and abnormal glucose metabolism), which limit routine use. Therefore, within these studies, harm was systemic rather than respiratory.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on the studies provided, oral corticosteroids have not been shown to be harmful for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis. In a 4‑year trial of alternate‑day prednisone in children, those on prednisone had better lung function and far fewer hospital admissions for cystic‑fibrosis–related lung disease, with no reported steroid side effects during the study period [1]. A 12‑week prednisolone study also showed improved breathing tests and reduced inflammatory markers, not worse lung outcomes [2]. However, this trial did detect non‑respiratory harms, including slowed growth and more abnormal blood sugar tests at higher doses, which limit long‑term use [3]. Overall, these studies suggest respiratory benefit, not respiratory harm, but important systemic risks.

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is oral corticosteroids a good choice for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is oral corticosteroids a bad choice for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**: Trials show some lung benefits from oral steroids in CF but significant long‑term side effects.

In children with mild–moderate CF, alternate‑day prednisone (about 1 mg/kg) improved lung function and reduced hospitalizations for lung disease over several years compared with placebo [1][3]. However, the large multicenter trial found important harms with long‑term use: growth slowed, especially at 2 mg/kg, and glucose metabolism problems increased; even 1 mg/kg impaired growth after 2 years [3]. The authors therefore only support 1 mg/kg alternate‑day treatment for carefully selected patients, and for less than 24 months [3].

You should only consider this under a cystic fibrosis specialist’s close supervision.

They show that alternate‑day prednisone or prednisolone can improve lung function, reduce hospitalizations, and lower inflammation markers. However, when doses are higher or treatment is prolonged, important side effects appear, especially poor growth and changes in blood sugar that could lead toward diabetes. Oral corticosteroids are not automatically a “bad” choice, but they have trade‑offs.

In children with mild–moderate cystic fibrosis, alternate‑day prednisone (about 1–2 mg/kg) improved lung function and reduced hospital admissions for lung problems over several years, with no major steroid‑side‑effects in one study [1]. A 12‑week prednisolone course also briefly improved breathing tests and lowered inflammation markers [2]. In a larger 4‑year trial, 1 mg/kg on alternate days improved lung function, especially in patients with Pseudomonas infection, and lowered IgG (an inflammation marker) [3].

However, higher doses (2 mg/kg) and longer treatment caused slowed growth and more abnormal blood sugar results, suggesting a risk of diabetes‑like problems [3]. Even 1 mg/kg affected growth after about 2 years [3].

So, oral steroids can help breathing but carry important long‑term risks, especially in children. They’re usually reserved for selected patients and limited duration, under a CF specialist’s close supervision and regular monitoring.

cost.positive_question: Is oral corticosteroids worth the money for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
cost.negative_question: Is oral corticosteroids not worth the money for respiratory complications in cystic fibrosis?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The trials did not directly measure cost or cost‑effectiveness, so “worth the money” must be inferred from clinical benefits versus harms, which drive health‑care costs. Oral corticosteroids improved lung function and reduced hospitalizations in mild–moderate cystic fibrosis, especially in selected patients [1][2][3]. However, longer‑term and higher‑dose use caused important side‑effects such as impaired growth and abnormal glucose metabolism [3], which carry medical and economic consequences. Thus, value depends on dose, duration, and patient selection.

- **Full Answer**:  
Oral corticosteroids can improve lung function and reduce hospital admissions in some children with cystic fibrosis who have mild to moderate lung disease. In a 4‑year study, alternate‑day prednisone led to better growth, breathing tests, and far fewer hospital stays for lung problems compared with placebo, with no clear steroid side‑effects reported [1]. Another trial showed short‑term improvements in breathing and reductions in inflammation markers after 12 weeks of prednisolone [2]. A large multicenter study found that 1 mg/kg alternate‑day prednisone improved lung function for up to 4 years, particularly in patients already colonized with Pseudomonas, but caused reduced growth after about 2 years; a higher 2 mg/kg dose also produced glucose (pre‑diabetes) problems [3]. Fewer hospitalizations suggest potential cost savings [1], but growth and metabolic complications can create future health costs [3]. Overall, limited‑duration, low‑dose alternate‑day prednisone may be “worth it” only for carefully selected patients under specialist supervision.
cost.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks if oral corticosteroids are “not worth the money” for lung problems in cystic fibrosis. The three trials provided do not report costs directly, so value must be judged by clinical benefits (lung function, hospitalizations) versus harms (side effects). Two long-term randomized studies of alternate‑day prednisone and one short‑term prednisolone study show meaningful improvements in lung function, inflammation, growth, and fewer hospital admissions, but also important side effects (growth slowing, glucose problems) at higher doses and longer durations. Thus, oral steroids appear potentially cost‑worthy only in carefully chosen patients, at moderate doses, for limited periods, with close monitoring.

- **Full Answer**:  
Oral corticosteroids for cystic fibrosis lung disease do have measurable benefits, but also important risks, and the studies did not directly measure cost.  

In children with mild‑to‑moderate cystic fibrosis, alternate‑day prednisone for several years improved lung function, growth, and reduced hospital admissions for lung problems, without clear steroid side‑effects in one study [1]. Another trial showed short‑term prednisolone improved breathing tests and lowered inflammation‑related blood markers [2]. A large multicenter study found that alternate‑day prednisone 1 mg/kg improved lung function for up to 4 years, especially in patients with Pseudomonas infection, and lowered IgG levels [3].  

However, the same long‑term trial showed growth slowing and more abnormal blood sugar tests, especially at higher doses and with longer use [3].  

Because better lung function and fewer hospitalizations can reduce healthcare costs, oral corticosteroids may be “worth it” for carefully selected patients, at moderate doses and limited duration, with close monitoring [1][3].

They show that oral corticosteroids (prednisone/prednisolone) can improve lung function and reduce hospitalizations in children with mild–moderate cystic fibrosis, at least for limited periods.
