effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is structured treatment interruptions for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is structured treatment interruptions for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across many trials in people with chronic HIV whose virus was well controlled on treatment, interrupting therapy on a schedule almost always led to the virus coming back quickly. Only a few patients maintained low virus levels without drugs, usually those who already had very strong immune responses. Short, frequent breaks often failed and sometimes allowed resistance to develop. Longer, CD4-guided breaks could be clinically safe for selected patients with high CD4 counts, but did not train the body to control HIV better. Benefits were mostly reduced drug exposure and some metabolic or psychological improvements, not better HIV control.

- **Full Answer**:  
Stopping HIV pills in a planned, repeated way (“structured treatment interruptions”) has generally not worked well for people with long‑term, suppressed HIV. In most studies, the virus rebounded to detectable levels within days to weeks after stopping, even after several interruption cycles [7][10][17][18][19][31]. Only a small minority kept low viral loads without drugs, and this was usually linked to unusually strong immune responses before stopping [27][31][33]. Short cycles such as 1‑week‑on/1‑week‑off led to frequent virologic failure and were stopped early [1][4][7][26]. Repeated interruptions can allow drug‑resistant virus to emerge, especially with prior suboptimal regimens [1][3][7][20][22][25][26]. CD4‑guided interruptions in people starting with very high CD4 counts appeared clinically safe over 1–3 years and reduced time on drugs, but did not improve the body’s long‑term control of HIV [1][14][15][21][23][31]. Some studies noted modest psychological or cholesterol improvements off therapy [2][24]. Overall, continuous antiretroviral therapy remains the more effective standard of HIV care.
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies in people with long‑term, well‑controlled HIV show that stopping and restarting treatment on a schedule almost always lets the virus come back quickly. Although a few patients keep lower viral loads off treatment, this is a small minority. Overall, structured interruptions do not give better control of HIV than just staying on therapy, and some interruption patterns clearly fail and may promote drug resistance.

- **Full Answer**:  
In chronic HIV infection with well‑suppressed virus, structured treatment interruptions (STIs) are largely ineffective at keeping HIV under control without medicines. Viral load typically rebounds within days to weeks of stopping therapy [6,16,18]. In a randomized trial, repeated 2‑, 4‑, and 6‑week treatment breaks did not prolong time to viral rebound compared with one final interruption after continuous therapy [9]. Large STI programs found only about 17% of patients had low viral load (<5,000 copies/mL) at 1 year off therapy and just 8% at 2 years [30]. “Week‑on/week‑off” or similar short‑cycle strategies had high virologic failure rates (about 31–53%) [0,25,38]. Many studies show no lasting lowering of the viral “set point” or durable immune control in chronically infected patients [8,12,21,24,31]. Some STI regimens also allow drug‑resistant virus to emerge as minor or major variants [6,19,21,25,28,34].

efficacy.positive_question: Does structured treatment interruptions work for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
efficacy.negative_question: Does structured treatment interruptions not work for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across many trials in people with long‑term, well‑suppressed HIV, stopping or cycling treatment almost always led to the virus returning in the blood within days to weeks [7][17][18][19][31]. Although structured treatment interruptions (STIs) can temporarily lower drug exposure, improve cholesterol and triglycerides [24], and may be psychologically acceptable with close monitoring [2], they rarely produce lasting control of HIV without medication. Most studies show only modest or no reduction in the new “set point” of viral load and no clear clinical advantage over continuous therapy [3][9][10][18][25][27][31][32]. STIs can also cause CD4 cell drops and immune activation [13][16][19], and repeated on‑off cycles sometimes select drug‑resistant virus, especially with short cycles like 1‑week on/1‑week off [1][7][20][22][26]. CD4‑guided longer interruptions appear relatively safe in carefully selected patients and do reduce time on drugs, but people generally need to restart therapy as CD4 counts fall [1][14][15][21][23].

- **Full Answer**:  
For people with chronic HIV whose viral load is already well controlled on antiretroviral therapy, structured treatment interruptions generally do **not** “work” as a way to control HIV without ongoing medication.

In most studies, the virus rebounded within days to weeks of stopping treatment [7][17][18][19][31]. Although some patients had partial immune boosting or a slightly lower viral set point, this rarely translated into durable control off therapy and offered no clear advantage over continuous treatment [3][9][10][18][25][27][31][32].  

Short, frequent cycles (like 1 week on/1 week off) had high failure rates and sometimes led to resistance [1][7][20][22][26]. Longer CD4‑count–guided interruptions can be relatively safe in carefully monitored people with high CD4 counts and do reduce total time on drugs, but most eventually need to restart when CD4 levels drop [1][14][15][21][23].  

Overall, continuous therapy remains the standard; STIs are considered experimental and should be done only in clinical trials.
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across many trials in chronically infected people whose HIV was already well controlled on antiretroviral therapy, stopping and restarting treatment almost always led to the virus rebounding quickly, usually back toward pretreatment levels. Different interruption patterns (short, long, CD4‑guided) did not produce durable control of HIV off drugs and sometimes allowed resistance mutations to appear. Immune responses often increased during the off‑drug periods, but this boost did not translate into lasting viral control once medications were stopped. A few carefully selected patients, or those receiving additional drugs like hydroxyurea, could stay off treatment longer with lower viral loads, but they were a small minority and benefits were usually temporary. Overall, the evidence shows structured interruptions are not a dependable replacement for continuous therapy in chronic, suppressed HIV.

- **Full Answer**:  
Structured treatment interruptions (STIs) have generally not worked as a reliable strategy for people with chronic HIV whose virus is well suppressed on treatment.  

In most studies, stopping drugs leads to rapid viral rebound within days to weeks, with levels returning to pretreatment “set points” despite repeated interruption cycles [7,10,17,18,19,27,31]. Short- and long-cycle STI schedules (including week‑on/week‑off and 4‑week off/8‑week on) showed high rates of virologic failure and no lasting immunologic or toxicity benefit compared with continuous therapy [1,3,4,24,26,30]. STIs can also allow resistant virus to emerge, even when drugs are restarted and viral load re-suppresses [7,8,20,21,22,28]. Although a minority of carefully selected patients with strong pre‑existing immune responses or added hydroxyurea maintained lower viral loads for some time off therapy, this was uncommon and often temporary [11,18,21,28,33].  

Overall, for chronic, suppressed HIV infection, STIs are experimental and are not recommended outside closely monitored clinical trials in routine care today.

safety.positive_question: Is structured treatment interruptions safe for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
safety.negative_question: Is structured treatment interruptions dangerous for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across many studies, stopping HIV treatment in a planned, “on‑off” way almost always led to a quick return of virus in the blood within days to weeks, along with immune activation and some CD4 cell loss [6,13–15,17–19,31]. Most people regained CD4 counts and viral control after restarting the same drugs [10,14,17,19,31]. Serious AIDS illnesses were rare in carefully selected patients with high CD4 counts and close monitoring [1,10,14,15,31]. However, certain interruption patterns—especially 1 week on/1 week off or similar short cycles—had high rates of virologic failure and sometimes selected drug‑resistant virus, leading to early trial stoppage [1,3,6,7,20,22,26,27,32]. Longer CD4‑guided interruptions reduced time on drugs without short‑term clinical harm in high‑CD4 patients, but did not improve long‑term virus control and still carried resistance and immune‑damage risks [1,10,14,15,25,31]. Overall, continuous therapy remains safer as routine care.

- **Full Answer**:  
For people with chronic HIV whose virus is well suppressed, structured treatment interruptions are not generally considered safe as routine care. In most studies, virus levels rebounded quickly each time treatment was stopped, and immune activation increased, with some fall in CD4 counts, even though counts usually recovered after restarting therapy [6,13–15,17–19,31]. Serious AIDS‑defining illnesses were uncommon in carefully chosen patients with high CD4 counts and close follow‑up [1,10,14,15,31]. However, short‑cycle strategies such as 1 week on/1 week off or similar designs showed high rates of virologic failure and sometimes selected drug‑resistant virus, leading to early termination of these arms [1,3,6,7,20,22,26,27,32]. Longer, CD4‑guided interruptions reduced time on drugs and appeared short‑term clinically safe in selected patients, but did not reliably improve long‑term control of the virus and still carried risks [1,10,14,15,25,31]. Continuous antiretroviral therapy therefore remains the safer standard outside of clinical trials.
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
In chronic HIV with suppressed virus, the key safety issues of structured treatment interruptions (STIs) are: clinical illness, CD4 cell trends, how fast the virus rebounds, and whether drug resistance appears. Randomized and cohort studies in carefully chosen patients with high CD4 counts found very few AIDS‑defining illnesses over 1–2 years, so short or CD4‑guided interruptions can be clinically safe under close monitoring [1][14][15][17][31]. However, almost everyone has rapid viral rebound within days to a few weeks, with immune activation and some CD4 loss [7][17][19][29]. Certain STI patterns, especially 1‑week‑on/1‑week‑off or long off‑periods, produced high rates of loss of viral control and drug‑resistant virus [1][3][20][22][26]. Trials designed to “train” the immune system rarely achieved lasting control of HIV off therapy [10][18][25][27][31]. Because benefits are limited and virologic risks are real, major studies advise keeping STIs within research settings, not routine care [3][7][25][31].

- **Full Answer**:  
Studies in people with long‑term viral suppression and high CD4 counts found that planned treatment interruptions rarely caused AIDS‑defining illnesses, and CD4 counts usually recovered after medicines were restarted [1][13][14][15][17][31]. But the virus almost always rebounded within days to weeks of stopping therapy [7][17][19], with immune activation and some CD4 loss, especially in those with lower past CD4 levels [13][15][16][19][29].

Several stop‑start patterns – particularly 1‑week‑on/1‑week‑off and 4‑weeks‑off/8‑weeks‑on cycles – led to frequent loss of viral control and emergence of drug‑resistant HIV, causing early trial termination [1][3][7][20][22][26]. Repeated interruptions also rarely produced lasting “immune control” of HIV; most patients ultimately needed to go back to continuous treatment [10][18][25][27][31].

So, while carefully supervised interruptions can sometimes be “safe,” they carry meaningful risks to viral suppression and future treatment options, and large trials conclude they should remain research tools, not routine care, for chronically infected patients with suppressed virus [3][7][25][31].

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing structured treatment interruptions is good for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing structured treatment interruptions is harmful for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across many trials in people with chronic HIV whose virus was already undetectable on antiretroviral therapy (ART), interrupting treatment almost always led to rapid viral rebound, immune activation, and sometimes CD4 decline and resistance, while rarely giving durable control off ART [7][10][15][16][19][20][22][26][31]. Some small, carefully monitored studies showed that interruptions can cut drug exposure and modestly improve cholesterol without short‑term AIDS events in selected high‑CD4 patients [1][4][14][15][21][24]. However, large randomized trials did not show better long‑term viral control or clear clinical benefit compared with staying on continuous therapy [3][10][25][30][31]. Only a small minority, usually with very favorable baseline profiles, maintained low viral loads long‑term without drugs [11][18][21][27][31][33]. Overall, evidence does not support structured interruptions as a generally beneficial strategy for chronically infected, suppressed patients.

- **Full Answer**:  
Many studies have tested structured treatment interruptions (STIs) in people with chronic HIV whose virus was well controlled on therapy. Most show that when drugs are stopped, the virus usually comes back within days to weeks, CD4 counts often fall, immune activation increases, and drug‑resistant virus can appear [7][15][16][19][20][22][26][31]. Randomized trials comparing STI with continuous treatment found no lasting benefit in keeping the virus low without drugs, and no clear improvement in side effects or lab markers overall [3][10][25][30][31]. Some small studies found that CD4‑guided or short‑cycle interruptions could reduce time on medications and improve cholesterol in carefully selected patients, without short‑term AIDS events [1][4][14][15][21][24]. A small minority maintained low viral loads long‑term off therapy, usually those with unusually strong immune responses or very low pre‑treatment viral loads [11][18][21][27][31][33]. Overall, current evidence does not support STIs as a generally “good” or routine strategy for chronically infected, suppressed patients in practice.
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Randomized and prospective studies of structured treatment interruptions (STIs) in people with chronic HIV and undetectable viral load on therapy have been done. Fixed on/off schedules often caused rapid viral rebound, CD4 cell declines, immune activation, and sometimes drug resistance. CD4‑guided interruptions in carefully selected, closely monitored patients looked safer, but did not clearly improve long‑term outcomes compared with staying on treatment. Overall, the literature shows that some STI strategies can be harmful, so they are generally considered experimental and not standard care for people doing well on continuous antiretroviral therapy.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. Randomized studies show some STI patterns are harmful in chronic, suppressed HIV. A week‑on/week‑off trial found 31% virologic failure and one AIDS event, so this strategy was judged “less useful” [1]. Another week‑on/week‑off study had 53% failure and new resistance mutations, and was stopped as unacceptable [23]. Long‑cycle interruptions (4 weeks off/8 weeks on) were halted early because resistance emerged and immune activation rose, without toxicity benefit [3]. Other work shows rapid viral rebound, CD4 drops, and immune‑cell dysfunction during interruptions [6][15][24]. CD4‑guided, closely monitored interruptions appeared safer but offered little lasting benefit over continuous therapy [13][14][25].

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is structured treatment interruptions a good choice for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is structured treatment interruptions a bad choice for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Most of the trials in chronically infected people on successful ART found that when treatment was stopped, viral load rebounded quickly, CD4 counts and immune markers worsened, and then improved again only after restarting the same regimen [5,6,12,14,18,20,24,28]. Different interruption patterns (fixed short cycles, longer cycles, and CD4‑guided stops) rarely produced durable, drug‑free control of HIV and did not clearly enhance immune control compared with staying on therapy [3,8,9,11,17,18,23,24,27,32]. Some approaches also led to high virologic failure and emergence of drug‑resistant virus, especially with frequent on‑off cycles [1,3,6,16,21,22,25,26,29]. A few small, highly selected cohorts tolerated CD4‑guided interruptions without short‑term AIDS events and reduced time on drugs [1,15,19,30,31]. Overall, benefits are uncertain and risks real, so routine STIs are not advisable outside clinical trials.

- **Full Answer**:  
Based on these studies, planned breaks from HIV treatment (“structured treatment interruptions”) are generally not a good choice for people with chronic, well‑suppressed HIV.

In almost all trials, the virus came back within days to weeks after stopping pills, often reaching pre‑treatment levels [6,14,18,24]. This rebound was accompanied by falls in CD4 counts and increased immune activation, even when numbers later improved after restarting therapy [5,12,13,14,20,24,28]. Many interruption strategies showed no lasting benefit in terms of immune control of HIV or long‑term drug‑free suppression [3,8,9,11,17,18,23,24,27,32]. Short‑cycle plans like one‑week‑on/one‑week‑off had high failure rates and sometimes selected drug‑resistant virus, leading to trials being stopped early [1,3,4,6,22,25,26,29]. 

Some carefully monitored CD4‑guided interruptions in people with very high CD4 counts appeared short‑term safe and reduced time on drugs, but still did not clearly improve health outcomes and remain experimental [1,15,19,30,31].

timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Most studies of structured treatment interruptions (STIs) in people with long‑term, well‑controlled chronic HIV show that the virus rebounds quickly when therapy is stopped, CD4 counts can drop, and immune activation increases [7,16,24]. Different STI schedules (short‑cycle, long‑cycle, CD4‑guided) rarely lead to lasting control off therapy and sometimes promote drug resistance [1,3,7,8,18,22,23,27,30,32,34]. Some short‑term safety and lipid benefits exist, but overall benefits are modest and uncertain [4,13,14,21,26,28,31,35,36].

For someone with chronic HIV whose virus is well suppressed, planned treatment breaks are generally a poor choice outside of a research study.  

In almost all interruption studies, HIV levels rose from undetectable to measurable within days to weeks after stopping therapy [7,16,24]. This rebound often caused CD4 counts to fall and markers of immune activation to rise, even when counts later recovered after restarting drugs [6,16,24]. Short‑cycle patterns such as 1‑week‑on/1‑week‑off led to very high rates of virologic failure [1,32], and several repeated‑interruption strategies selected drug‑resistant virus, especially with older or suboptimal regimens [3,7,8,18,22,30,34]. Attempts to use interruptions to “train” the immune system generally did not produce durable control of HIV off treatment [9,10,12,19,23,25,27,29,33].  

Some CD4‑guided interruption protocols in carefully selected patients appeared short‑term safe and reduced drug exposure [1,13,14,26,28,31,36], but these remain experimental.  

Discuss any desire to stop therapy with your HIV specialist; unsupervised interruptions are risky.

cost.positive_question: Is structured treatment interruptions worth the money for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
cost.negative_question: Is structured treatment interruptions not worth the money for chronic suppressed HIV infection?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
In people with long‑term viral suppression, most structured treatment interruption (STI) strategies led to quick viral rebound within days to weeks, so patients could not remain safely off medicines long term [1][3][7][10][13][17][31]. CD4‑count–guided interruptions in people starting with high CD4 levels can be relatively safe in the short to medium term and cut total time on drugs, but they still lead to viral rebound and are not a cure strategy [1][14][15].  

Only a small minority of patients maintain lower viral loads off therapy after STIs, and this is not predictable [11][21][27][31]. Continuous antiretroviral therapy remains the standard of care.

- **Rationale**:  
Clinical trials show that stopping or cycling HIV medicines in people with well‑controlled, chronic infection almost always leads to the virus coming back within days to weeks, with falling CD4 counts and increased immune activation [7,13,17,19]. Most studies did **not** find that structured interruptions “retrained” the immune system enough to keep the virus low without treatment [9,11,16,18,25,27,31]. Some strategies (like 1 week on/1 week off) had very high failure rates and were stopped early [1,24,26,32]. Repeated interruptions can allow drug‑resistant virus to emerge, even when resistance isn’t immediately obvious on standard tests [3,8,17,20,22,31].  

In a few carefully selected people with high CD4 counts, CD4‑guided interruptions were short‑term “safe” under close monitoring, but they didn’t improve long‑term viral control and remain experimental [1,13,14,15,21,27,29]. Testimonials don’t replace this evidence. Any interruption should only be done in a clinical trial or under strict specialist supervision.

- **Full Answer**:  
For people with long‑term, well‑suppressed HIV, structured treatment interruptions (STIs) have **not** been shown to be reliably effective or safe as a routine strategy.

When HIV medicines are stopped or cycled, the virus usually comes back within days to weeks, and CD4 counts often fall or fluctuate [7,13,17,19]. Large and smaller trials found that STIs did **not** produce lasting control of the virus off treatment, despite temporary boosts in immune responses [9,11,16,18,25,27,31]. “Short‑cycle” plans (such as 1 week on/1 week off) led to frequent virologic failure and were stopped early [1,24,26,32].  

Repeated interruptions can also allow drug‑resistant virus to appear, sometimes as minor variants that standard tests miss [3,8,17,20,22,31].  

In carefully chosen patients with high CD4 counts, doctor‑guided interruptions have reduced time on drugs without short‑term AIDS events, but they remain experimental and require very close monitoring [1,13,14,15,21,27,29].  

Based on current evidence, you **should not** start structured interruptions on your own. Discuss any interest in this approach with your HIV specialist; continuous therapy is still the standard of care.

- **Rationale**:  
Controlled studies in people with chronic HIV who are well suppressed on treatment show that most structured treatment interruption (STI) strategies cause the virus to rebound quickly (often within days to weeks) and do not provide lasting control off therapy [7,10,17,19,31]. Some small studies found that a minority of carefully selected patients could stay off treatment longer with somewhat lower viral loads, but this was uncommon and unpredictable [11,16,20,23,31]. STIs often lead to CD4 cell drops and immune activation [6,13,15,19,24,28], and several regimens—especially “week-on/week-off” or repeated cycles—had high rates of virologic failure and emergence of drug‑resistant virus [1,3,7,18,20–22,26,32]. While short interruptions can improve cholesterol and triglycerides in the very short term [4,22,24], overall, STIs remain experimental and are not considered generally safe or effective outside carefully monitored trials.

- **Full Answer**:  
For people with chronic HIV whose virus is well suppressed, structured treatment interruptions have **not** been shown to be reliably safe or effective in clinical trials.

In many studies, HIV rebounded to detectable levels within days to weeks of stopping treatment [7,17,19,31]. Most patients quickly lost viral control during longer interruptions, even after several cycles [10,16,25,31]. CD4 counts often fell and markers of immune activation rose during time off therapy [6,13,15,19,24,28].  

Certain STI patterns (especially 1‑week‑on/1‑week‑off and repeated cycling) led to high rates of virologic failure and sometimes drug‑resistant virus, even when resistance was not always obvious on standard tests [1,3,7,18,20–22,26,32].  

Large randomized trials comparing STIs with continuous therapy found **no clear benefit** in viral control, safety, or long‑term outcomes [3,10,25,30,31]. A few patients could stay off drugs longer with lower viral loads, but they were a small, unpredictable minority [11,16,20,23,31].  

Because of these risks and uncertainties, STI approaches are considered experimental and should only be done, if at all, in closely monitored research settings. For now, continuous antiretroviral therapy remains the standard of care for chronic suppressed HIV. Always discuss any change to your treatment—including interruptions—with your HIV specialist before proceeding.

Almost everyone’s viral load rebounded quickly once drugs were stopped, usually within days to a few weeks [7,16,29]. - **Full Answer**:  
Across many clinical trials in people with well‑controlled, chronic HIV, structured treatment interruptions (STI) have not delivered the hoped‑for benefits.

When ART was stopped in planned cycles, almost everyone’s virus rebounded within days to weeks [7,16,29]. Research in people with long‑term, well‑suppressed HIV shows that structured treatment interruptions (STIs) rarely provide meaningful control of the virus off medication [6] [21] [28]. In most studies, virus levels rebounded within days to weeks after stopping therapy [6] [21] [28]. ReviewTitle: Indomethacin for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA remains a significant cause of mortality and morbidity in premature infants. Indomethacin is an effective treatment to close a PDA, and has been used for many years with several treatment regimes, including prophylactic use in all at risk premature infants. There are however concerns regarding adverse side effects of indomethacin. By targeting a group of infants with an asymptomatic PDA, rather than treating all VLBW infants prophylactically, indomethacin use would be restricted, limiting the possibility of significant side effects to those with greater chance of benefit.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess whether in premature neonates with asymptomatic PDA, treatment with indomethacin improves short and long term outcomes; in particular: incidence of symptomatic PDA, mortality, chronic neonatal lung disease (CLD), intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH), retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), neurodevelopmental outcome, length of ventilation.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: Standard strategies of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group were used. Searches were made of the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, MEDLINE and EMBASE from 1966 to September 2002, CINAHL from 1982 to September 2002, and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (CENTRAL/CCTR) in The Cochrane Library, Issue 3, 2002. Searches were also made of previous reviews including cross-referencing, abstracts, and conference and symposia proceedings published in Pediatric Research.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: All randomised controlled trials of indomethacin compared with placebo or no intervention for the treatment of asymptomatic PDA in premature infants were eligible.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group were used. Trials identified by the search strategy were independently reviewed by each author and assessed for eligibility and trial quality. Data were then extracted independently by each author and compared, with any differences resolved following discussion. Any additional information required was requested from trial authors. Only published data was available for review. Results are expressed as typical relative risk and typical risk difference for dichotomous outcomes, and weighted mean difference for continuous variables.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Three small trials involving a total of 97 infants were included. Meta analysis of combined data was possible for seven outcomes. Treatment of an asymptomatic PDA with indomethacin significantly reduced the incidence of symptomatic PDA (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.19, 0.68) and duration of supplemental oxygen (WMD -12.5, 95% CI -23.8, -1.26). There was no evidence of effect on mortality (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.45, 3.86), CLD (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.62, 1.35), IVH (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.62, 2.37), ROP (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.26, 1.78), or length of ventilation (WMD -7.00 days, 95%CI -17.33, 3.34). Long term neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. One trial reported a significant reduction in the duration of supplemental oxygen following treatment with indomethacin in the subgroup of infants with birth weight less than 1000g.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: This review demonstrates a significant decrease in the incidence of symptomatic PDA following treatment of an asymptomatic PDA with indomethacin. There is also a small but statistically significant decrease in the duration of requirement for supplemental oxygen. There are no reported long term outcomes in the included trials, and so it is not possible to comment on possible long term effects. Further studies are required to determine the long term benefits or harms of closing a PDA prior to the onset of symptoms.

Inputs.Title: Failure of prophylactic indomethacin to improve the outcome of the very low birth weight infant.
Inputs.Abstract: Prophylactic closure of the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) has been recommended as a means of decreasing early respiratory distress, and thereby chronic respiratory sequelae in the very low birth weight (VLBW) neonate. This study was undertaken to evaluate some possible mechanisms for the observed failure of early indomethacin therapy to achieve such improvement. 24 VLBW infants with echocardiographic evidence of PDA were randomized to receive either indomethacin or placebo at 48 h of life; and then they were studied for clinical, metabolic and laboratory signs of ductal constriction and/or reopening. Early indomethacin conferred no improvement in respiratory sequelae. However, this was not secondary to a short-term therapeutic failure. Prophylactic indomethacin, even in the VLBW infant, was successful in decreasing dilator prostaglandin production, and probably in closing the PDA and in decreasing the number of recurrences. The implications are that even with effective ductal constriction, overall morbidity is not affected.

Inputs.Title: Prophylactic indomethacin therapy for patent ductus arteriosus in very-low-birth-weight infants.
Inputs.Abstract: We performed a double-blind, controlled study of prophylactic indomethacin therapy in 47 premature infants (less than 1700 g) who had subclinical patent ductus arteriosus. They received either indomethacin or placebo at a mean age of 2.9 days. Among the 25 infants weighing more than 1000 g, a hemodynamically important ductus shunt developed in only four of the 14 given placebo. The incidence of important shunts, the number of surgical ligations, and the duration of oxygen therapy were not appreciably different between the study groups. In contrast, among the 22 infants who weighed 1000 g or less, a major ductus shunt developed in 10 of the 12 given placebo. In the smaller infants indomethacin therapy was associated with a significantly lower incidence of major shunts, fewer surgical ligations, a decreased duration of oxygen therapy, and fewer days necessary to regain birth weight. We conclude that prophylactic indomethacin therapy in infants weighing under 1000 g prevents the later development of large ductus shunts and decreases morbidity.

Inputs.Title: Prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome.
Inputs.Abstract: Early treatment of premature infants with indomethacin has been proposed as a means of reducing the morbidity associated with respiratory distress syndrome complicated by symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus. We identified 26 infants less than 48 hours old with severe respiratory distress syndrome who had an asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus. These infants were treated with either indomethacin or placebo. There was a significant difference in the frequency of ductal closure after receiving indomethacin treatment. No significant difference was observed in the time required for mechanical ventilation, time receiving supplemental oxygen, or time in the hospital, and there were no significant differences in the incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, retinopathy of prematurity, or death between the two groups.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is indomethacin for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is indomethacin for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that giving indomethacin early can close or narrow an open duct (PDA) and prevent it from becoming a big problem, especially in the smallest preterm babies. However, closing the PDA early does not consistently improve long-term breathing problems or survival.

- **Full Answer**:  
Indomethacin is effective at causing an asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) to close or become smaller in preterm infants, as shown by more frequent ductal closure and reduced recurrences when compared with placebo [1][3]. In very small infants (≤1000 g), prophylactic indomethacin clearly lowers the chance that a large, hemodynamically important PDA will later develop, reduces the need for surgical ligation, shortens oxygen use, and speeds regaining birth weight [2].  

However, across studies, this early treatment does **not** improve major outcomes such as chronic lung disease, duration of ventilation, overall hospital stay, brain bleeding, eye disease of prematurity, or death [1][3].  

Overall, indomethacin is effective for closing an asymptomatic PDA and preventing large future shunts, especially in extremely low–birth-weight infants, but it has limited impact on long-term health outcomes [1][2][3].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**: Trials in preterm infants with asymptomatic or “silent” PDA show a clear pattern: indomethacin usually succeeds in narrowing or closing the duct, but this early closure rarely changes the outcomes that matter to families. Across studies, prophylactic treatment did not reduce chronic breathing problems, time on a ventilator or oxygen, length of hospital stay, or major complications such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, brain bleeding, eye damage, or death, except possibly in the very smallest babies.

- **Full Answer**: In very‑low‑birth‑weight infants, early indomethacin lowered prostaglandin levels and likely closed the PDA more often, but did not lessen respiratory problems or overall illness [1]. In a trial of infants with subclinical PDA, it failed to reduce important ductus shunts, surgery, or oxygen days in babies over 1000 g; benefits were seen only in those ≤1000 g [2]. In infants with severe RDS and asymptomatic PDA, closure improved, but lung, brain, eye, and survival outcomes did not [3].

efficacy.positive_question: Does indomethacin work for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
efficacy.negative_question: Does indomethacin not work for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Indomethacin reliably closes an asymptomatic PDA and, in the smallest preterm infants, reduces later large shunts and short‑term problems [1][2][3]. But it does not clearly improve long‑term outcomes for most preterm babies [1][3].

- **Full Answer**:  
Indomethacin can “work” in two ways: closing the duct early and improving the baby’s outcome.  

Trials in preterm infants with asymptomatic PDAs show that indomethacin usually closes or narrows the duct and reduces later duct reopening [1][3]. In infants ≤1000 g, this also leads to fewer large PDAs, less need for surgical ligation, shorter oxygen therapy, and faster return to birth weight [2].  

However, in somewhat larger preterm infants, early indomethacin does not reduce time on the ventilator or oxygen, hospital stay, chronic lung disease, brain bleeding, eye disease, or death [1][3].  

So, indomethacin can close an asymptomatic PDA and may help the tiniest babies, but it does not consistently improve long‑term outcomes for all preterm infants.
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that giving indomethacin early to preterm infants with an echocardiographic or asymptomatic PDA does what it is supposed to do at the heart level: it reduces prostaglandins, constricts the ductus, and increases the rate of closure, with fewer recurrences or large shunts, especially in the smallest infants [1][2][3]. However, in most preterm infants, this early treatment does *not* translate into better overall outcomes such as less chronic lung disease, shorter ventilation, shorter hospital stay, or lower rates of major complications or death [1][3]. One study found that in extremely small infants (≤1000 g), prophylactic indomethacin did reduce the later development of large, symptomatic PDAs, the need for surgery, and days on oxygen, suggesting some clinical benefit in this high‑risk group [2]. Thus, indomethacin “works” to close an asymptomatic PDA, but often does not improve broader outcomes, except possibly in the tiniest infants.

- **Full Answer**:  
Indomethacin does work to close an asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants, but its overall benefits are limited.

In very-low-birth-weight infants, prophylactic indomethacin reduces prostaglandin production, likely closes the PDA, and reduces recurrences, yet does not improve long‑term respiratory outcomes or overall morbidity [1].  

In infants with “subclinical” PDA, those weighing ≤1000 g benefited most: indomethacin reduced the development of large ductal shunts, the need for surgical ligation, days on oxygen, and days to regain birth weight [2]. In larger infants, these advantages were not seen [2].  

In preterm infants with severe respiratory distress and asymptomatic PDA, indomethacin increased ductal closure but did not shorten ventilation, oxygen use, hospital stay, or reduce bronchopulmonary dysplasia, brain bleeding, eye disease, or death compared with placebo [3].  

So, indomethacin effectively closes asymptomatic PDA, but usually does not improve major clinical outcomes, except possibly in the smallest, highest‑risk infants [1][2][3].

safety.positive_question: Is indomethacin safe for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
safety.negative_question: Is indomethacin dangerous for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is about safety, not just whether indomethacin closes a silent (asymptomatic) patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). All three trials gave indomethacin early to preterm infants with PDA that was not yet clinically problematic. Indomethacin clearly increased duct closure or prevented large shunts [1–3]. Safety is judged by whether important complications (like lung disease, brain bleeding, eye disease, or death) were higher with the drug. One study in very sick preterm infants found more duct closure but no differences in time on machines, oxygen, hospital stay, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, retinopathy of prematurity, or death [3]. Another found no change in overall illness despite effective duct constriction and reported no extra harms [1]. A study in the smallest infants (<1000 g) showed reduced PDA-related problems and no new safety concerns [2]. So, short‑term safety appears acceptable, but the clinical benefits are limited and mainly seen in the tiniest infants.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across three randomized trials, giving indomethacin to very preterm infants with an asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus did not increase major short‑term complications. In infants with severe respiratory distress syndrome and silent PDA, indomethacin closed the duct more often but did not change time on the ventilator, oxygen, length of stay, or rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, brain bleeding, eye disease of prematurity, or death [3]. In very‑low‑birth‑weight infants, prophylactic indomethacin reduced prostaglandin production and likely closed the duct, but overall illness burden did not improve, and no extra harms were reported [1]. In infants under 1000 g with subclinical PDA, indomethacin lowered the chance of developing a large shunt, reduced need for duct ligation, and shortened oxygen use and time to regain birth weight, again without noted safety signals [2]. These data suggest short‑term safety, but benefits are modest in the tiniest infants, so practice often varies considerably between centers [1–3].
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies looked at giving indomethacin early to preterm infants who had a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) but were not yet showing symptoms. They mainly assessed whether this reduced later problems and whether it caused harm. Across trials, indomethacin reliably promoted ductal closure but did not increase major complications, including death. In the smallest, most vulnerable infants, it even reduced later serious PDA-related problems. However, in broader groups of very-low-birth-weight infants, it did not improve overall illness or lung outcomes, meaning it was not clearly beneficial for everyone, but also not clearly dangerous in the short term.

- **Full Answer**:  
Across these studies, giving indomethacin early to preterm infants with an asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus closed the ductus more often but did not increase short‑term complications compared with placebo.  

In very‑low‑birth‑weight infants, prophylactic indomethacin reduced prostaglandin production and likely closed the ductus, but overall illness and lung outcomes were unchanged, suggesting neither clear benefit nor added harm for the group as a whole [1]. In another trial, infants under 1000 g who received indomethacin had fewer large later shunts, fewer surgical ligations, shorter oxygen use, and faster return to birth weight, without reported additional complications [2]. In infants with respiratory distress syndrome and asymptomatic ductus, indomethacin increased ductal closure but did not change time on the ventilator, oxygen, hospital stay, or rates of chronic lung disease, brain bleeding, eye disease, or death [3].  

Thus, within these trials, indomethacin was not shown to be dangerous for asymptomatic PDA.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing indomethacin is good for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing indomethacin is harmful for asymptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:

Another randomized study in infants under 1700 g with subclinical (asymptomatic) PDA found that indomethacin prevented later large PDA shunts. A third study in premature infants with severe respiratory distress and asymptomatic PDA showed more ductal closure with indomethacin but no improvement in ventilation time, oxygen use, hospital stay, major complications, or death [3]. Overall, the evidence supports that indomethacin closes asymptomatic PDA, but consistent clear clinical benefit is mainly seen in extremely small preterm infants, not across all preterm babies.

- **Full Answer**:  
Several randomized trials have tested indomethacin in premature infants with asymptomatic or “subclinical” patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

In very‑low‑birth‑weight infants, early indomethacin reliably reduced prostaglandin levels and likely closed the ductus, but this did not translate into better breathing outcomes [1].

In another study of infants under 1700 g with subclinical PDA, indomethacin prevented later large PDA shunts. Among the tiniest babies (≤1000 g), it also reduced the need for surgical ligation, shortened oxygen use, and helped them regain birth weight faster, suggesting some short‑term clinical benefit in this high‑risk group [2].

A third trial in premature infants with severe respiratory distress and asymptomatic PDA found more frequent ductal closure with indomethacin, but no differences in time on a ventilator, oxygen therapy, hospital stay, major complications, or death [3].

Overall, evidence shows indomethacin closes asymptomatic PDA, but consistent long‑term clinical benefits are limited mainly to the smallest preterm infants [1–3].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across the three randomized studies provided, indomethacin was given prophylactically to preterm infants with asymptomatic or subclinical patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The key safety question is whether these trials showed that indomethacin caused worse outcomes (harm) compared with placebo. The first study in very low birth weight infants found that early indomethacin likely closed the PDA but did not improve overall respiratory outcomes or morbidity; it did not report increased complications versus placebo [1]. The second study found that in the smallest infants (≤1000 g), prophylactic indomethacin reduced later large PDA shunts, surgeries, and oxygen use, indicating less morbidity rather than harm [2]. - **Full Answer**:  
The available studies do **not** show that indomethacin is harmful for asymptomatic PDA in preterm infants.  

In very low birth weight infants with echocardiographic PDA, early indomethacin likely closed the ductus and reduced recurrences, but did **not** change overall respiratory problems or general morbidity; importantly, no increase in complications was reported compared with placebo [1].

Thus, these studies do **not** provide evidence that prophylactic indomethacin is harmful; they show either neutral or beneficial effects on short‑term outcomes [1–3].

ReviewTitle: Non‐antiepileptic drugs for trigeminal neuralgia

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Trigeminal neuralgia was defined by the International Association for the Study of Pain as a sudden, usually unilateral, severe, brief, stabbing recurrent pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial nerve. Standard treatment is with anti-epileptic drugs. Non-antiepileptic drugs have been used in the management of trigeminal neuralgia since the 1970s. This is an update of a review first published in 2006 and previously updated in 2011.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To systematically review the efficacy and tolerability of non-antiepileptic drugs for trigeminal neuralgia.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: On 20 May 2013, for this updated review, we searched the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL (2013, Issue 4), MEDLINE (January 1966 to May 2013), EMBASE (January 1980 to May 2013), LILACS (January 1982 to May 2013) and the Chinese Biomedical Retrieval System (1978 to May 2013). We searched clinical trials registries for ongoing trials.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: We included double-blind, randomised controlled trials in which the active drug was used either alone or in combination with other non-antiepileptic drugs for at least two weeks.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two authors decided which trials fitted the inclusion criteria and independently graded risk of bias. We assessed the quality of the evidence according to the GRADE criteria for this update.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: In this 2013 update, we updated the searches, but identified only two new ongoing studies. The review includes four trials involving 139 participants. The primary outcome measure in each was pain relief. Three trials compared one of the oral non-antiepileptic drugs tizanidine, tocainide or pimozide with carbamazepine. The quality of evidence for all outcomes for which data were available was low. In a trial of tizanidine involving 12 participants (one dropped out due to unrelated disease), one of five participants treated with tizanidine and four of six treated with carbamazepine improved (risk ratio (RR) 0.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.05 to 1.89). Few side effects were noted with tizanidine. For pimozide, there was evidence of greater efficacy than carbamazepine at six weeks. Up to 83% of participants reported adverse effects but these did not lead to withdrawal; the report did not provide comparable data for carbamazepine. Limited data meant that we could not assess the effects of tocainide; however, data from non-randomised studies (not included in this review) indicate that serious haematological adverse events can occur. A trial involving 47 participants compared 0.5% proparacaine hydrochloride eyedrops with placebo but did not show any significant benefits, again according to low-quality evidence. The report did not mention adverse events. The proparacaine trial was at low risk of bias; the other trials were at unclear risk of bias overall.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: There is low-quality evidence that the effect of tizanidine is not significantly different than that of carbamazepine in treating trigeminal neuralgia. Pimozide is more effective than carbamazepine, although the evidence is of low quality and the data did not allow comparison of adverse event rates. There is also low-quality evidence that 0.5% proparacaine hydrochloride eye drops have no benefit over placebo. Limitations in the data for tocainide prevent any conclusions being drawn. There is insufficient evidence from randomised controlled trials to show significant benefit from non-antiepileptic drugs in trigeminal neuralgia. More research is needed.

Inputs.Title: The effect of single-application topical ophthalmic anesthesia in patients with trigeminal neuralgia. A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract: To evaluate the reported benefit of ipsilateral single-application ophthalmic anesthetic eyedrops in patients with typical trigeminal neuralgia, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial was performed. Forty-seven patients were randomly assigned to receive two drops of either proparacaine (25 cases) or saline placebo (22 cases). The experimental and placebo groups were equivalent in regard to patient age, distribution of trigeminal neuralgia pain, duration of pain, current medication regimens, and number of prior procedures performed. Pain response was assessed at 3, 10, and 30 days after instillation using two pain rating scales and a measure of pain frequency. Treatment failure was defined in advance as any of the following: a lack of clinical response, the need for an increase in medication, or the need for surgery. No significant difference in outcomes was found between the two groups either when using a verbal pain rating scale (p = 0.24) or when comparing overall pain status (unchanged, improved throughout the study period, or temporarily improved) (p = 0.98). No difference in the frequency of trigeminal neuralgia attacks between the two treatment groups (scaled within five levels of pain frequency) was detected (p = 0.09). During follow-up monitoring, 11 patients in the test drug group and 14 in the placebo group required surgery because of persistent pain (p = 0.24). The results of this study indicate that single-application topical ophthalmic anesthesia reduces neither the severity nor the frequency of pain in comparison to placebo administration. Although a simple and safe treatment, the single application of topical ophthalmic eyedrops provides no short- or long-term benefit to patients with trigeminal neuralgia.

Inputs.Title: The analgesic effect of tocainide in trigeminal neuralgia.
Inputs.Abstract: Tocainide is a derivative of lidocaine with anti-arrhythmic action and, unlike lidocaine, can be used for oral treatment. Tocainide was alternatively with carbamazepine given to 12 patients with trigeminal neuralgia in a double-blind cross-over study for 2 weeks. The analgesic effect was estimated each day by the patients using a 0-10-point scale summarizing the frequency and severity of the attacks. The similarity in analgesic effect of the two drugs was striking. A possible analgesic mechanism could be that tocainide blocks the sodium channels in the hyperexcitable nerve membranes in the pain-producing foci in trigeminal neuralgia.

Inputs.Title: Pimozide therapy for trigeminal neuralgia.
Inputs.Abstract: Pimozide was compared with carbamazepine in a double-blind crossover trial in 48 patients with trigeminal neuralgia who were refractory to medical therapy. Pimozide treatment produced greater reduction in trigeminal neuralgia symptoms than carbamazepine treatment. All of the pimozide-treated patients improved, while only 56% of carbamazepine-treated patients were relieved of their pain. Although both drugs provoked some adverse effects, it was not necessary to interrupt the trial in any case. After this 24-week trial, all patients began receiving pimozide and were followed up according to an open-label study design. In all cases, the pimozide dosage was progressively reduced until the minimal effective dose was reached. Central and peripheral mechanisms that may underlie pimozide-induced improvement are discussed.

Inputs.Title: Tizanidine in the management of trigeminal neuralgia.
Inputs.Abstract: In a double-blind study the efficacy and tolerability of tizanidine was compared with those of carbamazepine in the management of trigeminal neuralgia. Six patients were allocated to treatment with tizanidine and six to carbamazepine. After individual titration the maximum daily doses were 18 mg and 900 mg, respectively. Among the efficacy factors used, the visual analog scale (VAS) and the overall efficacy as assessed by patients and investigator turned out to be the most appropriate. The results indicate that tizanidine was well tolerated, but the effects, if any, were inferior to those of carbamazepine.

ReviewTitle: Low bacterial diet versus control diet to prevent infection in cancer patients treated with chemotherapy causing episodes of neutropenia

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Neutropenia is a potentially serious side effect of chemotherapy and a major risk factor for infection, which can be life-threatening. It has been hypothesised that a low bacterial diet (LBD) can prevent infection and (infection-related) mortality in cancer patients receiving chemotherapy that causes episodes of neutropenia, but much remains unclear. This review is an update of a previously published Cochrane review.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: The primary objective of this review was to determine the efficacy of an LBD versus a control diet in preventing infection and in decreasing (infection-related) mortality in adult and paediatric cancer patients receiving chemotherapy that causes episodes of neutropenia. Secondary objectives were to assess time to first febrile episode, need for empirical antibiotic therapy, diet acceptability and quality of life.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text:
We searched the following electronic databases: the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (2015, Issue 4), the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE) (2015, Issue 4), PubMed (from 1946 to 4 May 2015), EMBASE (from 1980 to 4 May 2015) and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) (from 1981 to 4 May 2015).
In addition, we searched the reference lists of relevant articles and conference proceedings of American Society of Hematology (ASH; from 2000 to 2015), European Bone Marrow Transplantation (EBMT; from 2000 to 2015), Oncology Nurses Society (ONS; from 2000 to 2015), International Society for Paediatric Oncology (SIOP; from 2000 to 2014), Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC; from 2000 to 2015), American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO; from 2000 to 2015), Interscience Conference of Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy (ICAAC; from 2000 to 2015), European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN; from 2000 to 2015), American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN; from 2000 to 2015) and European Hematology Association (EHA; from 2000 to 2015). In May 2015, we scanned the National Institutes of Health Register via clinicaltrials.gov and the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN) Register (www.controlled-trials.com).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing use of an LBD versus a control diet with regard to infection rate, (infection-related) mortality, time to first febrile episode, need for empirical antibiotic therapy, diet acceptability and quality of life in adult and paediatric cancer patients receiving chemotherapy causing episodes of neutropenia.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two review authors independently performed study selection, 'Risk of bias' assessment and data extraction. We performed analyses according to the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: In the original version of this review, we identified three RCTs that assessed different intervention and control diets in 192 participants (97 randomised to intervention diet; 95 to control diet) with different types of malignancies. For the update, we identified no eligible new studies. Co-interventions (e.g. protective environment, antimicrobial prophylaxis, central venous catheter care, oral care, hygiene practices, colony-stimulating factors) and outcome definitions also differed between studies. In all included studies, it was standard policy to give empirical antibiotics (and sometimes also antimycotics) to (some of) the participants diagnosed with an infection. Two studies included adults and one study included children. In all studies, only a scant description of treatment regimens was provided. All studies had methodological limitations. Pooling of results of included studies was not possible. In two individual studies, no statistically significant differences in infection rate were identified between intervention and control diets; another study showed no significant differences between treatment groups in the number of chemotherapy cycles with an infection. None of the studies mentioned infection-related mortality, but in one study, no significant difference in overall survival was observed between treatment groups. Time from onset of neutropenia to fever, duration of empirical antibiotics and antimycotics, diet acceptability (i.e. following the diet easily and following the diet throughout all chemotherapy cycles) and quality of life were all evaluated by only one study; for all outcomes, no statistically significant differences between treatment arms were identified.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: At the moment, no evidence from individual RCTs in children and adults with different malignancies underscores use of an LBD for prevention of infection and related outcomes. All studies differed with regard to co-interventions, outcome definitions and intervention and control diets. As pooling of results was not possible, and as all studies had serious methodological limitations, we could reach no definitive conclusions. It should be noted that 'no evidence of effect', as identified in this review, is not the same as 'evidence of no effect'. On the basis of currently available evidence, we are not able to provide recommendations for clinical practice. Additional high-quality research is needed.

Inputs.Title: Normal hospital and low-bacterial diet in patients with cytopenia after intensive chemotherapy for hematological malignancy: a study of safety.
Inputs.Abstract:
The purpose of this randomized, controlled pilot study is to address the question whether normal hospital diet (NHD) is safe when compared with low-bacterial diet (LBD) given to prevent infections in cytopenic patients who receive antimicrobial prophylaxis (AP).
                The patients were randomized into two groups: one group to receive AP and LBD, the other to receive the same AP and NHD. The primary outcome parameter is colonization of the digestive tract with aerobic gram-negative bacilli and yeasts. Secondary outcome parameters were infections and total societal costs.
                No statistically significant differences between treatment groups were observed regarding the primary outcome parameter, gut colonization by yeasts or gram-negative bacilli, or infections, use of antimicrobials, days with fever and total societal costs.
                On the basis of the results of this pilot study, NHD appears to be as safe as LBD in patients with chemotherapy-induced cytopenia. Furthermore, the results indicate that LBD may offer no additional benefit as an infection preventive measure to the measures already implemented, such as AP. Thus, a larger randomized study, powered adequately to determine noninferiority of NHD to LBD is warranted and safe to be carried out.

Inputs.Title: Randomized comparison of cooked and noncooked diets in patients undergoing remission induction therapy for acute myeloid leukemia.
Inputs.Abstract:
A neutropenic diet is often used to prevent infection in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Although such a diet potentially entails inconvenience, its value is uncertain.
                One hundred fifty-three patients admitted to a high-efficiency particulate air-filtered room (protected environment [PE]) to receive induction therapy for newly diagnosed AML were randomly assigned to a diet containing no raw fruits or vegetables (cooked diet) or to a diet containing fresh fruit and fresh vegetables (raw diet). Stratification was based on the patients' early risk of mortality (ERM) score. All patients received antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis and remained on study until they were discharged from the PE. The outcomes of principal interest were major infection (pneumonia, bacteremia, or fungemia) and death; if the true probability of either event was 20% on the cooked arm and 40% on the raw arm, then the probability that the cooked arm would be selected as superior was 83%.
                Seventy-eight patients were randomly assigned to the cooked arm, and 75 were assigned to the raw arm. The two groups were similar with respect to age, ERM, chemotherapy received, and days at risk. Twenty-nine percent of patients in the cooked group and 35% of patients in the raw group developed a major infection (P = .60). Time to major infection and survival time were similar in the two groups. Fever of unknown origin occurred in 51% of the cooked group and 36% of the raw group.
                In patients treated in a PE, a neutropenic diet did not prevent major infection or death.

Inputs.Title: Feasibility and safety of a pilot randomized trial of infection rate: neutropenic diet versus standard food safety guidelines.
Inputs.Abstract: The neutropenic diet is an intervention that excludes certain foods, especially fresh fruits and vegetables, from the diets of pediatric oncology patients to reduce infection rate. The purpose of this study was to demonstrate a safe and feasible methodology to evaluate the infection rate in pediatric cancer patients randomized to the neutropenic diet or to Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved food safety guidelines. Pediatric oncology patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy were randomized to the neutropenic diet or to FDA food safety guidelines and followed through one chemotherapy cycle. The primary outcome was febrile neutropenia. Secondary outcomes were adherence and diet tolerability. Nineteen patients were enrolled. Four patients on each diet arm developed febrile neutropenia. The adherence rate was 94% for the neutropenic diet and 100% for the food safety guidelines. Although patients were able to tolerate both diets, there was more reported difficulty adhering to the neutropenic diet. Infection rates for children with cancer on the neutropenic diet were similar to those for patients following food safety guidelines. The results of this study suggest that a larger randomized trial to determine the effectiveness of food safety guidelines in minimizing the risk of food borne infection is safe and feasible in children with cancer.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is low bacterial diet for infection?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is low bacterial diet for infection?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across three small randomized studies in people with very low white blood cell counts from chemotherapy, low‑bacterial or “neutropenic” diets (which restrict raw fruits, vegetables, and other foods) did **not** lower infection rates compared with less restrictive diets that used standard food safety and antimicrobial precautions. This suggests that careful food handling and routine infection‑prevention measures matter more than severely limiting what patients eat.

- **Full Answer**:  
A low‑bacterial (neutropenic) diet does **not** appear to be more effective than a normal diet for preventing infections when usual infection‑prevention steps are used.  

In adults with blood cancers and chemotherapy‑related low blood counts, infection rates, gut germ colonization, fevers, antibiotic use, and costs were similar whether patients ate a low‑bacterial diet or a normal hospital diet, as long as they also received antimicrobial prophylaxis [1].  

In adults with acute myeloid leukemia, avoiding all raw fruits and vegetables (cooked diet) did **not** reduce major infections or deaths compared with a diet that allowed fresh produce [2].  

In children with cancer, infection rates were the same with a neutropenic diet and with standard FDA food‑safety guidelines, though the neutropenic diet was harder to follow [3].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies compare low‑bacterial/neutropenic diets with more liberal diets in patients at high risk for infection (due to chemotherapy/neutropenia). Across adults and children, infection outcomes—major infections, febrile neutropenia, death, gut colonization—were essentially the same regardless of diet. This means the low‑bacterial diet did not measurably improve infection prevention when standard medical infection‑control measures were already used.

- **Full Answer**:  
In several randomized studies, a low‑bacterial or “neutropenic” diet did not reduce infections compared with more liberal diets when standard infection‑prevention steps (like antimicrobial drugs and clean hospital environments) were already in place.  

In adults with blood cancers after intensive chemotherapy, infection rates, gut colonization with harmful bacteria or yeast, days with fever, and antibiotic use were all similar whether patients received a low‑bacterial diet or a normal hospital diet [1]. In adults with acute myeloid leukemia kept in specialized filtered rooms, avoiding all raw fruits and vegetables (cooked diet) did not lower rates of serious infections or death compared with a diet that allowed fresh produce [2]. In children on chemotherapy, febrile neutropenia occurred equally in those on a neutropenic diet and those just following standard FDA food‑safety rules [3]. Overall, these trials show no clear infection‑prevention benefit from a low‑bacterial diet [1–3]. They add restrictions without proven benefit.

In adults with blood cancers, infection rates, fevers, antibiotic use, and gut colonization with germs were the same with normal and low‑bacterial diets [1]. ReviewTitle: Diuretics for transient tachypnoea of the newborn

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN) results from delayed clearance of lung liquid and is a common cause of admission of full-term infants to neonatal intensive care units. The condition is particularly common after elective caesarean section. Conventional treatment involves appropriate oxygen administration and continuous positive airway pressure in some cases. Most infants receive antibiotic therapy. Hastening the clearance of lung liquid may shorten the duration of the symptoms and reduce complications.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To determine whether diuretic administration reduces the duration of oxygen therapy and respiratory symptoms and shortens hospital stay in term infants presenting with transient tachypnoea of the newborn.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: An updated search was carried out in September 2015 of the following databases: the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (The Cochrane Library issue 9, 2015), MEDLINE via Ovid, EMBASE, PubMed, and CINAHL via OVID.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: We included randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials that compared the effect of diuretics administration versus placebo or no treatment in infants of less than seven days of age, born at 37 or more weeks of gestation with the clinical picture of transient tachypnoea of the newborn.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: We extracted and analysed data according to the methods outlined in the latest Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Two review authors assessed trial quality in each potentially eligible manuscript and two review authors extracted data.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Our previous systematic review included two trials enrolling a total of 100 infants with transient tachypnoea of the newborn (Wiswell 1985; Karabayir 2006). The updated search revealed no new trials. Wiswell 1985 randomised 50 infants to receive either oral furosemide (2 mg/kg body weight at time of diagnosis followed by a 1 mg/kg dose 12 hours later if the tachypnoea persisted) or placebo. Karabayir 2006 randomised 50 infants to receive either intravenous furosemide (2 mg/kg body weight) or an equal volume of normal saline placebo. Neither trial reported on the need for respiratory support. Neither trial demonstrated a statistically significant impact of furosemide on transient tachypnoea of the newborn regarding duration of symptoms or length of hospitalisation.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: Diuretics cannot be recommended as treatment for transient tachypnoea of the newborn and it should not be used unless additional data become available. This finding suggests that either furosemide is not effective in promoting resorption of lung fluid, or factors other than delayed resorption of this fluid contribute to the pathogenesis of transient tachypnoea of the newborn. The question remains as to whether furosemide given to the infant (or even to the mother before caesarean section) might shorten the duration of the illness. As elective caesarean section continues at a high level, these two interventions might be worthy of trials.

Inputs.Title: Effect of furosemide on the clinical course of transient tachypnea of the newborn.
Inputs.Abstract: The effect of furosemide on the course of transient tachypnea of the newborn was evaluated in a controlled, prospective study. Fifty infants with transient tachypnea of the newborn were randomly assigned to control or treatment groups. Those in the treatment group were given furosemide, 2 mg/kg orally, at the time of diagnosis followed by 1 mg/kg 12 hours later if the symptoms persisted. Infants in the control group received a placebo. Compared with infants in the control group, the furosemide-treated group demonstrated no significant difference in the duration of tachypnea nor in the length of hospitalization. It is concluded that oral furosemide, at the doses used in this study, does not significantly affect the clinical course of transient tachypnea of the newborn.

Inputs.Title: Intravenous frusemide for transient tachypnoea of the newborn: a randomised controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract:
To investigate the effect of intravenous frusemide on the course of transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN).
                Fifty term infant with TTN were randomised at the time of diagnosis to receive either intravenous frusemide 2 mg/kg or saline placebo. Outcomes assessed included duration of supplemental oxygen requirement, the period of tachypnoea, time to discharge from hospital and weight loss in the first 24 h of life and before discharge.
                The two groups were similar with respect to sex, birthweight, mode of delivery and age at presentation. The study group lost significantly more weight in the first 24 h after birth. There were no significant differences between the two groups in the duration of oxygen requirements, the period of tachypnoea and the time to hospital discharge.
                A single dose of intravenous frusemide (2 mg/kg) does not improve the clinical course of TTN. This finding suggests that either frusemide is not effective in promoting resorption of lung fluid or factors other than delayed resorption of this fluid contribute to the pathogenesis of TTN.
