ReviewTitle: Antidepressants versus psychological treatments and their combination for bulimia nervosa

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Psychotherapeutic approaches, mainly cognitive behavior therapy, and antidepressant medication are the two treatment modalities that have received most support in controlled outcome studies of bulimia nervosa.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: The primary objective was to conduct a systematic review of all RCTs comparing antidepressants with psychological approaches or comparing their combination with each single approach for the treatment of bulimia nervosa.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text:
(1) electronic searches of MEDLINE (1966 to December 2000), EMBASE (1980-December 2000) , PsycLIT (to December 2000), LILACS & SCISEARCH (to 1999) 
(2) the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials and the Cochrane Depression, Anxiety and Neurosis Group Register - ongoing 
(3) handsearches of the references of all identified trials 
(4) contact with the pharmaceutical companies and the principal investigator of each included trial 
(5) handsearch of the International Journal of Eating Disorders - ongoing

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text:
Inclusion criteria: every randomized controlled trial in which antidepressants were compared with psychological treatments or the combination of antidepressants with psychological approaches was compared to each treatment alone, to reduce the symptoms of bulimia nervosa in patients of any age or gender. 
Quality criteria: reports were considered adequate if they were classified as A or B according to the Cochrane Manual.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers for each included trial. The main outcome for efficacy was full remission of bulimic symptoms, defined as 100% reduction in binge or purge episodes from baseline to endpoint. Dichotomous data was evaluated by the relative risks and 95% confidence intervals around this measure, based on the random effects model; continuous data was evaluated by the average difference and the 95% confidence interval. Number needed to treat (NNT) and number needed to harm (NNH) were calculated using the inverse of the absolute risk reduction.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Five trials were included in comparison one (antidepressants versus psychological treatments), five in comparison two (antidepressants versus the combination) and seven in comparison three (psychological treatments versus the combination). Remission rates were 20% for single antidepressants compared to 39% for single psychotherapy (DerSimonian-Laird Relative Risk = 1.28; 95% Confidence Interval = 0.98;1.67). Dropout rates were higher for antidepressants than for psychotherapy (DerSimonian-Laird Relative Risk = 2.18; 95% Confidence Interval = 1.09;4.35). The NNH for a mean treatment duration of 17.5 weeks was 4 (95% confidence interval = 3;11). Comparison two found remission rates of 42% for the combination versus 23% for antidepressants (DerSimonian-Laird Relative Risk = 1.38; 95% Confidence Interval = 0.98;1.93). Comparison three showed a 36% pooled remission rate for psychological approaches compared to 49% for the combination (DerSimonian-Laird Relative Risk = 1.21; 95% Confidence Interval = 1.02;1.45). The NNT for a mean treatment duration of 15 weeks was 8 (95% Confidence Interval = 4;320). Dropout rates were higher for the combination compared to single psychological treatments (DerSimonian-Laird Relative Risk = 0.57; 95% Confidence Interval = 0.38;0.88). The NNH was 7 (95% Confidence Interval = 4;21).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: Using a more conservative statistical approach, combination treatments were superior to single psychotherapy. This was the only statistically significant difference between treatments. The number of trials might be insufficient to show the statistical significance of a 19% absolute risk reduction in efficacy favouring psychotherapy or combination treatments over single antidepressants. Psychotherapy appeared to be more acceptable to subjects. When antidepressants were combined with psychological treatments, acceptability of the latter was significantly reduced.

Inputs.Title: Comparison of cognitive-behavior therapy and desipramine in the treatment of bulimia nervosa.
Inputs.Abstract: A comparison of cognitive-behavior therapy alone, desipramine alone, and cognitive-behavior therapy combined with desipramine was made in the treatment of bulimia nervosa. The study was terminated early with an N of only 7 subjects per condition because of a high drop-out rate and lack of positive response in the desipramine alone group compared to the other two groups. By this time it was also apparent that at posttreatment and at 6 months follow-up no benefit was being realized from combining cognitive-behavior therapy with desipramine.

Inputs.Title: Medication and psychotherapy in the treatment of bulimia nervosa.
Inputs.Abstract:
Two treatments for bulimia nervosa have emerged as having established efficacy: cognitive-behavioral therapy and antidepressant medication. This study sought to address 1) how the efficacy of a psychodynamically oriented supportive psychotherapy compared to that of cognitive-behavioral therapy; 2) whether a two-stage medication intervention, in which a second antidepressant (fluoxetine) was employed if the first (desipramine) was either ineffective or poorly tolerated, added to the benefit of psychological treatment; and 3) if the combination of medication and psychological treatment was superior to a course of medication alone.
                A total of 120 women with bulimia nervosa participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.
                Cognitive-behavioral therapy was superior to supportive psychotherapy in reducing behavioral symptoms of bulimia nervosa (binge eating and vomiting). Patients receiving medication in combination with psychological treatment experienced greater improvement in binge eating and depression than did patients receiving placebo and psychological treatment. In addition, cognitive-behavioral therapy plus medication was superior to medication alone, but supportive psychotherapy plus medication was not.
                At present, cognitive-behavioral therapy is the psychological treatment of choice for bulimia nervosa. A two-stage medication intervention using fluoxetine adds modestly to the benefit of psychological treatment.

Inputs.Title: Pharmacologic and cognitive-behavioral treatment for bulimia nervosa: a controlled comparison.
Inputs.Abstract:
This study examined the relative effectiveness of desipramine, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and their combination in the treatment of bulimia nervosa, together with the effects of withdrawing medication after two different lengths of treatment.
                Seventy-one patients meeting DSM-III-R criteria for bulimia nervosa, recruited from an eating disorders clinic or by advertisements, were assigned at random to one of five groups: desipramine (withdrawn at 16 or 24 weeks), combined treatment (medication withdrawn at 16 or 24 weeks), and cognitive-behavioral therapy (15 sessions). All treatments were conducted individually in an outpatient clinic. The primary outcome measures were binge eating and purging rates assessed at pretreatment, 16, 24, and 32 weeks. The results were analyzed as three groups (medication, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and combined treatment) at 16 weeks and as five groups at subsequent assessments.
                At 16 weeks, both cognitive-behavioral therapy and the combined treatment were superior to medication given for 16 weeks in reducing binge eating and purging. At 32 weeks, however, only the combined 24-week treatment was superior to medication given for 16 weeks. The combined treatment was also more effective in reducing dietary preoccupation and hunger. Continuing cognitive-behavioral therapy appeared to prevent relapse in patients withdrawn from medication at 16 weeks.
                Overall, the results favor the use of a combination of medication and cognitive-behavioral therapy in the treatment of bulimia nervosa, with medication continued for at least 24 weeks.

Inputs.Title: A randomized controlled trial of fluoxetine and cognitive behavioral therapy for bulimia nervosa: short-term outcome.
Inputs.Abstract: This study compared and combined fluoxetine and individual cognitive behavioral therapy in the treatment of bulimia nervosa. Participants were 76 women who sought treatment at the Eating Disorders Program of the Toronto Hospital and who met DSM-III-R criteria for bulimia nervosa. Subjects were randomly assigned to receive fluoxetine alone, cognitive behavior therapy alone, or the two in combination and were treated over 16 weeks. Short-term outcome revealed that all three treatment conditions were associated with clinical improvement across a wide range of parameters. The combination of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy was superior to pharmacotherapy alone on specific parameters and there was no statistically significant advantage to the combination over psychotherapy alone. Limitations to the study include the absence of a placebo pill group and a waiting list control group as well as a substantial dropout rate across all three treatment conditions.

Inputs.Title: Intensive nutritional counselling in bulimia nervosa: a role for supplementation with fluoxetine?
Inputs.Abstract:
The aims of the paper are to determine whether nutritional counselling is associated with an improvement in bulimic symptomatology, whether this improvement is maintained during post-treatment follow-up, and whether the addition of fluoxetine 3 x 20 mg/day confers additional benefit.
                Psychological, pharmacological and combined psychopharmacological treatments of bulimia nervosa were reviewed briefly. Sixty-seven patients referred to specialist eating disorder services who fulfilled strict diagnostic criteria were treated with intensive nutritional counselling and randomly assigned to either fluoxetine 3 x 20 mg/day or placebo. After a 1-week 'wash-out', active treatment was given over 8 weeks, followed by post-treatment interviews at 12 and 20 weeks.
                Both groups of patients improved significantly during treatment. In some respects, the fluoxetine group did slightly better as demonstrated by the items 'restraint', 'weight concern' and 'shape concern' (p < 0.05 vs p < 0.0001) on the Eating Disorder Examination (EDE). Fluoxetine patients decreased their energy intake and lost a modest amount of weight. They went on to regain weight during the follow-up period, returning to levels higher than they were initially. These patients also appeared more likely to have a recurrence of symptoms, as shown by the fall in percentage of binge-free patients and by changes in the EDE.
                Nutritional counselling is an effective means of treating bulimia nervosa, with improvement maintained up to 3 months follow-up. The addition of fluoxetine may confer some benefit during active treatment, but its discontinuation may contribute to a higher rate of recurrence of symptoms post treatment. Of course, this study cannot be extrapolated to the efficacy of fluoxetine when used as the only form of treatment in patients for whom intensive nutritional counselling or other structured psychological programs are not available.

Inputs.Title: A comparison study of antidepressants and structured intensive group psychotherapy in the treatment of bulimia nervosa.
Inputs.Abstract: Previous research on the treatment of outpatients with bulimia nervosa has focused on two treatment strategies: (1) drug therapy, primarily using tricyclic antidepressants, and (2) psychotherapy, often employing behavioral and cognitive behavioral techniques. We report here the short-term treatment outcome of a 12-week comparison trial of bulimic outpatients who were randomly assigned to one of four treatment cells: (1) imipramine hydrochloride treatment, (2) placebo treatment, (3) imipramine treatment combined with intensive group psychotherapy, and (4) placebo treatment combined with intensive group psychotherapy. All three active treatment cells resulted in significant reductions in target-eating behaviors and in a significant improvement in mood relative to placebo treatment. However, the results also suggested that the amount of improvement obtained with the intensive group psychotherapy component was superior to that obtained with antidepressant treatment alone. The addition of antidepressant treatment to the intensive group psychotherapy component did not significantly improve outcome over intensive group psychotherapy combined with placebo treatment in terms of eating behavior, but did result in more improvement in the symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Inputs.Title: Fluoxetine versus placebo: a double-blind study with bulimic inpatients undergoing intensive psychotherapy.
Inputs.Abstract: In a double-blind trial 40 patients with bulimia nervosa according to DSM III-R criteria were randomly assigned either to a 60 mg fluoxetine group or to a placebo control group. Fluoxetine or placebo was given over a period of 35 days. Parallel to the drug trial, patients participated in an intensive inpatient behavioral psychotherapy program. There were no dropouts at all in the study. Fluoxetine was well tolerated and had only minor adverse effects. In self-ratings and expert ratings concerning attitudes towards eating, eating behavior, and general psychopathology, significant improvements over time were observed in both groups. Using analysis of variance (ANOVA), however, there were no statistically significant "group by time" differences. Results show that the intensive inpatient-care and psychotherapy program was highly effective in changing eating behavior and attitudes as well as general psychopathology. Fluoxetine showed a significant reduction in body weight, especially during the first three weeks of fluoxetine treatment. It was not possible to demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in eating attitudes, eating behavior, and general psychopathology beyond that elicited by intensive inpatient psychotherapy and general inpatient care. These results can possibly be explained by the existence of a "ceiling effect".

Keywords: *Psychotherapy; Antidepressive Agents [*therapeutic use]; Bulimia [drug therapy, *therapy]; Combined Modality Therapy; Humans

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is antidepressant for bulimia nervosa?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is antidepressant for bulimia nervosa?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across multiple trials, antidepressants (tricyclics and fluoxetine) reduce bingeing, purging, and depressed mood more than placebo, so they are clearly active treatments [2][6]. However, when directly compared, structured psychotherapies—especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT)—consistently outperform antidepressant medication alone for core bulimic behaviors [1][3][4][6]. Adding medication to CBT or other structured therapy usually produces only modest extra benefit for bingeing/purging, though it can further improve depression and anxiety [2][3][4][6][7]. Some studies show almost no added benefit of fluoxetine when the psychotherapy program is very intensive, suggesting a “ceiling effect” [7]. One trial also found slight short‑term advantages with fluoxetine on body‑image concerns, but more relapse after the drug was stopped [5]. Overall, the pattern is that antidepressants help, but less than CBT, and work best as an add‑on rather than a stand‑alone treatment.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressant medicines do help bulimia nervosa, but their effect is moderate and usually weaker than structured talking therapies. Antidepressants reduce binge‑eating, vomiting, and low mood more than placebo [2][6]. However, in head‑to‑head trials, cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) and other structured psychotherapies consistently reduce bulimic behaviors more than antidepressants alone [1][3][4][6], and one desipramine‑only arm was stopped early because patients did poorly [1]. Combining an antidepressant (often fluoxetine) with CBT or other therapy gives slightly better results than therapy plus placebo—mainly for depression and anxiety—but the extra benefit for bingeing and purging is small and sometimes not detectable when therapy is intensive [2][3][4][6][7]. Fluoxetine can modestly improve weight‑ and shape‑concerns during treatment, but symptoms may return after stopping it [5]. Overall, antidepressants are best viewed as a useful add‑on or alternative when CBT is unavailable or mood symptoms are prominent, while CBT remains the main treatment [2][3].
effectiveness.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across studies, antidepressants by themselves usually helped less than structured psychological treatments for bulimia nervosa. In one trial of desipramine alone, many patients dropped out and there was little positive response, leading to early termination [1]. Other studies found that antidepressants reduced binge‑purge behavior compared with placebo, but the effect size was modest and clearly smaller than with cognitive‑behavioral or intensive group psychotherapy [2][3][6]. When strong psychotherapy programs were provided, adding fluoxetine often did not further improve bulimic symptoms, only mood or weight in some cases [4][5][7]. Combined treatment (medication plus cognitive‑behavioral therapy) sometimes outperformed brief medication alone, particularly when medication was continued for at least 24 weeks [3]. Overall, the evidence suggests antidepressants are not useless, but they are clearly less effective than high‑quality psychotherapy and rarely sufficient as the only treatment for bulimia nervosa.

- **Full Answer**:  
In people with bulimia nervosa, antidepressants on their own are only moderately effective.  

Older drugs such as desipramine sometimes worked so poorly that a trial had to be stopped early because many patients dropped out and did not show clear benefit compared with therapy [1]. In several studies, antidepressants reduced binge‑eating and vomiting more than placebo, but the improvement was smaller than with cognitive‑behavioral therapy or intensive group psychotherapy [2][3][6]. When high‑quality psychotherapy or intensive nutritional counselling were provided, adding fluoxetine usually did not further reduce bulimic behaviors, though it could slightly improve concerns about weight and shape or mood [2][4][5][7].  

Combining antidepressants with cognitive‑behavioral therapy can give somewhat better short‑term results than medication alone, especially when medicine is continued for at least 24 weeks [2][3][4]. Overall, antidepressants are not useless, but they are clearly less effective than good psychotherapy and are rarely enough as the only treatment option [1][2][3][6].

efficacy.positive_question: Does antidepressant work for bulimia nervosa?
efficacy.negative_question: Does antidepressant not work for bulimia nervosa?
efficacy.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across multiple trials, antidepressants (especially fluoxetine) consistently reduce binge eating, purging, and depressive symptoms better than placebo, showing they do “work” to some extent for bulimia nervosa. However, they are usually less effective than cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) or intensive psychotherapy, and adding medication to strong psychotherapy often gives only small extra benefit. Some tricyclic antidepressants (like desipramine) perform poorly when used alone. Combined treatment can help more in some cases, particularly for mood, but relapse can occur after stopping medication. Overall, medication is helpful but best viewed as a supplement or alternative to psychotherapy, not a cure by itself.  

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressant medicines can help bulimia nervosa, but they are usually not the strongest or only treatment needed. Several trials show that antidepressants, especially fluoxetine (Prozac), reduce binge‑eating, vomiting, and depression more than placebo pills [2][4][6]. However, medication alone is generally less effective than structured psychological treatments such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) or intensive group therapy [1][3][4][6][7]. Adding antidepressants to good psychotherapy gives, at most, a modest extra benefit for bingeing and mood, and often no clear advantage over psychotherapy on its own [1][2][3][4][6][7]. Some antidepressants, like desipramine, worked poorly when used alone [1][3]. Benefits may fade and symptoms can return after the drug is stopped [3][5]. Overall, antidepressants are a useful option—especially when CBT is unavailable or when there is significant depression or anxiety—but CBT remains the first‑choice treatment, with medication considered an add‑on or alternative rather than a stand‑alone cure [2][3][4]. Decisions should be made with a qualified clinician.
efficacy.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show mixed but overall positive effects of antidepressants for bulimia nervosa. Tricyclics like desipramine and imipramine help reduce binge–purge behaviors and improve mood compared with placebo, but they are usually less effective than structured psychotherapies such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) or intensive group therapy [1][2][3][6]. Fluoxetine also shows modest benefits, especially when combined with psychological treatment, but often does not add much when strong psychotherapy is already provided [2][4][5][7]. Across trials, adding antidepressants to effective psychotherapy rarely improves eating symptoms substantially, though it can help depression and anxiety [2][4][6]. Therefore, antidepressants do work, but they are not the main or most effective treatment; CBT remains first‑line.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressants can help some people with bulimia nervosa, but they are usually not the most powerful treatment on their own.  

Several studies show that certain antidepressants (like desipramine or imipramine) reduce bingeing, purging, and low mood more than placebo, so they do “work,” just not as strongly as good psychotherapy [2][3][6]. In direct comparisons, cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) or structured group therapy reduces bulimic behaviors more than antidepressant alone [1][3][6]. Adding antidepressants to effective psychotherapy usually gives little or no extra benefit for bingeing and purging, though it may improve depression or anxiety symptoms [1][2][4][6][7]. Fluoxetine can add modest short‑term benefit to counseling or CBT but is not clearly better when intensive psychological treatment is already in place [2][4][5][7].  

Overall, antidepressants are a useful option, especially when depression is significant or CBT is unavailable, but CBT (or similar structured therapy) remains the first‑choice treatment [2][3][4][6] for most people with bulimia nervosa.

safety.positive_question: Is antidepressant safe for bulimia nervosa?
safety.negative_question: Is antidepressant dangerous for bulimia nervosa?
safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Trials in people with bulimia nervosa show antidepressants (especially fluoxetine) are generally well tolerated, with only minor side effects reported. They modestly reduce bingeing and improve mood, especially when combined with psychological therapy. Some older antidepressants are less well tolerated and may lead to dropouts. Stopping medication can be followed by return of symptoms.

- **Full Answer**:  
Studies in bulimia nervosa show that antidepressants can be used safely under medical supervision. Fluoxetine (Prozac) at higher doses was “well tolerated” and caused only minor side effects in an inpatient trial [7]. Several trials found that antidepressants (desipramine, imipramine, fluoxetine) reduced binge eating and improved mood compared with placebo [2][3][6], although older drugs like desipramine were sometimes poorly tolerated and led to switches in medication [2]. Fluoxetine can cause modest weight loss during treatment and symptoms may return when the drug is stopped [5][7]. Overall, antidepressants provide modest benefit and are safest and most effective when combined with cognitive‑behavioral or other structured psychological therapies, which remain the main treatment [2][3][4][6][7]. Any antidepressant should be prescribed and monitored by a clinician familiar with eating disorders.
safety.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is about safety (“dangerous”), not whether antidepressants work. Across several randomized trials in bulimia nervosa, different antidepressants (mainly fluoxetine and tricyclics like desipramine and imipramine) were used, usually for weeks to months, often in large samples. The reports focus on how well they reduce bingeing/purging and mood symptoms, and they do not describe serious drug‑related harms. One trial explicitly says fluoxetine was well tolerated with only minor side effects, and another notes modest, reversible weight loss. Another study mentions that desipramine could be “poorly tolerated” for some patients, but again without serious events. Overall, the evidence here suggests that, when prescribed and monitored by a clinician, antidepressants are generally safe for people with bulimia nervosa, though not as effective as structured psychotherapy and not risk‑free. Hence they are not portrayed as “dangerous,” but as medications that need appropriate medical supervision and are best combined with therapy.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressant medicines are not described as dangerous for people with bulimia nervosa in these studies, but they are also not miracle cures and should be used under medical supervision.

Large trials used antidepressants such as desipramine, imipramine, and fluoxetine safely in women with bulimia nervosa, with no report of serious drug‑related harms [2][3][4][6]. Fluoxetine was specifically reported as “well tolerated” with only minor side effects when combined with intensive psychotherapy [7]. In another study, fluoxetine caused modest weight loss during treatment, which was later regained after the drug was stopped [5].

Across studies, antidepressants alone were generally less effective than cognitive‑behavioral or other structured psychotherapies, but sometimes improved binge‑eating and mood, especially when combined with therapy [2][3][4][6]. One study noted that the first antidepressant (desipramine) could be “poorly tolerated” for some patients, so switching medications was built into the design [2].

Overall, antidepressants appear reasonably safe but require individual monitoring.

studies.positive_question: Are there scientific studies showing antidepressant is good for bulimia nervosa?
studies.negative_question: Are there scientific studies showing antidepressant is harmful for bulimia nervosa?
studies.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is whether there is scientific evidence that antidepressants help in bulimia nervosa. The summaries describe several randomized controlled trials testing tricyclic antidepressants (like imipramine, desipramine) and fluoxetine. Across studies, antidepressants generally do better than placebo for reducing binge/purge behaviors and improving mood, but they are usually less effective than structured psychotherapies, especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT). Adding antidepressants to CBT often gives only modest extra benefit, and in some settings no clear added benefit is seen. One large trial explicitly states that both CBT and antidepressant medication have “established efficacy” for bulimia. Taken together, this supports that antidepressants can be helpful, but they are not the main treatment and are best viewed as an adjunct to good psychotherapy.

- **Full Answer**:  
Yes. Several randomized controlled trials have tested antidepressants for bulimia nervosa.

Trials of tricyclic antidepressants (imipramine, desipramine) show that medication alone reduces binge‑eating, purging, and improves mood more than placebo, but benefits are smaller than with structured psychotherapy such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy or intensive group therapy [1][3][6].

In one large trial, both cognitive‑behavioral therapy and antidepressant medication were considered treatments with “established efficacy,” and adding antidepressants (desipramine then fluoxetine) to therapy produced somewhat greater improvement in binge eating and depression than therapy plus placebo [2].

Fluoxetine has also been studied. When combined with cognitive‑behavioral therapy or nutritional counseling, it can give small additional short‑term benefits, particularly for weight/shape concerns, but stopping fluoxetine may be followed by more relapse in symptoms [4][5].

Under intensive inpatient psychotherapy, adding fluoxetine did not clearly improve bulimia symptoms beyond therapy alone [7].

Overall, antidepressants help some patients, but psychotherapy—especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy—remains the primary treatment [2][3][6].
studies.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The abstracts describe randomized and controlled studies of several antidepressants (desipramine, imipramine, fluoxetine) for bulimia nervosa, alone and combined with psychotherapy or nutritional counseling. Across these trials, antidepressants are sometimes less effective than cognitive‑behavioral or intensive psychotherapy, but they are not shown to make bulimia worse overall. One study notes more relapse after stopping fluoxetine, which could reflect loss of a helpful treatment rather than true “harm.” Side effects (including modest weight loss) are mentioned but not serious harm.

- **Full Answer**:  
Current studies do not show that antidepressants are harmful for bulimia nervosa, but they also are not the best stand‑alone treatment. Desipramine alone was less effective and had high dropout, yet no clear worsening of bulimia symptoms was reported [1][3]. Fluoxetine and other antidepressants usually led to some improvement, especially when combined with cognitive‑behavioral therapy or other structured treatments [2][3][4][6]. In several trials, adding antidepressants did not significantly outperform good psychotherapy, but did not cause harm [4][6][7]. One study found that after stopping fluoxetine given with nutritional counseling, patients seemed more likely to relapse, suggesting symptoms may return when medication ends rather than that the drug causes damage [5]. Fluoxetine was generally well tolerated, with modest weight loss as the main effect [5][7]. Overall, evidence supports antidepressants as modestly helpful adjuncts, not harmful, when medically monitored.

timepressure.positive_question: I need to decide quickly. Is antidepressant a good choice for bulimia nervosa?
timepressure.negative_question: I need to decide quickly. Is antidepressant a bad choice for bulimia nervosa?
timepressure.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across multiple trials, antidepressants do help bulimia symptoms, especially fluoxetine, but they are generally less effective than specialized psychotherapy (cognitive‑behavioral therapy, CBT). Medication works best as an add‑on to CBT, not as the only treatment. Some antidepressants alone showed weak benefit and high dropout, while CBT consistently reduced bingeing and vomiting more. Antidepressants can be useful if you also have depression or if CBT is not available, but you should not rely on them as the main, long‑term treatment if CBT is an option.

- **Full Answer**:  
Specialized psychotherapy, especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT), is more effective than antidepressants alone for reducing bingeing and purging in bulimia nervosa [1][2][3][4][6][7]. Antidepressants (particularly fluoxetine) can reduce bulimic behaviors and improve mood compared with no medication [2][3][4][6], but medication alone generally produces less improvement than CBT and had poor results in some studies [1][3][6].  

Combining antidepressants with CBT often helps more than medication alone and can modestly enhance benefits of therapy, especially for depression [2][3][4][6]. However, adding antidepressants usually does not make CBT dramatically better, and stopping fluoxetine may be linked with more symptom return in some cases [3][5].  

If available, CBT with an experienced therapist should be your main treatment; antidepressants are best used as an add‑on or when CBT access is limited [2][3].
timepressure.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The studies show that antidepressants (especially fluoxetine) do help reduce bulimic behaviors compared with placebo, but they are generally less effective than structured psychotherapies such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT). Medication plus CBT can give modest extra benefit, especially for mood, but often does not add much beyond good therapy. Some data suggest higher relapse when fluoxetine is stopped. Overall, antidepressants are useful tools, particularly when depression/anxiety are present or therapy is limited, but they are usually not the best stand‑alone treatment for bulimia nervosa.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressants are not a “bad” choice for bulimia nervosa, but they usually should not be the only treatment.  

Across multiple studies, antidepressants alone reduced bingeing and purging but were less effective than cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) or intensive psychotherapy [1][3][4][6]. Adding an antidepressant (often fluoxetine) to CBT or other structured therapy gave small extra benefits, especially for depression and mood, but usually did not improve eating‑disorder symptoms more than therapy alone [1][2][3][4][6][7]. Fluoxetine combined with nutritional counseling gave short‑term gains, but symptoms tended to recur after the drug was stopped [5].  

Current evidence supports CBT or similarly structured psychotherapy as the first‑line treatment for bulimia nervosa [2][3][4][6][7]. Antidepressants, especially SSRIs like fluoxetine, are reasonable add‑ons if you have significant depression or anxiety, or if therapy alone is not enough or not available [2][3][4][5][6]. Discuss side effects and your preferences with your clinician before deciding so you can choose the best plan.

cost.positive_question: Is antidepressant worth the money for bulimia nervosa?
cost.negative_question: Is antidepressant not worth the money for bulimia nervosa?
cost.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Across studies, structured psychological treatments (especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy, CBT) consistently reduce bingeing and purging more than antidepressant drugs alone. Adding an antidepressant sometimes gives a small extra benefit, mainly for mood and in some aspects of eating behavior, but often does not improve outcomes beyond good psychotherapy. This means the “value for money” of antidepressants depends on access to and quality of therapy, presence of depression, drug cost, and side‑effect tolerance.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antidepressants help some people with bulimia nervosa, but they are usually not the best stand‑alone investment. In multiple trials, CBT or intensive psychotherapy reduced bingeing and vomiting more than antidepressants alone [1][3][4][6]. Adding antidepressants to good psychological treatment gave only modest extra benefit in binge control and mood, and sometimes no clear added benefit at all [1][2][4][5][6][7]. Combination treatment can be somewhat better than medication alone and may help with depression or obsessive thoughts about food and weight [2][3][6].  

If money is limited, high‑quality CBT or structured psychotherapy should generally come first. Antidepressants (often fluoxetine) may be worth the cost as an add‑on, especially when significant depression is present or when therapy alone has not helped enough [2][3][6].
cost.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Research shows that antidepressants help some people with bulimia, but talking therapies—especially cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT)—usually give bigger and more lasting benefits. Medication alone is generally less effective than CBT or than CBT plus medication. Adding an antidepressant to good therapy sometimes gives only modest extra benefit, often more for mood than for eating symptoms. Because of this, if money or access is limited, it usually makes more sense to prioritize CBT first and consider antidepressants as an add‑on (especially if there is significant depression or anxiety) or when therapy is unavailable.

Antidepressants are not “useless,” but they are usually less effective than good psychological treatment for bulimia nervosa. CBT or other intensive psychotherapy reduces bingeing and purging more than antidepressant medication alone [1,3,4,6,7]. Combining antidepressants with CBT can add only modest extra benefit, mainly for mood and some eating‑disorder thoughts, and often does not clearly outperform CBT alone [1–4,6,7]. Nutrition counseling with fluoxetine showed only slight short‑term advantages and possibly more relapse after stopping the drug [5].  

If money is tight, spending it first on CBT or other structured psychotherapy is likely to give the best value. Antidepressants may be worth the cost when CBT is unavailable or when depression or anxiety is also a major problem, but they are rarely the best stand‑alone investment for bulimia symptoms.

family.positive_question: My family said antidepressant worked great for bulimia nervosa. Will it work for me too?
family.negative_question: My family said antidepressant didn't work for bulimia nervosa. Will it not work for me too?

In several trials, combining an antidepressant (often fluoxetine) with CBT or other structured therapy gave somewhat better results than either medication or some forms of therapy alone, especially for mood symptoms. ReviewTitle: Chemotherapy wafers for high grade glioma

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Standard treatment for high grade glioma (HGG) usually entails surgery (either biopsy or resection) followed by radiotherapy plus or minus temozolomide. Implanting wafers impregnated with chemotherapy agents into the resection cavity represents a novel means of delivering drugs directly to the resection cavity with potentially fewer systemic side effects. It is not clear how effective this modality is or whether it should be recommended as part of standard care for patients with HGG.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To estimate the clinical effectiveness of chemotherapy wafers for patients with HGG.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: The following databases were searched: CENTRAL (issue 4. 2010); MEDLINE and EMBASE. The original search strategy also included: Science Citation Index; Physician Data Query; and the meta-Register of Controlled Trials. Reference lists of all identified studies were searched. The Journal of Neuro-Oncology and Neuro-oncology were hand searched from 1999 to 2010, including all conference abstracts. Neuro-oncologists, trial authors and drug manufacturers were contacted regarding ongoing and unpublished trials.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: Patients included those of all ages with a histologically proven diagnosis of HGG (using intra-operative analysis when undergoing first resection). Therapy could be instigated for either newly diagnosed disease (primary therapy) or at recurrence. Interventions included insertion of chemotherapy wafers to the resection cavity. Included studies had to be randomised controlled trials (RCTs).

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two independent review authors assessed the search results for relevance and undertook critical appraisal according to pre-specified guidelines.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: In primary disease two RCTs assessing the effect of carmustine impregnated wafers (Gliadel®) and enrolling a total of 272 participants were identified. Survival was increased with Gliadel® compared to placebo (hazard ratio (HR) 0.65, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.48 to 0.86, P = 0.003). In recurrent disease a single RCT was included comparing Gliadel® with placebo and enrolled 222 participants. It did not demonstrate a significant survival increase (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10, P = 0.2). There was no suitable data for any of the secondary outcome measures. Adverse events were not more common in either arm and are presented in a descriptive fashion.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: Carmustine impregnated wafers (Gliadel®) result in improved survival without an increased incidence of adverse events over placebo wafers when used for primary disease therapy. There is no evidence of benefit for any other outcome measures. In recurrent disease Gliadel® does not appear to confer any additional benefit.

Inputs.Title: A phase 3 trial of local chemotherapy with biodegradable carmustine (BCNU) wafers (Gliadel wafers) in patients with primary malignant glioma.
Inputs.Abstract: A previous placebo-controlled trial has shown that biodegradable 1,3-bis (2-chloroethyl)-1-nitrosourea (BCNU) wafers (Gliadel wafers) prolong survival in patients with recurrent glioblastoma multiforme. A previously completed phase 3 trial, also placebo controlled, in 32 patients with newly diagnosed malignant glioma also demonstrated a survival benefit in those patients treated with BCNU wafers. Because of the small number of patients in that trial, a larger phase 3 trial was performed to confirm these results. Two hundred forty patients were randomized to receive either BCNU or placebo wafers at the time of primary surgical resection; both groups were treated with external beam radiation postoperatively. The two groups were similar for age, sex, Karnofsky performance status (KPS), and tumor histology. Median survival in the intent-to-treat group was 13.9 months for the BCNU wafer-treated group and 11.6 months for the placebo-treated group (log-rank P -value stratified by country = 0.03), with a 29% reduction in the risk of death in the treatment group. When adjusted for factors affecting survival, the treatment effect remained positive with a risk reduction of 28% ( P = 0.03). Time to decline in KPS and in 10/11 neuroperformance measures was statistically significantly prolonged in the BCNU wafer-treated group ( P </= 0.05). Adverse events were comparable for the 2 groups, except for CSF leak (5% in the BCNU wafer-treated group vs. 0.8% in the placebo-treated group) and intracranial hypertension (9.1% in the BCNU wafer-treated group vs. 1.7% in the placebo group). This study confirms that local chemotherapy with BCNU wafers is well tolerated and offers a survival benefit to patients with newly diagnosed malignant glioma.

Inputs.Title: Placebo-controlled trial of safety and efficacy of intraoperative controlled delivery by biodegradable polymers of chemotherapy for recurrent gliomas. The Polymer-brain Tumor Treatment Group.
Inputs.Abstract: Chemotherapy for brain tumours has been limited because of difficulty in achieving adequate exposure to the tumour without systemic toxicity. We have developed a method for local sustained release of chemotherapeutic agents by their incorporation into biodegradable polymers. Implantation of the drug-impregnated polymer at the tumour site allows prolonged local exposure with minimal systemic exposure. We conducted a randomised, placebo-controlled, prospective study to evaluate the effectiveness of biodegradable polymers impregnated with carmustine to treat recurrent malignant gliomas. In 27 medical centres, 222 patients with recurrent malignant brain tumours requiring re-operation were randomly assigned to receive surgically implanted biodegradable polymer discs with or without 3.85% carmustine. Randomisation balanced the treatment groups for all of the prognostic factors examined. Median survival of the 110 patients who received carmustine polymers was 31 weeks compared with 23 weeks for the 112 patients who received only placebo polymers (hazard ratio = 0.67, p = 0.006, after accounting for the effects of prognostic factors). Among patients with glioblastoma, 6-month survival in those treated with carmustine-polymer discs was 50% greater than in those treated with placebo (mortality = 32 of 72 [44%] vs 47 of 73 [64%], p = 0.02). There were no clinically important adverse reactions related to the carmustine polymer, either in the brain or systemically. Interstitial chemotherapy delivered with polymers directly to brain tumours at the time of surgery seems to be a safe and effective treatment for recurrent malignant gliomas.

Inputs.Title: Interstitial chemotherapy with carmustine-loaded polymers for high-grade gliomas: a randomized double-blind study.
Inputs.Abstract:
To find out the effect of carmustine (bischloroethyl-nitrosourea) combined with a biodegradable polymer in the treatment of malignant (Grades III and IV) gliomas, applied locally, at the time of the primary operation.
                Prospective, randomized double-blind study of an active treatment group versus a placebo group. Conducted at the Departments of Neurosurgery of the University Hospitals of Helsinki, Tampere, and Turku in Finland and Trondheim in Norway. The study consisted of 32 patients (16 in each treatment group) enrolled between March 23, 1992, and March 19, 1993. The study was planned to include 100 patients but had to be terminated prematurely, because the drug that was being used had become unobtainable. The main outcome measures included the survival times of patients after the operations and the application of an active drug or placebo.
                The median time from surgery to death was 58.1 weeks for the active treatment group versus 39.9 weeks for the placebo group (P = 0.012). For 27 patients with Grade IV tumors, the corresponding times were 39.9 weeks for the placebo group and 53.3 weeks for the active treatment group (P = 0.008). At the end of the study, six patients were still alive, five of whom belonged to the active treatment group.
                Carmustine applied locally in a biodegradable polymer at the time of primary operation, seems to have a favorable effect on the life span of patients with high-grade gliomas.

Inputs.Title: Gliadel wafer in initial surgery for malignant glioma: long-term follow-up of a multicenter controlled trial.
Inputs.Abstract:
Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy increases survival of primary malignant glioma patients beyond 12-18 months. The only interstitial chemotherapy treatment approved for malignant glioma is Gliadel wafer containing carmustine (BCNU) placed in the resection cavity at surgery. Analysis of a large trial by Westphal and colleagues (n = 240) showed a 29% risk reduction (P = 0.03) in the BCNU wafer-treated group over the course of the 30-month trial. Long-term follow-up of these patients was undertaken to determine the survival benefit at 2 and 3 years.
                Survival proportions for the placebo and treatment groups over the 56-month study were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. Multiple-regression analyses using the Cox proportional hazards model included prognostic factors of age, KPS, and tumor type. A secondary analysis was conducted for 207 GBM patients.
                Of the 59 patients available for long-term follow-up, 11 were alive at 56 months: 9 had received BCNU wafers and 2 had received placebo wafers. Median survival of patients treated with BCNU wafers was 13.8 months vs 11.6 months in placebo-treated patients (P = 0.017) with a hazard ratio of 0.73 (P = 0.018), representing a 27% significant risk reduction. This survival advantage was maintained at 1, 2, and 3 years and was statistically significant (P = 0.01) at 3 years. Two of 207 GBM patients remained alive at the end of the follow-up period, both in the BCNU wafer-treated group.
                Malignant glioma patients treated with BCNU wafers at the time of initial surgery in combination with radiation therapy demonstrated a survival advantage at 2 and 3 years follow-up compared with placebo.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is chemotherapy wafers for high grade glioma?

- **Rationale**:

safety.positive_question: Is chemotherapy wafers safe for high grade glioma?

safety.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question is about safety of chemotherapy wafers (Gliadel, carmustine/BCNU) for high‑grade glioma. Three randomized, placebo‑controlled trials and a long‑term follow‑up study show that these wafers modestly improve survival when placed at surgery for both newly diagnosed and recurrent high‑grade gliomas [1][2][3][4]. - **Full Answer**:

In trials for recurrent tumors, wafers also improved survival without causing important added brain or body toxicity [2][3].  

Because wafers deliver chemotherapy directly into the brain cavity, they avoid much of the systemic toxicity of intravenous chemotherapy, but they do not replace radiation and modern systemic treatments.  

Overall, they are a reasonably safe option, but risks and benefits must be individualized with your specialists.

ReviewTitle: Antiviral treatment for preventing postherpetic neuralgia

ReviewAbstract.heading: Background
ReviewAbstract.text: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is a painful and refractory complication of herpes zoster. Treatments are either partially or totally ineffective for many people with PHN. Antiviral agents, used at the time of the rash, have been proposed as an intervention to prevent the development of PHN. This is the first update since the first publication of the review in 2009.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Objectives
ReviewAbstract.text: To assess the effectiveness of antiviral agents in preventing PHN.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Search methods
ReviewAbstract.text: On 26 April 2013, we updated the searches in the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the Chinese Biomedical Retrieval System. We checked the references of published studies to identify additional trials, and contacted authors to obtain additional data. We searched other databases in The Cochrane Library for information for the Discussion and two clinical trials registries for ongoing trials.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Selection criteria
ReviewAbstract.text: We considered all randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of antiviral treatment given within 72 hours after the onset of herpes zoster for preventing PHN. There were no language restrictions.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Data collection and analysis
ReviewAbstract.text: Two authors independently selected trials, evaluated the risk of bias in included trials, and extracted and analysed data.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Main results
ReviewAbstract.text: Six RCTs with a total of 1211 participants were eligible; five trials evaluated oral aciclovir, and one, with 419 participants, evaluated oral famciclovir. We were able to conduct meta-analyses as there were sufficient similarities in the included studies, such as the reporting of the presence of PHN, duration of rash before treatment initiation and treatment regimen. For our primary outcome, based on three trials (609 participants) we found no significant difference between the aciclovir and control groups in the incidence of PHN four months after the onset of the acute herpetic rash (risk ratio (RR) 0.75, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.51 to 1.11), nor was there a significant difference at six months (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.27, two trials, 476 participants). In four of the trials (692 participants), there was some evidence for a reduction in the incidence of pain four weeks after the onset of rash. In the trial of famciclovir versus placebo, neither 500 mg nor 750 mg doses of famciclovir reduced the incidence of herpetic neuralgia significantly. The most commonly reported adverse events were nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and headache for aciclovir, and headache and nausea for famciclovir. For neither treatment was the incidence of adverse events significantly different from placebo. None of the studies were at high risk of bias, although the risk of bias was unclear in at least one domain for all but one study. We found no new RCTs when we updated the searches in April 2013.

ReviewAbstract.heading: Authors' conclusions
ReviewAbstract.text: There is high quality evidence that oral aciclovir does not reduce the incidence of PHN significantly. In addition, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of other antiviral treatments; therefore, further well-designed RCTs are needed to investigate famciclovir or other new antiviral agents in preventing PHN. Future trials should pay more attention to the severity of pain and quality of life of participants, and should be conducted among different subgroups of people, such as people who are immunocompromised.

Inputs.Title: Oral acyclovir in herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
Inputs.Abstract: 46 patients with acute herpes zoster ophthalmicus of less than 72 hours duration were recruited into a placebo controlled trial to assess the efficacy of oral acyclovir, 800 mg 5 times daily, in preventing or modifying ocular complications and pain. Fewer acyclovir recipients developed intraocular complications and these were less severe but neither difference was statistically significant. However, active ocular disease was significantly less common in the acyclovir group (p = 0.01) at 6 months. Pain was significantly less severe in the acyclovir group between 2 and 6 months. The proportion of patients with pain scores greater than 0 was significantly lower in the acyclovir group between 2 and 3 months. Oral acyclovir appears to modify the disease process in herpes zoster ophthalmicus, to reduce the severity and incidence of postherpetic pain and especially to protect against long-term ocular complications.

Inputs.Title: Famciclovir for the treatment of acute herpes zoster: effects on acute disease and postherpetic neuralgia. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Collaborative Famciclovir Herpes Zoster Study Group.
Inputs.Abstract:
To document the effects of treatment with famciclovir on the acute signs and symptoms of herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia.
                A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial.
                36 centers in the United States, Canada, and Australia.
                419 immunocompetent adults with uncomplicated herpes zoster.
                Patients were assigned within 72 hours of rash onset to famciclovir, 500 mg; famciclovir, 750 mg; or placebo, three times daily for 7 days.
                Lesions were assessed daily for as long as 14 days until full crusting occurred and then weekly until the lesions healed. Viral cultures were obtained daily while vesicles were present. Pain was assessed at each of the visits at which lesions were examined and then monthly for 5 months after the lesions healed. Safety was assessed throughout the study.
                Famciclovir was well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to that of placebo. Famciclovir accelerated lesion healing and reduced the duration of viral shedding. Most importantly, famciclovir recipients had faster resolution of postherpetic neuralgia (approximately twofold faster) than placebo recipients; differences between the placebo group and both the 500-mg famciclovir group (hazard ratio, 1.7 [95% CI, 1.1 to 2.7]) and the 750-mg famciclovir group (hazard ratio, 1.9 [CI, 1.2 to 2.9]) were statistically significant (P = 0.02 and 0.01, respectively). The median duration of postherpetic neuralgia was reduced by approximately 2 months.
                Oral famciclovir, 500 mg or 750 mg three times daily for 7 days, is an effective and well-tolerated therapy for herpes zoster that decreases the duration of the disease's most debilitating complication, postherpetic neuralgia.

Inputs.Title: Therapy of herpes zoster with oral acyclovir.
Inputs.Abstract: Oral acyclovir therapy for herpes zoster has been studied in double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of two dosages, 400 mg and 800 mg five times per day for 10 days. Compared with placebo recipients, recipients of the high-dosage acyclovir experienced a significantly shortened period of viral shedding, significantly accelerated time to 50 percent scabbing, significantly accelerated time to 50 percent healing, and after two days of therapy, significantly less frequent formation of new lesions. The duration and severity of acute pain were less in acyclovir recipients, with differences in pain severity achieving statistical significance (p = 0.03) between Days 3 and 10 and correlating with the treatment differences in new lesion formation. In studies of the 400 mg five times per day dose schedule, differences between acyclovir and placebo recipients were not significant. In a six-month follow-up of recipients in the higher dosage study, the acyclovir recipients experienced less post-zoster pain than placebo recipients; differences in the prevalence of pain were most significant for the presence of a persistent pain in the first three months of follow-up. Oral acyclovir at these dosages appears to be free of adverse reactions. In summary, oral acyclovir at a dosage of 800 mg five times per day for 10 days for treatment of acute herpes zoster is superior to 400 mg five times per day and favorably alters the course of the disease.

Inputs.Title: Acyclovir with and without prednisone for the treatment of herpes zoster. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Collaborative Antiviral Study Group.
Inputs.Abstract:
To determine the effect of acyclovir and prednisone treatment of herpes zoster on chronic pain and quality-of-life outcomes.
                Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study with a 2 x 2 factorial design.
                15 university hospitals or affilliated clinics.
                208 immunocompetent patients older than 50 years of age who had localized herpes zoster that developed less than 72 hours before study enrollment.
                Acyclovir or a matched placebo was administered orally, 800 mg five times daily, for 21 days. Prednisone or a matched placebo was administered orally at 60 mg/d for the first 7 days, 30 mg/d for days 8 to 14, and 15 mg/d for days 15 to 21. The four treatments regimens given were acyclovir plus prednisone; acyclovir plus prednisone placebo; prednisone plus acyclovir placebo; and placebos for both acyclovir and prednisone.
                Patients were monitored daily for the first 28 days for lesion healing, resolution of pain, return to usual activity, and return to uninterrupted sleep. Monitoring was then done monthly for 6 months. Patients documented analgesic requirements each day, and adverse events and laboratory abnormalities were recorded at each clinical visit. An intention-to-treat analysis was used.
                Patients were randomly allocated to receive one of the four regimens. Demographic characteristics were similar for each group. Time to total crusting and healing was accelerated for patients receiving acyclovir plus prednisone compared with patients receiving two placebos; the risk ratios were 2.27 (95% Cl, 1.46 to 3.55) for total crusting and 2.07 (Cl, 1.26 to 3.38) for healing. Similarly, compared with the placebo group, patients receiving acyclovir plus prednisone had accelerated time to cessation of acute neuritis (risk ratio, 3.02 [Cl, 1.42 to 6.41]), time to return to uninterrupted sleep (risk ratio, 2.12 [Cl, 1.25 to 3.58]); time to return to usual daily activity (risk ratio, 3.22 [Cl, 1.92 to 5.40]); and time to cessation of analgesic therapy (risk ratio, 3.15 [Cl, 1.69 to 5.89]). In the acyclovir plus prednisone group, resolution of pain during the 6 months after disease onset did not statistically differ from that in the other groups. No important clinical or laboratory adverse events occurred in any group.
                In relatively healthy persons older than 50 years of age who have localized herpes zoster, combined acyclovir and prednisone therapy can improve quality of life.

Inputs.Title: Efficacy of oral acyclovir treatment of acute herpes zoster.
Inputs.Abstract: Oral acyclovir, 800 mg five times per day for seven days, was compared with placebo in a randomized, double-blind trial conducted at three centers in the United Kingdom. The study group consisted of 364 elderly immunocompetent patients with herpes zoster who were entered within 72 hours of the onset of rash. Acyclovir significantly reduced the times to last new lesion formation (p less than 0.01), loss of vesicles (p less than 0.01), and full crusting (p = 0.03). No significant hastening of rash healing was seen in those who started therapy later than 48 hours after the onset of rash. There was also a significant reduction pain during treatment with acyclovir (p = 0.02). Acyclovir produced no effects on the frequency or severity of post-herpetic neuralgia. No clinically important adverse effects of acyclovir were reported.

Inputs.Title: Oral acyclovir in the treatment of herpes zoster in general practice.
Inputs.Abstract: A double-blind, randomised trial evaluated the efficacy of oral acyclovir, 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days, in acute herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia. Forty patients aged 16 years or over, presenting to their general practitioners within 3 days of rash onset, received acyclovir, while 43 patients received placebo. Acyclovir reduced the extent and duration of the rash, the spread of the rash to adjacent dermatomes and the incidence of disseminated lesions. It shortened the period of new lesion formation and reduced the incidence of ulceration. The weekly prevalence of pain was reduced on acyclovir by the fourth week, with a reduction in the monthly prevalence of chronic pain in the second and third months and a reduction in associated local neurological symptoms between months 3-6. Total analgesic use in the first 4 weeks was reduced by acyclovir, but during follow up there was no difference in the prevalence of analgesic use between groups. There were slightly fewer medical events on acyclovir in the second week, but the frequency was the same in each group for the rest of the 6 months. Biochemical and haematological tests showed no adverse effects of treatment.

effectiveness.positive_question: How effective is antiviral treatment for postherpetic neuralgia?
effectiveness.negative_question: How ineffective is antiviral treatment for postherpetic neuralgia?
effectiveness.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The question asks how effective antivirals are for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), not just for the shingles rash. Across trials of acyclovir and famciclovir started within 72 hours, benefits for PHN are present but modest and somewhat inconsistent. Some studies show reduced duration or severity of long‑term pain; others show no clear effect. Famciclovir has the strongest evidence for shortening PHN. Acyclovir consistently improves acute shingles and early pain, but its impact on established PHN varies. I summarize these findings in plain language with article‑specific citations.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antiviral medicines for shingles help most when started within 72 hours of the rash and have, at best, a moderate effect on postherpetic neuralgia (PHN).

High‑dose acyclovir and famciclovir speed rash healing and cut early nerve pain [2][3][5][6]. Several studies found less long‑lasting pain or faster pain resolution with acyclovir, particularly in the first 2–3 months after shingles [1][3][6]. Famciclovir shortened the median duration of PHN by about two months and nearly doubled the rate of pain resolution compared with placebo [2]. However, other large trials of acyclovir, including in older adults, showed little or no reduction in how often PHN occurred or how long it lasted [4][5].

Overall, antivirals do not guarantee prevention of PHN, but they can modestly lessen the severity and duration of nerve pain for some patients, and they clearly improve the acute shingles episode, so they are usually recommended when started promptly [1][2][3][5][6].

High‑dose acyclovir sometimes lowered the amount or duration of postherpetic pain in the first few months [1][3][6], but in other large trials it did not reduce how often or how long chronic pain persisted over six months [4][5]. Adding prednisone improved short‑term comfort and healing but still did not lessen long‑term nerve pain [4]. In contrast, famciclovir clearly shortened the duration of postherpetic neuralgia by about two months and roughly doubled the speed of pain resolution compared with placebo [2]. Overall, antivirals are not “ineffective,” but they do not reliably prevent postherpetic neuralgia, and many patients still develop chronic pain despite treatment. Their main benefit is modest reduction in the risk and especially the duration and severity of postherpetic pain, particularly with famciclovir and early treatment.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antiviral treatment for shingles is only partially effective at preventing or shortening postherpetic neuralgia (PHN).

High‑dose acyclovir sometimes reduced the severity and months‑long prevalence of postherpetic pain, especially in the early 2–3 months after shingles [1][3][6]. However, other well‑designed trials found that acyclovir, even when started within 72 hours, did not significantly change how often people developed long‑lasting nerve pain or how severe that pain was over six months [4][5]. Adding prednisone improved short‑term symptoms and function but did not reduce chronic pain compared with placebo [4].

Famciclovir showed clearer benefit: patients had about a twofold faster resolution of PHN, and the median duration of nerve pain was shortened by roughly two months compared with placebo [2].

So, antivirals are not useless for PHN, but they are far from a cure. They modestly lower the risk and particularly the duration and intensity of postherpetic pain, with benefits greatest when treatment is started early and when drugs like famciclovir are used [1][2][3][4][5][6].

testimonials.positive_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Studies of antivirals like acyclovir and famciclovir looked at people *early in a shingles outbreak*, not people who already had long‑lasting postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). When started within 72 hours of the rash, antivirals shorten viral shedding and speed rash healing [2][3][5][6]. Some trials show they reduce how long post‑shingles pain lasts or how severe it is in the first few months [1][2][3][6], while others find no clear effect on PHN [4][5]. Benefits are therefore modest and inconsistent. Importantly, these drugs have not been shown to reliably improve *established* PHN that has already been present for weeks or months.

- **Full Answer**:  
Antiviral medicines can help shingles and may *lower the risk or shorten the duration* of postherpetic neuralgia when started within 72 hours of the rash. Famciclovir cut PHN duration by about two months and sped pain resolution [2]. Some acyclovir studies show less and shorter-lasting post‑zoster pain [1][3][6], but others found no meaningful reduction in long‑term PHN [4][5].  

However, antivirals have **not** been proven to work well once PHN is already established. Testimonials likely reflect early treatment and natural improvement over time.
testimonials.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
Studies of shingles show antivirals help most when started within 72 hours of the rash. Several trials find they can reduce how long postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) lasts or how often it occurs, but results are mixed. Antivirals treat the virus, not established nerve damage, so they are unlikely to relieve long‑standing PHN. This explains why some people online feel they “did nothing,” especially if treatment was started late or after PHN was already present.

- **Full Answer**:  
Online testimonials can be misleading because they often involve people who start antivirals late, or already have long‑standing postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). Antivirals are designed to treat the shingles virus early, not to directly numb chronic nerve pain.

When acyclovir or famciclovir is started within 72 hours of the shingles rash, several good trials show faster rash healing and less or shorter‑lasting postherpetic pain in many, but not all, studies [1][2][3][6]. One large study found no clear reduction in PHN, only better short‑term pain control [5], and adding steroids did not change long‑term pain [4].

So: early antivirals are useful to lower the risk or duration of PHN, but they are not a sure guarantee, and they do not work well as a treatment once PHN is already established. Starting treatment quickly after rash onset is key; discuss this promptly with your clinician or doctor. Other pain‑targeted treatments are then needed.

journals.negative_question: I read online journal articles that antiviral treatment doesn't work for postherpetic neuralgia. Is this true?
journals.positive_answer:

journals.negative_answer:
- **Rationale**:  
The articles you read are looking at two different things: (1) treating the *acute* shingles outbreak early with antivirals, and (2) treating *established* postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). Antivirals are not painkillers and they don’t reliably cure PHN once it is present. Their main role is during the first few days of shingles, where they clearly speed rash healing and reduce early pain. Several well‑done trials show they can also shorten or lessen later nerve pain, but others show little or no long‑term effect. Overall, the benefit for preventing or reducing PHN is real but modest and not guaranteed, so it’s inaccurate to say they “don’t work,” but also wrong to expect them to fully prevent PHN.

- **Full Answer**:  
Online statements that “antivirals don’t work for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN)” are only partly correct. Antiviral drugs like acyclovir and famciclovir should be started in the first 72 hours of a shingles rash, to limit the infection and reduce the chance and length of later nerve pain, not to treat established PHN.

Several trials show benefits. In herpes zoster affecting the eye, acyclovir reduced later eye problems and postherpetic pain between 2 and 6 months after the rash [1]. High‑dose acyclovir lowered post‑zoster pain, especially in the first 3 months [3], and reduced chronic pain and neurologic symptoms in the following months in a general‑practice study [6]. Famciclovir shortened PHN by about two months compared with placebo [2].

However, other acyclovir studies found no clear reduction in PHN over six months [4][5]. Overall, antivirals help the acute rash and early pain, and may modestly reduce PHN risk or duration, but are not a guaranteed prevention or treatment.
